### TO THE
## HONOURABLE AND RIGHT REVEREND
# SHUTE BARRINGTON, LL.D.
<note>original: "LL.D."; this stands for *Legum Doctor*, or Doctor of Laws.</note>
## LORD BISHOP OF DURHAM.

<insert>PUBLIC LIBRARY OF THE CITY OF BOSTON</insert>

**MY LORD,**

THE following work was undertaken at your Lordship’s recommendation and, among other motives, for the purpose of making the most fitting return I could for a great and important benefit conferred upon me.

It may be unnecessary, yet perhaps not entirely out of place, to state to your Lordship and to the reader the several inducements that have led me once more to publish. The favor of my first and ever-honored patron <note>This likely refers to Edmund Law, the Bishop of Carlisle, who was Paley's early mentor.</note> had put me in possession of such a generous provision <term>provision</term><note>In this context, a "provision" refers to a "living" or "benefice"—a permanent church appointment that provided a steady income and a home.</note> in the church as to abundantly satisfy my needs and far exceed my own expectations <note>original: "pretensions"; here meaning one's claims or what one feels they deserve.</note>. Your Lordship’s generosity <note>original: "munificence"</note>, in conjunction with...

Paley reflects on how the generous clerical positions he has been granted have more than satisfied his personal needs.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dedication of William Paley's "Natural Theology" to Shute Barrington, the Bishop of Durham. Paley is explaining how the Bishop's patronage and his own health issues led him to write this book.</meta>

-># DEDICATION.<-

...along with the support of other excellent prelates <term>prelates</term><note>High-ranking members of the clergy, such as bishops or archbishops.</note> who viewed my services with the same kind partiality as your Lordship, has since placed me in church positions <note>original: "ecclesiastical situations"</note> more than sufficient to satisfy any reasonable ambition. 

Meanwhile, a weak and recently painful state of health has deprived me of the ability to perform the duties of my position in a way that matches my own sense of responsibility or my heartfelt wishes for them. My inability to perform the public functions of my profession has, among other consequences, left me with much free time. That time was not to be wasted. It was only in my study that I could make up for my shortcomings in the church. It was only through the printing press that I could speak. 

These circumstances especially gave your Lordship the right to call upon me for the only kind of effort I was still capable of. They also made me ready to obey that call without hesitation, in the best way I could. Regarding the choice of a subject, I had no reason to doubt what it should be. In saying this, I am not referring so much to the supreme importance of the topic, or to the skepticism regarding it that is common today, but rather to its connection with the subjects I treated in my previous publications. The following discussion was the only part missing to complete my works into a coherent system. In these works, for whatever they are worth, the public now has before them,

<summary>Paley explains that his declining health made him unable to perform public church duties, leading him to use his "leisure" to write this book. He views "Natural Theology" as the final piece needed to complete his entire philosophical and theological system.</summary>
<keywords>William Paley, Bishop Shute Barrington, clerical duties, chronic illness, authorship, theological system, religious skepticism</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication of William Paley's "Natural Theology" to Shute Barrington, the Bishop of Durham. Paley is explaining how this book completes his life's work as a systematic defense of religious belief.</meta>

-># DEDICATION.<-

...the evidences for natural religion <note>Natural religion refers to truths about God that can be discovered through reason and the study of nature, rather than through scripture.</note>, the evidences for revealed religion <note>Revealed religion refers to truths communicated to humanity by God, specifically through the Bible.</note>, and an account of the duties that result from both. It is of little importance that they were written in the exact opposite order of how they should be read. I therefore entrust this current volume to your Lordship's protection, not only as what will likely be my final work, but as the completion of a consistent and thorough plan.

Until now, My Lord, I have been speaking about myself rather than my patron. Your Lordship does not need the praise of a dedication, nor any testimony from me. I am simply following my own inclination when I declare that no part of my relationship with your Lordship has been more rewarding than the opportunities it has given me to observe your sincere, active, and tireless concern <term>solicitude</term> for the advancement of essential Christianity. This is a concern accompanied by a fair-mindedness <term>candor</term> <note>In the 18th century, "candor" meant being free from prejudice, fair, and kind, rather than just being bluntly honest.</note> that allows no minor differences of opinion to cause any loss of respect or decrease in favor, as long as there is agreement on the main purpose and goal. It is lucky for a country, and an honor to its government, when qualities and attitudes like these are placed in high-ranking and influential positions. This is the sincere judgment I have formed of your Lordship’s character and its value to the public:

<summary>Paley frames "Natural Theology" as the final installment of his comprehensive system of religious thought and praises the Bishop of Durham for his sincere and tolerant support of Christianity.</summary>

<term>Natural Theology</term>: The study of God based on observed facts and experience in the natural world, rather than on divine revelation.
<term>State of the Argument</term>: The current standing or summary of the logical case being made.
<term>Mechanical Arrangement</term>: The organization of physical parts to achieve a specific function, much like a machine.
<term>Immechanical functions</term>: Natural processes (like digestion or sensation) that do not appear to be governed by the laws of simple mechanics.
<term>Animal Bodies</term>: The physical anatomy of living creatures.
<term>Comparative Anatomy</term>: The study of the similarities and differences in the structures of different species.
<term>Prospective Contrivances</term>: Features in nature that seem designed specifically to prepare for a future event or need.
<term>Instincts</term>: Inherited, natural behaviors that occur without being learned.
<term>Astronomy</term>: The scientific study of stars, planets, and the physical universe.
<term>Personality of the Deity</term>: The philosophical argument that God is an intelligent, conscious being with a will.
<term>Unity of the Deity</term>: The concept that there is only one God, evidenced by the uniformity of the laws of nature.
<term>Goodness of the Deity</term>: The argument that the design of the world proves God’s benevolence and care for living things.

<meta>This page begins the main text of William Paley's "Natural Theology," following the Table of Contents. It introduces the foundational "Watchmaker Analogy," which is the central metaphor of the book.</meta>

# NATURAL THEOLOGY;

->OR,<-

## EVIDENCES OF THE EXISTENCE AND ATTRIBUTES
## OF THE DEITY,

### COLLECTED FROM THE APPEARANCES OF NATURE.

---

## CHAPTER I.

---

### STATE OF THE ARGUMENT.

In crossing a heath <note>A large area of open, uncultivated land.</note>, suppose I struck my foot against a *stone* and was asked how the stone came to be there. I might possibly answer that, for anything I knew to the contrary, it had lain there forever; nor would it perhaps be very easy to show the absurdity of this answer. But suppose I had found a *watch* upon the ground, and it was asked how the watch happened to be in that place. I would hardly think of the answer I had given before—that, for anything I knew, the watch might have always been there. Yet why should this answer not serve for the watch as well as for the stone? Why is it not just as acceptable in the second case as in the first? For this reason, and for no other: namely, that when we come to inspect the watch, we perceive (what we could not discover in

<summary>William Paley introduces his famous "Watchmaker Analogy," arguing that the complexity of a watch necessitates a designer in a way that a simple stone does not. This serves as the starting point for his argument that the complexity of nature proves the existence of God.</summary>
<keywords>William Paley, Watchmaker Analogy, Argument from Design, Natural Theology, Teleology, Existence of God</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the "State of the Argument" from Chapter I, elaborating on the specific mechanical details of the watch to justify the conclusion of intentional design.</meta>

<header>STATE OF THE ARGUMENT.</header>

<margin><image-desc>Faint circular ink stamp from the Trinity College Library, Dublin.</image-desc></margin>
the stone) that its various parts are framed and put together for a purpose; for example, that they are so formed and adjusted as to produce motion, and that motion is so regulated as to point out the hour of the day. We perceive that if the various parts had been shaped differently from how they are, or were a different size than they are, or were placed in any other manner or order than that in which they are placed, either no motion at all would have been carried on in the machine, or none which would have served the purpose that is now served by it. 

To list a few of the simplest of these parts and their functions, all leading toward one result: we see a cylindrical box containing a coiled elastic spring which, by its effort to unwind itself, turns the box around. We next observe a flexible chain (skillfully crafted to be bendable) conveying the action of the spring from the box to the <term>fusee</term> <note>A cone-shaped pulley used in mechanical watches to equalize the pull of the mainspring as it unwinds.</note>. We then find a series of wheels whose teeth catch and connect with each other, conducting the motion from the <term>fusee</term> to the <term>balance</term> <note>The balance wheel is the timekeeping element in a mechanical watch that swings back and forth to regulate time.</note>, and from the <term>balance</term> to the pointer. At the same time, by the size and shape of those wheels, that motion is regulated so that it results in causing an <term>index</term> <note>The hand or pointer on the watch face.</note>, through a steady and measured progression, to pass over a specific space in a specific time. 

We notice that the wheels are made of brass to prevent them from rusting, and the springs are made of steel, as no other metal is so elastic. We also see that a glass is placed over the face of the watch—a material used in no other part of the work—but if any substance other than a transparent one had been used in its place, the hour could not be seen without opening the case. Once this mechanism is observed (and it indeed requires an examination of the instrument, and perhaps some prior knowledge of the subject, to perceive and understand it; but once it is...

<summary>Paley describes the intricate internal components of a watch, such as the spring, fusee, and balance, arguing that their specific arrangement and materials prove the device was designed for a clear purpose.</summary>
<keywords>William Paley, Watchmaker Analogy, mechanical design, teleology, functional complexity, horology, Natural Theology</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the "State of the Argument" from Chapter I, moving from the description of the watch’s internal mechanics to the logical conclusion that such complexity requires an intelligent designer.</meta>

->### STATE OF THE ARGUMENT.<-

...as we have already observed and understood), the inference, we think, is inevitable: the watch must have had a maker. There must have existed, at some time and at some place or another, a <term>artificer</term> <note>A skilled craftsman or inventor.</note> or craftsmen who formed it for the purpose which we find it *actually* serves; who understood its construction and designed its use.

I. Nor would it, I believe, weaken the conclusion if we had never seen a watch being made, if we had never known a craftsman capable of making one, or if we were completely incapable of executing such a piece of workmanship ourselves or understanding the manner in which it was performed. All of this is no more than what is true of some magnificent remains of ancient art, of certain "lost arts," and, for the majority of mankind, of the more complex productions of modern manufacturing. Does one man in a million know how oval frames are <term>turned</term>? <note>Refers to "engine turning" on a lathe, a complex mechanical process used to create elliptical or decorative patterns in the 18th century.</note> Ignorance of this kind increases our opinion of the unseen and unknown artist’s skill (if he is indeed unknown), but it raises no doubt in our minds about the existence and actions of such an artist at some former time and in some place or another. Nor can I see that the inference changes at all whether the question concerns a human agent, an agent of a different species, or an agent possessing a different nature in some respects.

II. Secondly, it would not invalidate our conclusion if the watch sometimes malfunctioned, or if it seldom kept exactly the right time. The purpose of the machinery, the design, and the designer would still be evident—and in this case, would remain evident—regardless of how we accounted for the irregularity of the movement, or even if we could not account for it at all. It is not necessary for a machine to be perfect in order to show the design with which it was made; it is even less necessary where the only...

<summary>Paley argues that the complexity of a watch necessitates a designer, regardless of whether we have seen it made or if the machine functions perfectly.</summary>
<keywords>teleological argument, watchmaker analogy, intelligent design, William Paley, craftsmanship, mechanical perfection</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the "State of the Argument" from Chapter I, finishing the point that a malfunctioning watch still proves the existence of a designer, and moving into arguments regarding unknown or seemingly redundant parts.</meta>

->### STATE OF THE ARGUMENT.<-

The question is simply whether it was made with any design at all.

III. Thirdly, it would not create any uncertainty in the argument if there were a few parts of the watch whose function we could not discover, or had not yet discovered, or even some parts where we could not determine if they contributed to the general effect in any way at all. 

For the first part of this case: if the movement of the watch were actually stopped, disturbed, or slowed down by the loss, disorder, or decay of the parts in question, no doubt would remain in our minds as to the utility or intention of these parts. This remains true even if we were unable to investigate the manner in which they worked, or the connection by which the final effect depended upon their action. Furthermore, the more complex a machine is, the more likely this obscurity is to arise. 

Then, for the second point: suppose there were parts that could be removed without <term>prejudice</term> <note>Without causing harm or detriment to the function.</note> to the movement of the watch, and we had proved this by experiment. These superfluous parts, even if we were completely certain they were unnecessary, would not <term>vacate</term> <note>Invalidate or void.</note> the reasoning we had established concerning the other parts. The indication of <term>contrivance</term> <note>A term for a purposefully designed device or mechanism.</note> would remain for those other parts nearly exactly as it was before.

IV. Fourthly, no person in their right mind would think the existence of the watch, with its various machinery, was accounted for by being told that it was merely one out of many possible combinations of material forms. It is not enough to argue that whatever a person found in that place must have contained some internal <term>configuration</term> <note>The specific arrangement or shape of parts.</note> or another, and that this configuration might just as easily be the structure of a watch as any other structure.

V. Fifth, it would not satisfy his inquiry to be told that there existed in things a "principle of order" which had arranged the parts of the watch into their present form and position. He has never known a watch to be made by a principle of order; nor can he even form an idea of what is meant by a principle of order that is distinct from the intelligence of the watchmaker.

VI. Sixth, he would be surprised to hear that the mechanism of the watch was not proof of <term>contrivance</term> <note>Purposeful design or invention.</note>, but only a motive to induce the mind to think so.

VII. He would be no less surprised to be informed that the watch in his hand was nothing more than the result of the laws of *metallic nature*. It is a misuse of language to assign any "law" as the efficient, active cause of anything. A law presupposes an agent; for a law is only the method according to which an agent proceeds. It implies a power; for it is the order according to which that power acts. Without this agent and without this power—which are both distinct from the law itself—the *law* does nothing and is nothing. The expression "the law of metallic nature" may sound strange and harsh to a scientific ear, but it seems quite as justifiable as some other phrases more familiar to him, such as "the law of vegetable nature," "the law of animal nature," or indeed "the law of nature" in general, when these are cited as the cause of <term>phenomena</term> <note>Observable facts or events.</note> in a way that excludes agency and power, or when a "law" is substituted in their place.

VIII. Finally, our observer would not be driven from his conclusion, or from his confidence in its truth, by being told that he knew nothing at all about the matter. He knows enough for his argument. He knows the utility of the end result; he knows the usefulness and adaptation of the means to that end. These points being known, his ignorance of...

## CHAPTER II.

->### STATE OF THE ARGUMENT CONTINUED.<-

Suppose, next, that the person who found the watch should, after some time, discover that it possessed an unexpected property in addition to all the qualities he had previously observed. Suppose that, in the course of its movement, it produced another watch like itself (a thing that is certainly conceivable). Imagine that it contained within it a mechanism—a system of parts, such as a mold or a complex arrangement of <term>lathes</term><note>The original text uses "laths," referring to the components of a lathe or similar machine tool used for shaping parts.</note>, files, and other tools—evidently and separately designed for this purpose. Let us inquire: what effect should such a discovery have on his former conclusion?

I. The first effect would be to increase his admiration of the <term>contrivance</term><note>A purposeful design, invention, or mechanical device.</note> and his conviction of the ultimate skill of the designer. Whether he considered the purpose of the design, the distinct equipment, or the intricate (yet in many parts understandable) mechanism by which it was carried out, he would see in this new observation only an additional reason for doing what he had already done: attributing the construction of the watch to intentional design and to <term>supreme art</term><note>Highest level of skill or craftsmanship.</note>. 

If the construction of the watch *without* this property—or before this property had been noticed—proved that intention and skill had been employed in its creation, then the proof would appear even stronger when he learned of this further property, which serves as the crown and perfection of all the rest.

<summary>Paley argues that if a watch were discovered to have the ability to reproduce itself, this complexity would only strengthen the observer's conviction that it was created by an intelligent designer.</summary>

II. He would reflect that, although the watch before him was, in a sense, the maker of the second watch produced during its movements, it was "the maker" in a very different sense from how a carpenter, for example, is the maker of a chair. The carpenter is the author of the chair's <term>contrivance</term><note>A purposeful design or invention.</note> and the cause of the relationship between its parts and their function. Regarding these aspects, the first watch was not the cause of the second watch at all. It was not the creator of the structure and order of the parts within the new watch, nor of the parts used as tools to produce it. We might say, speaking very loosely, that a stream of water ground the corn; but no amount of loose language or speculation would lead us to think that the stream of water *built* the mill, even if the mill were so old that we did not know who the builder was. What the stream of water does in this situation is simply this: by applying a mindless force to a mechanism already set up—set up independently of the water and designed by an intelligent mind—an effect is produced: specifically, the corn is ground. But that effect results from the arrangement of the machine. The force of the stream cannot be called the cause or author of the effect, much less the author of the arrangement itself. Intelligence and planning were still necessary to build the mill, regardless of the role the water plays in grinding the corn. Yet, the water's role is exactly the same as the role the first watch would play in producing the new watch, according to the scenario we assumed in the previous section. Therefore:

Evidence of design and <term>contrivance</term><note>A purposeful design or invention.</note> are no better explained now than they were before. Within the same object, we may look for the causes of different properties. We may ask for the cause of a body's color, its hardness, or its heat; and these causes may all be different. We are currently asking for the cause of that usefulness for a purpose—that relationship to a goal—which we have noted in the watch before us. Telling us that a previous watch produced it provides no answer to this question. There cannot be design without a designer, or an invention without an inventor. There cannot be order without choice, or an arrangement without something capable of arranging things. Usefulness and relationship to a purpose cannot exist without something that could intend a purpose. Finally, tools cannot be suited to a goal and perform their function in achieving that goal unless the goal was first envisioned and the tools adapted to reach it.

The arrangement and positioning of parts, the usefulness of tools for a specific goal, and the relationship of instruments to a function all imply the presence of intelligence and mind. Therefore, no one can rationally believe that the unfeeling, lifeless watch that produced the one before us was the actual cause of the mechanism we so admire. It cannot truly be said to have constructed the instrument, arranged its parts, assigned their functions, or determined their order, movement, and mutual dependence. Nor can it be said to have combined their various motions into a single result—especially a result that serves the needs of other beings. Therefore, all these properties remain just as unexplained as they were before.

Going back even further brings us no closer to a satisfying answer on this subject. <term>Contrivance</term><note>The act of planning or inventing a complex mechanism; purposeful design.</note> is still unexplained. We still need a <term>contriver</term><note>A designer or inventor.</note>. A <term>designing mind</term><note>An intelligent consciousness capable of planning for a specific purpose.</note> is neither provided by this assumption, nor can it be done without. If the difficulty decreased the further back we went, then by going back infinitely, we might eventually resolve it. And this is the only situation where this type of reasoning applies. 

Where there is a trend—or, as we increase the number of terms, a steady approach toward a limit—*there*, by assuming the number of terms is what we call infinite, we can imagine the limit being reached. But where there is no such trend or approach, nothing is gained by lengthening the series. Regarding the point in question (regardless of any other differences), there is no distinction between one series and another; between a series that is finite and a series that is infinite. 

A chain made of an infinite number of links can no more support its own weight than a chain made of a limited number of links. We are certain of this (even though we *can* never actually perform the experiment) because by increasing the number of links—from ten, for example, to a hundred, or from a hundred to a thousand, and so on—we do not come even slightly closer to self-support, nor do we see the slightest trend toward it. In this regard (though they may differ in many other ways), there is no difference between a longer or shorter chain, or between one that is finite and one that is indefinite. 

This situation is very similar to the case we are considering. The machine we are examining demonstrates, through its construction, purposeful design and planning. Purposeful design must have had a designer, and planning must have had a planner, regardless of whether the machine was produced directly by another machine or not. That circumstance does not change the situation. That other machine...

In whatever other respects they may differ, they do not differ in this. In all cases equally, the existence of design and planning remains unexplained.

The question is not simply, "How did the first watch come into existence?" One might claim that this question is dismissed by assuming the series of watches produced from one another has been infinite, and consequently had no such *first* watch that required a cause. This might have been the state of the question if we were looking at nothing more than an unorganized, non-mechanical substance, showing no mark or indication of design. It might be difficult to show that such a substance could not have existed from eternity, either in a sequence (if it were possible for unorganized bodies to produce one another, which I do not think it is) or by lasting forever as an individual object. 

But that is not the question now. To assume it is would be to assume that it makes no difference whether we had found a watch or a stone. As it is, the <term>metaphysics</term><note>The branch of philosophy dealing with the fundamental nature of reality and existence.</note> of that question have no place here; for, in the watch we are examining, we see design and planning; a goal and a purpose; the means to achieve that goal, and the adaptation of parts for that purpose. And the question which irresistibly presses upon our thoughts is: where did this design and planning come from? What is required is the intending mind, the adapting hand, the

It is simply working with one set of tools instead of another.

The conclusion is irrefutable. A *second* examination presents us with a new discovery. Can this be argued without absurdity? Yet this is the essence of atheism.

## CHAPTER III.

### APPLICATION OF THE ARGUMENT.

THIS is the essence of atheism: every sign of intentional planning and every manifestation of design that existed in the watch also exists in the works of nature. The difference is that nature’s designs are greater and more complex to a degree that exceeds all calculation. I mean that the mechanisms of nature surpass human inventions in their complexity, subtlety, and intricate detail; they go even further beyond them, if possible, in their sheer number and variety. Yet, in countless cases, natural structures are just as clearly mechanical, just as clearly planned, and just as clearly adapted to their specific purpose or function as the most perfect products of human ingenuity.

I know of no better way to introduce such a vast subject than by comparing two individual things: an eye, for example, with a telescope. As far as the examination of the instrument itself goes, there is exactly the same proof that the eye was made for vision as there is that the telescope was made to assist it. They are both built upon the same principles; both are adjusted to the laws by which the transmission and refraction <term>refraction</term><note>The bending of light as it passes from one medium, such as air, into another, such as glass or water.</note> of rays of light are regulated. I am not speaking here of the origin of the laws of physics themselves; but, since those laws are fixed, the construction in both cases is specifically adapted to them. For instance, to produce the same visual effect, these laws require that the rays of light, in passing from—

Accordingly, we find that the eye of a fish—specifically the part called the crystalline lens—is much rounder than the eye of land-dwelling animals. What clearer evidence of design could there be than this difference? What more could a maker of mathematical instruments have done to show his understanding of the principles, his application of that knowledge, and his ability to adapt his means to an end? I will not say to show off the range or excellence of his skill and art—for in these matters, any comparison is improper—but to demonstrate planning, choice, consideration, and purpose.

To some, the fact that the eye is a *perceiving organ* while the telescope is an *unperceiving instrument* might seem like a difference great enough to destroy any similarity between them. The fact is, however, that they are both instruments. As far as the mechanism is concerned—at least regarding the use of a mechanism and even the specific type used—this distinction does not change the analogy at all. Consider the physical structure of the eye. To produce clear vision, it is necessary for an image or picture of the object to be formed at the back of the eye. Where this necessity comes from, or how that picture connects to or contributes to our sensation of sight, may be difficult—or even, we might admit, impossible—for us to discover. But the current question does not depend on that inquiry. It may be true that in this and other cases, we can follow the mechanical design up to a certain point, and then we encounter something that is not mechanical or is completely mysterious. However, this does not undermine the certainty of our investigation regarding the parts we have already understood. The difference between an animal and an automated statue <term>automatic statue</term><note>An automaton; a self-operating machine or robot designed to follow a sequence of operations.</note> consists of this: in the animal, we can trace the mechanism to a certain point, and then we are stopped—

In contrast, in a machine like an automaton—because of the relatively few movements of which it is capable—we can trace the mechanism from beginning to end. In the example we are now considering, it is a matter of certainty (because it is a fact that experience and observation demonstrate) that the formation of an image at the back of the eye is necessary for perfect vision. The image itself can be shown. Anything that affects the clarity of the image also affects the clarity of the vision. Since the formation of such an image is necessary (regardless of how) for the sense of sight and the exercise of that sense, the apparatus by which it is formed is constructed and put together not only with infinitely more skill, but upon the exact same principles of art as in the telescope or the <term>camera obscura</term> <note>A device consisting of a box or room with a hole in one side that projects an image of its surroundings onto a screen.</note>. 

The question of how perception arises from the image can be set aside; for the purpose of producing the image, these are instruments of the same kind. The goal is the same; the means are the same. The purpose in both is identical, and the <term>contrivance</term> <note>a phrase used here to mean "purposeful design" or "invention"</note> for accomplishing that purpose is identical in both. The lenses of the telescope and the humors <term>the transparent fluids (aqueous, crystalline, and vitreous)</term> of the eye bear a complete resemblance to one another in their shape, their position, and in their power over the rays of light—specifically, in focusing each beam of light to a point at the correct distance from the lens. In the eye, this is the exact place where the membrane <note>the retina</note> is spread out to receive it. Given such a close similarity and the same level of evidence, how is it possible to deny design in the one, yet acknowledge the proof of design in the other as the plainest and clearest of all propositions?

The resemblance between the two cases is even more precise and holds true in more ways than we have shown so far, or than we might realize at first glance. In refracting telescopes <term>dioptric telescopes</term> <note>telescopes that use lenses to gather and focus light</note>, there is a specific kind of flaw. Rays of light <term>pencils of light</term> <note>narrow beams or bundles of light rays</note>, when passing through glass lenses, separate into different colors. This tints the object—especially its edges—as if it were being seen through a prism. To correct this inconvenience had long been a desired goal <term>desideratum</term> <note>something that is needed or wanted</note> in the field of optics. 

Finally, it occurred to a wise <term>sagacious</term> optician to investigate how this issue was handled in the eye, which faces the exact same challenge as the telescope. His observations taught him that in the eye, the problem was solved by combining lenses made of different materials—that is, substances with different light-bending powers <term>refracting powers</term>. Our craftsman <term>artist</term> <note>referring here to the optician/instrument maker</note> took his cue from this discovery. He corrected the defect by using different types of glass to imitate the effects of the various fluids <term>humors</term> <note>the transparent substances or fluids within the eye</note> that light rays pass through before reaching the back of the eye. Could this feature exist in the eye without a purpose, when it was the very thing that showed the optician the only effective way to achieve that same goal?

Furthermore, there are other points that perhaps show less of a strict resemblance and more the superiority of the eye over the telescope. Yet, because this superiority is based on the same laws that govern both, it provides a basis for a fair and accurate comparison. The eye required two things that the telescope did not—at least not to the same degree. These were: first, the adaptation of the organ to different levels of light; and second, the adaptation to the enormous range of distances at which we see objects with the naked eye—namely <term>viz.</term>, from a few inches to many miles. These challenges do not present themselves to the maker of the telescope. He wants all the light he can get, and he never directs his instrument toward objects near at hand. In the eye, both of these requirements had to be provided for; and for the purpose of providing for them, a subtle and appropriate mechanism is introduced.

I. In order to exclude excess light when it is too bright, and to make objects visible in dimmer conditions when no more light can be had, the hole or opening <term>aperture</term> in the eye through which the light enters is formed so as to contract or expand <term>dilate</term> itself. This serves the purpose of admitting a greater or lesser number of rays at the same time. The chamber of the eye is a dark room <term>camera obscura</term> <note>original: "camera obscura"; Latin for "dark chamber," a device that projects an image through a small hole</note> which can enlarge its opening when the light is too faint and contract it again when the light is too strong; and it does this without any assistance other than its own exquisite machinery. Furthermore, it should be observed in the human subject that this hole in the eye, which we call the pupil, retains its exact circular shape throughout all its different dimensions. Let a craftsman <term>artist</term> only try to execute the same. According to the laws of optics <term>optics</term>—that is, the fixed laws regulating the transmission of light—this could not be achieved without the organ itself undergoing a physical change and an adjustment. This adjustment must correspond to the requirements of the situation; specifically, it must account for the different angles at which rays of light reach the eye. 

Rays coming from points located a short distance from the eye enter in a spreading or <term>diverging order</term> <note>rays that move away from each other as they travel from a source</note>. Using the same optical instrument in the same state, these rays cannot be focused to a single point—that is, they cannot form an image in the same location—as rays coming from objects situated at a much greater distance. Those distant rays arrive at the eye in directions that are nearly, and practically speaking, parallel. 

Focusing near objects requires a rounder lens. The <term>point of concourse</term> <note>the focal point where light rays meet to form a clear image</note> behind the lens must fall precisely upon the retina <term>retina</term>, or the vision will be blurred. Yet, by the unchanging properties of light, this point is pushed further back when the rays come from a near object than when they are sent from a remote one. 

A person using an optical instrument would handle this matter by changing his lens or his telescope as the situation required, or by adjusting the distance of his glasses by hand or with a screw. But how is it to be managed in the eye? What the change was, in what part of the eye it occurred, or by what means it was achieved had long been a subject of inquiry and speculation. (For if the known laws governing the refraction <term>refraction</term> <note>the bending of light as it passes through a lens</note> of light are to be maintained, there must be some change in the state of the organ.) The change, though sufficient for the purpose, is so tiny that it escapes ordinary observation. Some very recent discoveries, resulting from a laborious and highly accurate inspection of the structure and operation of the organ, seem at last to have identified the mechanism.

The fact is, two unique features are found in the eyes of birds, both of which help the eye adjust to different distances. The first is a bony, yet flexible, rim or hoop found in most species. It surrounds the widest part of the eye. By restricting the movement of the muscles to that specific area, it increases the side pressure on the eyeball <term>orb</term>. This pressure elongates the axis of the eye so the bird can focus on very near objects. Because of these mechanisms, birds' eyes can shift between extremes of focus more easily and quickly than the eyes of other animals.

There is one property, however, common, I believe, to all eyes—at least all those that have been examined*—namely, that the optic nerve enters the back of the eye not in the center, but slightly to one side. It enters not at the point where the axis of the eye meets the retina, but between that point and the nose. The advantage of this arrangement is that no part of an object is invisible to both eyes at the same time.

One question may have stayed in the reader’s mind while reading these observations: namely, why shouldn't the Deity have given the animal the faculty of vision *directly*? Why use this indirect method of perception and the employment of so many means? An element <note>light</note> was provided for the purpose, which reflects off opaque substances and refracts through transparent ones, both according to precise laws. Then, a complex organ—an intricate and artificial apparatus—was created so that, through the operation of this light and in accordance with the restrictions of these laws, an image could be produced upon a membrane communicating with the brain.

What does this structure actually consist of? It includes: an external ear (the <term>concha</term> <note>the bowl-shaped part of the outer ear</note>), designed like an ear-trumpet to catch and collect the pulses we mentioned. In large four-legged animals, this part turns toward the sound and has a shape and range of motion clearly suited for that task. It also consists of a tube leading into the head, located at the base of the outer ear, with folds and curves that guide the air into it. There is a thin membrane, like the skin of a drum, stretched across this passage on a bony rim. There is a chain of movable and incredibly intricate bones that form a connection—the only observable connection—between that membrane and the inner channels and recesses of the skull. There are cavities shaped like musical wind instruments, either spiral or circular in form. There is the <term>Eustachian tube</term>, which acts like the vent hole in a drum to allow air to pass freely in and out of the "barrel" of the ear as the membrane vibrates or as the temperature changes. Finally, the entire <term>labyrinth</term> <note>the complex structure of the inner ear</note> is carved out of rock—that is, it is fashioned into the substance of the hardest bone in the body. This collection of connected parts forms an apparatus clearly related to the transmission of sound (or the impulses received from sound); our only regret is that it is not yet better understood.

The internal connection formed by the small bones of the ear looks more like what we usually call machinery than anything else I have seen in animal bodies. It seems evi-

This occurs when solid objects are pressed against the bones of the skull, such as when a metal bar is held at one end between the teeth while its other end touches a vibrating body. The benefit of the Eustachian tube to the ear can be explained based on known pneumatic principles <note>principles regarding the physical properties of air and gases</note>. Behind the eardrum is a second cavity or barrel, called the **tympanum**. The Eustachian tube is a slender pipe—sufficient for air to pass through—leading from this cavity into the back part of the mouth. 

Now, it would not have worked to have a vacuum in this cavity; for, in that case, the external atmospheric pressure would have burst the membrane covering it. Nor would it have worked to fill the cavity with lymph <note>a clear bodily fluid</note> or any other secretion, which would necessarily have obstructed both the vibration of the membrane and the movement of the small bones. Finally, it would not have worked to occupy the space with trapped air, because the expansion of that air by heat, or its contraction by cold, would have stretched or loosened the covering membrane to a degree that would interfere with its intended purpose. The only remaining solution—and the one for which the Eustachian tube serves—is to open a communication between this cavity and the external air. In short, it serves exactly the same purpose as the vent hole in a drum.

The *membrana tympani* <note>the eardrum</note> itself also deserves a thorough examination. It is not found in the ears of fish; this provides additional proof of what its entire structure suggests: it is specifically designed to react to air or an elastic medium. It bears an obvious resemblance to the pelt <note>the skin or head of a drum</note> or head of a drum, from which it takes its name. It also resembles a drumhead in its most important property: its function depends on its tension. Being under tension is its essential state. This muscle he suggests is designed to bring the membrane into harmony with different sounds. However, he also discovered that this muscle itself cannot function unless the membrane is stretched and kept in a proper state of tightness by what may be called an external force: namely, the action of the muscles of the malleus. Our author <note>referring to Everard Home</note>, assuming his explanation of the use of these parts to be correct, is well-justified in the reflection he makes upon it: "*this method of adapting the ear to different sounds is one of the most beautiful applications of muscles in the body; the mechanism is so simple, and the variety of effects is so great.*"

# CHAPTER IV.

## OF THE SUCCESSION OF PLANTS AND ANIMALS.

The reproduction of an animal explains the design of the eye or ear no more than—following the scenario described in a previous chapter—the creation of a watch by the movement and mechanics of a previous watch would explain the skill and intent shown in the new watch. It would not explain the arrangement of the wheels, the way their teeth interlock, the relationship between the various parts and their shared goal, the suitability of their shapes and positions for their functions, their connections, their operation, or the useful results of those operations. I insist most strongly on the accuracy of this comparison; it applies to every method of species reproduction. Whatever was true of the watch in that hypothetical scenario is equally true for plants and animals.

I. To begin with the production of seeds and fruit <term>fructification</term> in plants: Can it be doubted that the seed contains a specific organizational structure? Whether it is a hidden plant embryo <term>plantule</term> along with the means for its temporary nutrition, or whatever else it may be, it contains a structure suited for the growth <term>germination</term> of a new plant. Does the plant that produced the seed have anything more to do with that structure than the first watch would have had to do with the design of the second watch produced through its mechanical movements? To be clear: does the parent plant have anything at all to do with the actual design <term>contrivance</term>? The maker...

He specifically applies this to the complex organizational structure found within plant seeds.</summary>

...and designer of one watch, when he inserted within it a mechanism suited to the production of another watch, was in truth the maker and designer of that other watch. All the properties of the new watch were to be attributed to his work <term>agency</term>: the design shown in it to his intention; the art to him as the artist; the arrangement of each part to his placement; and the action, effect, and use to his deliberation, intelligence, and workmanship. In producing it through the medium of a previous watch, he was only working with one set of tools instead of another. 

The same applies to the plant and the seed it produces. Can any distinction be made between the two cases—between the watch that produces and the plant that produces? Both are passive, unconscious substances; both, through the organization that was given to them, produce their likeness without understanding or design; both, in other words, are merely instruments.

II. From plants we may move on to egg-laying <term>oviparous</term> animals; from seeds to eggs. Now I argue that the bird has the same level of involvement in the formation of the egg she lays as the plant has in the seed it drops—and no more, nor greater. The internal makeup of the egg is as much a secret to the hen as if the hen were inanimate. Her will cannot alter it, or change a single feather of the chick. She can neither foresee nor determine the sex of her brood, or how many there will be of either sex; yet the creature produced shall be, from the beginning, very different in its physical makeup according to the sex it bears. 

Therefore, far from adapting the means to reach an end, she is not even aware of the effect beforehand. If there is concealed within that smooth shell a provision and a preparation for the production and nourishment of a new animal, they are not of her providing or preparing; if there is design <term>contrivance</term>, it is none of hers. Therefore, even if there is a difference in life and perception between the animal and the plant, it is a difference that does not change the calculation. It is an irrelevant factor. Now, a cause that has this relationship to the effect—conscious design—is what we require in order to explain the suitability of means to an end, and the fitting of one thing to another. This cause is something the parent plant or animal does not provide.

It is further observable concerning the <term>propagation</term> <note>reproduction</note> of plants and animals that the apparatus employed shows no resemblance to the thing produced; in this respect, it is similar to the instruments and tools of an artist. The <term>filaments</term>, <term>antherae</term>, and <term>stigmata</term> <note>the pollen-bearing and pollen-receiving parts of a flower</note> of flowers bear no more resemblance to the young plant, or even to the seed formed through them, than a chisel or a <term>plane</term> <note>a tool for smoothing wood</note> does to a table or a chair. What then are the filaments, antherae, and stigmata of plants, but instruments in the strictest sense of the word?

## CHAPTER 5.

### CONTINUING THE APPLICATION OF THE ARGUMENT.

Every observation made in our first chapter regarding the watch can be applied with perfect accuracy to the eye, to animals, to plants, and indeed to all organized parts of the natural world. For example:

I. When we are simply investigating the *existence* of an intelligent Creator, imperfections, inaccuracies, a susceptibility to disorder, or occasional irregularities may exist to a significant degree without causing any doubt about the main question. Just as a watch may frequently run poorly, or perhaps rarely run perfectly—it may be faulty or defective in some parts—without giving us the slightest reason to suspect that it was not actually a watch, that it was not manufactured, or that it was not designed for its intended purpose. When faults are pointed out, and when questions are raised concerning the skill of the artist or the dexterity <term>dexterity: manual skill or cleverness in execution</term> with which the work was performed, then we must defend these qualities against criticism. To do so, we must be able to either show some unmanageable nature or imperfection in the materials, or point out some insurmountable difficulty in the construction to which the complaint can be attributed. If we cannot do this, we must provide other examples of such perfect skill and contrivance <term>contrivance: a clever or complex mechanical device or design</term> originating from the same hand, which may convince the inquirer of the existence, in the case before him, of

IV. There is another explanation which leads to the same conclusion as attributing everything to chance. However, there is no foundation whatsoever for this theory in anything we observe in nature. No such experiments are occurring today, and no such force exists that would constantly push new varieties of beings into existence. Every possible variety of being has, at one time or another, found its way into existence (though by what cause or in what manner is not explained), and those which were poorly formed perished. Furthermore, the idea of a "principle of order" acting blindly and without choice is disproven by the observation that order is not universal. If order originated from a constant and necessary principle, it would be found everywhere; if it originated from an unintelligent principle, it would be distributed randomly. We find order exactly where it is needed; where order is not needed—that is, where it would be useless if it existed—we do not find it. In the structure of the eye (to stick with our previous example), the most precise order is maintained in the shape and position of its various parts. However, in the shapes of rocks and mountains, in the lines that mark the coasts of continents and islands, and in the shapes of bays and headlands <term>promontories: high points of land that jut out into a body of water</term>, no order is perceived at all, because such order would have been unnecessary <term>superfluous: unnecessary or redundant</term>. No useful purpose would have been served by shaping rocks and mountains into perfect geometric solids, defining the boundaries of the ocean with mathematical curves, or having the map of the world look like a table of diagrams in *Euclid’s Elements* or *Simpson’s Conic Sections* <note>Euclid's Elements is a fundamental work of geometry; Thomas Simpson's work on Conic Sections was a standard mathematical textbook in the 18th century.</note>.

## CHAPTER VI.

### THE CUMULATIVE ARGUMENT.

If there were no other example of design <term>contrivance: a mechanical device or clever arrangement</term> in the world except for the *eye*, it alone would be sufficient to support the conclusion we draw from it regarding the necessity of an intelligent Creator. This argument could never be dismissed, because it cannot be explained by any other hypothesis that does not contradict all the principles of knowledge we possess—the very principles by which things are proven true or false whenever they are tested by experience. 

The eye's layers <term>coats: the membranes or tissues covering the eyeball</term> and fluids <term>humours: the transparent liquid substances within the eye</term> are constructed just as the lenses of a telescope are made: to refract <term>refraction: the bending of light as it passes through different materials</term> light rays to a single point, which is the primary function of the organ. The provision of muscular tendons for turning the pupil toward an object is similar to the screws used to aim a telescope; the eye's ability to function as an optical instrument depends entirely on this power of direction. Furthermore, there are provisions for its defense and for its constant lubrication <term>lubricity: the state of being smooth or slippery</term> and moisture. We see this in the socket and the eyelids, in the gland that secretes tears, and in the duct—its communication with the nose—for draining the liquid after the eye has been washed by it. 

Taken together, these features compose an apparatus, a system of parts, and a coordination of means so obvious in their design, so exquisite in their construction, so successful in their result, and so precious and infinitely beneficial in their use, that they are, in my opinion, enough to overcome all...

<summary>The author argues that the complex, telescope-like anatomy of the eye—including its lenses, muscles, and tear systems—is sufficient on its own to prove the existence of an intelligent Creator. He asserts that the eye's design is so perfect and beneficial that it outweighs any skeptical objections.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the cumulative nature of the argument for design, emphasizing that each biological example stands as an independent proof of a Creator, regardless of whether other parts of nature are understood.</meta>

<page-num>56</page-num>

->**THE CUMULATIVE ARGUMENT.**<-

No doubt can be raised on this subject. In this chapter, I want to point out that even if other parts of nature were impossible for us to study, or if they seemed completely chaotic and disordered, the strength of this single example would remain unchanged. If there were only one watch in the entire world, it would be just as certain that it had a maker. Even if we had only ever seen a single type of water-powered machine <term>hydraulic machine: a device operated by the pressure or movement of liquid</term>, as long as we understood how it worked and what it was for, we would be just as sure that it was created by the skill and planning of a craftsman as if we had visited a museum and seen twenty different water pumps or a thousand different machines for other uses. 

Every single machine serves as proof on its own, regardless of any others. The same is true for the evidence of divine action <term>divine agency: the operation or power of God acting in the world</term>. The proof is not a single conclusion at the end of a long chain of reasoning where each instance of design <term>contrivance: a mechanical device or purposeful arrangement</term> is just a link. In such a chain, if one link fails, the whole argument collapses. Instead, the argument is independently supported by every individual example. 

An error in describing one example only affects that specific case. The argument is "cumulative" in the fullest sense of that word. The eye proves the point even without the ear; the ear proves it without the eye. The proof in each instance is complete in itself. Once the purpose of a part and the way its structure serves that purpose are shown, the mind can be satisfied. No further evidence can take away from the power of that specific example.

<summary>Paley argues that the evidence for a Creator is cumulative, meaning each individual instance of design in nature—like the eye—stands as a complete and independent proof, regardless of other examples.</summary>

# CHAPTER VII.

## OF THE MECHANICAL AND IMMECHANICAL PARTS AND FUNCTIONS OF ANIMALS AND PLANTS.

It is not that *every* part of an animal or plant <term>vegetable: in this context, any living organism that is not an animal; a plant</term> has not originated from a designing mind. Nor is it that every part is not constructed with its own specific purpose in mind, according to the laws governing the substances or actions used in that part. Furthermore, it is not that each part is not designed to achieve its goal while operating according to those laws. Rather, we make the distinction proposed here—between "mechanical" parts and other parts of animals and plants—simply because those laws themselves are not equally understood in all cases. Or, what amounts to nearly the same thing, those laws are not as clearly demonstrated in simpler processes or simpler machines.

For example, the principle of muscular motion—namely, what cause makes the center of a muscle swell and its tendons <term>tendons: tough cords of tissue connecting muscle to bone</term> subsequently contract, whether by an act of will or by involuntary irritation—is completely unknown to us. The substance involved—whether it is fluid, gas, elastic, electricity, none of these, or nothing like them—is also unknown to us. Consequently, the laws belonging to that substance, which regulate its actions, are also unknown. We see nothing similar to this contraction in any machine we can build or any process we can carry out.

<meta>catchword: So</meta>

<summary>Paley distinguishes between "mechanical" biological functions (those we can understand through physics) and "immechanical" ones (like muscle contraction) whose underlying physical laws remain unknown to science.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the distinction between the "mechanical" and "immechanical" functions of organisms, specifically focusing on how muscle arrangement functions like a machine despite the mysterious nature of the "nervous influence" that triggers movement.</meta>

<page-num>58</page-num>

-> MECHANICAL AND IMMECHANICAL PARTS <-

We admit that we are ignorant up to this point, but no further. Once we assume the existence of this power and principle (whatever its cause may be), the arrangement of the fibers to receive that principle and the placement of the muscles to use and apply that power is mechanical. It is as easy to understand as the adjustment of the wires and strings used to move a puppet. 

We see, therefore, regarding our current subject, what is mechanical in the animal body and what is not. The "nervous influence" (we often have to name things we know little about)—that is, the influence that causes the belly or middle of the muscle to swell—is not mechanical. We perceive the usefulness of the result; however, we do not understand the means, or the preparation of means, by which it is produced. 

But our lack of clarity regarding the origin of muscular motion does not cast doubt on our observations of the rest of the process. These observations relate: 

1. To the makeup of the muscle, where the swelling of the middle part is necessarily and mechanically followed by the contraction of the tendons.
2. To the vast number and variety of muscles and the many useful abilities they provide to the animal, which is truly astonishing.
3. To the judicious (if we may use that word when speaking of the Creator or the works of nature), wise, and well-designed arrangement of each muscle for its specific purpose—moving a joint in various directions and pulling the part it is attached to in a specific, predetermined way. 

This is a mechanical operation, demonstrated in many examples. To use any obscurity, difficulty, or controversy in the theory of magnetism as an objection to our knowledge of the device's design—or the evidence of design shown in the automaton—would be logically flawed. It would be exactly the same as using our admitted ignorance of the cause of nerve function, or even of the substance and structure of the nerves themselves, as a reason to question or doubt the reasoning we establish concerning the mechanical parts of our own bodies. 

The proposition that an animal is a machine is neither entirely true nor completely false. The distinction we have been discussing shows how far the comparison implied by this expression holds true and where it fails. I contend, therefore, that there is mechanism in animals; that this mechanism is just as truly a machine as those made by human art; and that this mechanism is understandable and certain. It is no less certain simply because it often begins or ends with something that is not mechanical. Whenever it is understandable and certain, it demonstrates intention and design <term>contrivance: a purpose-built mechanical device or clever design</term>, both in the works of nature and in those of art; and it is the best demonstration that either can provide.

But, while I argue for these propositions, I do not mean to suggest that there are not other cases where we cannot display a mechanical process, or prove indeed that mechanism is employed. Even in those cases, we do not lack sufficient evidence to lead us to the same conclusion of design.

What conclusion does its location, properties, action, surprising efficacy, and invaluable use authorize us to draw regarding a creative design?

Another most subtle and curious function of animal bodies is secretion. This function is semi-chemical and semi-mechanical; it is exceedingly important and diverse in its effects, yet obscure in both its process and its apparatus. The importance of the secretory organs is only too well proven by the diseases that an excessive, deficient, or corrupted <note>original: "vitiated"</note> secretion is almost certain to produce. If just one secretion goes wrong, it is enough to make life miserable, or sometimes to destroy it. 

The variety of these secretions is no less remarkable than their importance. From the exact same blood (speaking here of the human body), about twenty different fluids are separated. In their observable properties—taste, smell, color, and consistency—they are as different from one another as possible: thick, thin, salty, bitter, or sweet. If we look beyond ourselves to other species of animals, we find secretions with not only the most various but also the most opposite properties: the most nutritious food and the deadliest poison; the sweetest perfumes and the most foul-smelling odors. 

The greater part of these—such as the gastric juice, the saliva, the bile, the slippery <term>mucilage</term> <note>synovial fluid</note> which lubricates the joints, the tears which moisten the eye, and the wax which protects the ear—are used within the <term>animal economy</term> <note>the functional system of a living body</note> after they are secreted. They are clearly subservient to and actually contribute to the needs of the animal itself. Other fluids seem to be separated only to be rejected. That this is also necessary (though why it was originally necessary, we cannot say) is shown by the consequences of this separation being long suspended; those consequences are disease and death.

My goal in the present chapter has been to teach three things: 

First, that it is a mistake to suppose that, when reasoning from the appearances of nature, the limits of our knowledge proportionally affect the certainty of our conclusion; in many cases, our lack of full knowledge does not affect that certainty at all.

## CHAPTER VIII.

### MECHANICAL ARRANGEMENT IN THE HUMAN BODY <term>frame</term> <note>the physical structure of the human body</note>.

We will therefore proceed to propose specific examples taken from this class of mechanical parts. We have chosen those which, among all that we know, seem to be the most striking and the best understood. However, we must prioritize a third requirement: that the example must be capable of being explained without the use of diagrams, illustrations, or technical language.

### THE BONES.

I. I challenge anyone to produce, in the joints and pivots of the most complex or flexible machine ever invented <term>contrived</term>, a construction more skillfully engineered <term>artificial</term> <note>In this context, "artificial" refers to something crafted with great human-like skill and design, rather than something "fake"</note>—or more obviously designed—than what is seen in the vertebrae of the *human neck*. Two specific functions had to be achieved. The head needed the power to bend forward and backward, as if nodding, stooping, or looking up and down; and, at the same time, it needed the ability to turn itself around on the body to a certain extent—say, a quarter-circle <term>quadrant</term>, or rather, perhaps, a hundred and twenty degrees of a circle. To achieve these two purposes, two distinct mechanisms <term>contrivances</term> are used. First, the head rests directly upon the highest of the vertebrae and is joined to it by a *hinge joint*. Upon this joint, the head moves freely forward and back—

Therefore, secondly, to enable the head to do this, a further mechanism is introduced; not between the head and the uppermost bone of the neck where the hinge is, but between that bone and the bone immediately underneath it. It is a mechanism resembling a *mortise and tenon* <term>tenon and mortice</term> <note>a joint used in woodworking where a projection (tenon) fits into a hole (mortise)</note>. This second bone (the uppermost bone but one) has what anatomists call a process <term>process</term> <note>a natural projection or outgrowth on a bone</note>—that is, a projection somewhat similar in size and shape to a tooth. This "tooth," entering a corresponding hole or socket in the bone above it, forms a pivot or axle. Upon this axle, that upper bone—together with the head which it supports—turns freely in a circle, as far as the attached muscles permit the head to turn. Thus, both motions are perfected without interfering with each other. When we nod the head, we use the hinge joint which lies between the head and the first bone of the neck. When we turn the head around, we use the mortise and tenon joint which runs between the first bone of the neck and the second.

We see the same mechanical solution <term>contrivance</term>, and the same principle, employed in the frame or mounting of a telescope. It is occasionally necessary that the lens end <term>object end</term> of the instrument be moved up and down, as well as horizontally (or equatorially). For the vertical motion, there is a hinge upon which the telescope pivots; for the horizontal or equatorial motion, there is an axis upon which the telescope and the hinge turn together. And this is exactly the mechanism which is applied to the movement of the head. No one here will doubt the existence of deliberate planning <term>counsel</term> and design, unless it is by that weakness <term>debility</term> of mind which cannot trust its own reasoning in anything.

II. Another mechanical design <term>contrivance</term>, similar in purpose to the last but different and original in its execution, is seen in what anatomists call the *forearm*; that is, the part of the arm between the elbow and the wrist. Here, for the limb to be fully useful, two motions are required: a back-and-forth motion at the elbow, which is called a reciprocal motion; and a rotating <term>rotatory</term> motion, by which the palm of the hand may be turned upward as needed. How is this managed? The forearm, as is well known, consists of two bones <note>the radius and the ulna</note>, lying alongside each other but touching only near their ends. Only one of these bones is joined to the upper arm <term>cubit</term> at the elbow; the other bone alone is joined to the hand at the wrist. The first bone, by means of a hinge joint at the elbow (which allows movement only in a single plane), swings backward and forward, carrying the other bone and the entire forearm with it. Meanwhile, whenever there is a need to turn the palm upward, that other bone, to which the hand is attached, rolls upon the first. This is aided by a groove or hollow near each end of one bone, into which a corresponding projection <term>prominence</term> on the other bone is fitted. If both bones had been joined to the upper arm at the elbow, or both to the hand at the wrist, this rotation could not have been achieved. The first bone had to be free at one end, and the second at the other; by this means, the two actions may be performed together. III. The spine, or backbone, is a chain of joints of truly wonderful construction. Various, difficult, and almost contradictory functions <term>offices</term> had to be performed by the same structure. It had to be firm, yet flexible. It must be *firm* to support the body’s upright position, yet *flexible* to allow the torso to bend in every degree of curvature. Furthermore, it served another entirely distinct purpose: to act as a pipe or conduit for the safe passage from the brain of the most important fluid in the animal body—the one upon which all voluntary motion depends: the spinal cord <term>spinal marrow</term>. Now, the spine was intended not only to provide the main conduit for the passage of the spinal cord <term>medullary substance</term> from the brain, but also to send out, along its path, small pipes from it. These, being afterwards indefinitely subdivided under the name of nerves, distribute this vital supply to every part of the body. This same spine was also to serve another purpose no less necessary than the preceding: namely, to provide a pivot <term>fulcrum</term>, support, or foundation (or more accurately, a series of these) for the attachment of the muscles which are spread over the torso. In the torso, there are no cylindrical bones like those in the limbs to which muscles can be fastened; the spine also serves a similar use by providing a support for the ends of the ribs to rest upon.

Ask a craftsman to create a piece of machinery which shall fulfill all these purposes, and let him set about designing it. Let him try his skill upon it; let him feel the difficulty of accomplishing the task before he is told how the same thing is achieved in the animal body. Nothing will enable him to judge the wisdom that has been employed so well, and nothing will lead him to think of it so accurately. 

First, regarding the firmness and yet flexibility of the spine: it is composed of a great number of bones (twenty-four in the human subject) joined to one another and compacted together by broad bases. The width of the bases upon which the parts individually rest, and the closeness of the junction, give the chain its firmness and stability. The number of parts, and the resulting frequency of joints, provide its flexibility. We may also observe that this flexibility varies in different parts of the chain: it is least in the back, where strength is needed more than bending <term>flexure</term>, and greater in the lower back <term>loins</term>, which it was necessary should be more supple than...

Secondly, to provide a passage for the descent of the spinal cord <term>medullary substance</term>, each of these bones is perforated in the middle. They are arranged in such a manner that, when put together, the hole in one bone aligns perfectly with the holes in the two adjacent bones. By this means, the perforated pieces form a complete, enclosed, and uninterrupted channel—at least while the spine is upright and at rest. 

However, because a fixed posture is incompatible with its use, a great difficulty still remained: how to prevent the vertebrae from shifting against one another and breaking the line of the canal whenever the body moves or twists; and how to prevent the joints from gaping open on the outside whenever the body is bent forward and the spine is forced into the shape of a bow. These mechanical dangers are addressed through mechanical solutions. The vertebrae—by means of their bony processes, projections, and the joints <term>articulations</term> which some of these form with one another at their ends—are locked together and confined. This maintains the relative position of the broad surfaces of the bones (called the "bodies") nearly unchanged. This design shifts the change and pressure produced by bending <term>flexion</term> almost entirely onto the intervening cartilages <note>the intervertebral discs</note>. The springy and flexible nature of this substance allows for all necessary motion without creating any gap from a separation of the parts. 

I say "all necessary motion" because, although we can bend our backs to almost any degree of inclination, the movement of each individual vertebra is actually very small. This is the advantage we receive from the chain being composed of so many links, and the spine of so many bones. Had it consisted of only three or four bones, then in bending the body, the spinal

In a structure involving so many joints, where a misalignment in any one of them would have been fatal, security became a matter of careful design. For this purpose, the vertebrae are joined together—that is, the movable joints between them are formed—by those projections of their substance which we have mentioned under the name of processes. These lock into and overlap one another so effectively that they secure the body of the vertebrae not only from accidentally slipping, but even from being pushed out of place by any force short of that which would break the bone. 

I have often noticed and admired this structure in the backbone <term>chine</term> of a hare. In this, as in many instances, an ordinary observer of biological systems <term>animal economy</term> can avoid the unpleasantness of attending human dissections. It will move neither forward, backward, nor to either side. Now, this is the very same design employed in the famous iron bridge near my home at Bishopwearmouth <note>The Wearmouth Bridge, completed in 1796, was one of the longest iron-arch bridges of its time and a marvel of contemporary engineering.</note>, and for the same purpose of stability: namely, the sides <term>cheeks</term> of the bars, which pass between the arches, sit across the joints where the pieces of each arch are united. Each crossbar rests upon two of these pieces at their point of junction; by that position, it resists—at least in one direction—any tendency for either piece to slip out of its place. 

Thus perfectly, by one method or another, the danger of the bones slipping sideways or being drawn out of the line of the back is guarded against. Furthermore, to prevent the bones from being pulled apart lengthwise—or along the direction of the spine—a strong membrane runs from one end of the chain to the other. This is sufficient to resist any force that is ever likely to act in the direction of the back, or parallel to it, and consequently secures the entire structure in place. The general result is that not only are the motions of the human body necessary for the ordinary tasks of life performed with safety, but it is an accident hardly ever heard of that even the extreme contortions <term>gesticulations</term> of an acrobat <term>harlequin</term> distort his spine.

The structure of the spine is generally similar across different animals. Among the snake tribe, however, it is significantly varied, though with strict attention to the requirements <term>conveniency</term> of the animal. For instance, while four-legged animals have between thirty and forty vertebrae, snakes have nearly one hundred and fifty. Furthermore, while in humans and quadrupeds the bone surfaces are flat—pressed against each other and bound tight by ligaments—in the snake, the bones fit into one another like a ball and socket*, so that they move freely against one another in every direction. In other words, in humans and quadrupeds, stability is the primary consideration; in snakes, it is flexibility. Yet even this flexibility is not achieved at the cost of safety. The backbone of a snake, in terms of its structural integrity and flexibility, is one of the most remarkable examples of biological mechanism with which we are acquainted. The chain of a watch—specifically the chain that passes between the spring-barrel and the fusee <note>A fusee is a conical pulley used in old mechanical watches to equalize the force of the mainspring as it unwinds.</note>—which is designed for these same properties, is only a clumsy piece of craftsmanship compared to the structure we are discussing.

Since the ends of the ribs are fixed at the spine, the result of their downward slant is that whenever they are pulled upward, they are necessarily drawn outward at the same time. As the ribs are brought to a right angle with the spine in the back, the <term>sternum</term> <note>The breastbone.</note>, or the part of the chest to which they are attached in the front, is pushed forward. Furthermore, if each rib had been a rigid bone joined at both ends to fixed bases, the entire chest would have been immovable. 

James Keill <note>An influential 17th-century physician and anatomist.</note> observed that the breastbone is pushed out one-tenth of an inch during a relaxed breath. When a deeper and more forceful breath is necessary, the expansion of the chest can be so increased by effort that the lungs may be filled with seventy or a hundred such cubic inches. Schelhammer <note>Gunther Christoph Schelhammer, a German physician.</note> says that the <term>thorax</term> forms a kind of bellows, the likes of which have never been—and probably never will be—made by any human craftsman.
