I. The examples mentioned above are just a few bones made remarkable by their shape. However, almost all bones have *joints*; and in these, even more clearly than in the form or shape of the bones themselves, we see both intentional design and the wisdom of the designer. Every joint is a marvel and is also strictly mechanical. There is the hinge joint and the <term>mortise and tenon</term> <note>A woodworking joint where a projection (tenon) fits into a hole (mortise); here used to describe the ball and socket joint.</note> joint. Each is as clearly recognizable and as accurately defined as any joint produced in a carpenter's workshop. One or the other is used depending on which is best suited for the required movement. 

For example, a ball and socket joint is not required at the knee, because the leg only needs to move backward and forward in a single plane; for this, a hinge joint is sufficient. However, a ball and socket joint is necessary at the hip so that not only can the forward step be taken, but the space between the limbs can be widened or narrowed as desired. 

Now, consider how inconvenient it would be—resulting in both unnecessary movement and a failure of proper <term>articulation</term>—if the situation were reversed. Imagine if the ball and socket joint were at the knee and the hinge joint were at the hip. The thighs would have to be kept constantly pressed together, while the legs would be loose and wobbly. There would be no known benefit in being able to turn the calves of the legs forward, yet there would be great restriction in limiting the movement of the thighs to a single plane.

The *hinge joint* is not formed by a bolt passing through the two parts of the hinge to keep them in their places; instead, it uses a different method. A strong, tough, parchment-like membrane rises from the receiving bones and is attached all around the inserted bones just below their heads, enclosing the joint on every side. This membrane ties, confines, and holds the ends of the bones together, keeping the corresponding parts of the joint—that is, the relative curves and hollows—in close contact with each other.

For the *ball and socket joint*, besides the membrane already described, some important joints have an additional security: a short, strong, yet flexible ligament. This is inserted at one end into the head of the ball and at the other into the bottom of the cup. This ligament keeps the two parts of the joint so firmly in place that none of the natural motions of the limb—nor the usual jerks and twists to which it is liable—can pull them apart. Indeed, nothing less than extreme and unnatural force can separate them. It is difficult to imagine how much force is required even to stretch, let alone break, this ligament; yet it is so flexible that it does not hinder the suppleness of the joint. Furthermore, because of its location, it is protected from injury by sharp edges. Just as its strength prevents it from being ruptured, its position ensures it cannot be cut, except by an accident severe enough to sever the limb entirely. If I were permitted to create a proof of <term>contrivance</term> <note>Intentional design or a cleverly made device.</note>—one that might satisfy even the most skeptical inquirer—I do not know if I could have chosen a more clear or indisputable example of mechanism than this ligament. Another equally important joint, which is also of the *hinge joint* <term>ginglymus</term> variety, is the *ankle*. Although it is important, it is small—perhaps to preserve the symmetry and lightness of the limb—and, for that reason, more liable to injury. This joint is strengthened (that is, protected from dislocation) by two remarkable bony projections or extensions of the leg bones. These extensions form the bumps that we call the inner and outer ankle. Each bone has a part that extends lower than the rest, thereby overlapping the joint. Consequently, if the joint is in danger of slipping outward, it is restrained by the inner projection (that of the *tibia*); if it is in danger of slipping inward, it is held by the outer projection (that of the *fibula*). Between these two, it is locked in its position. I know of no explanation that can be given for this structure except for its usefulness. Why should the *tibia* end at its lower extremity with a double point, and the *fibula* do the same, if not to barricade the joint on both sides by extending part of the bone's thickness over it?

When the *shoulder* joint is compared with the *hip* joint—though both are ball-and-socket joints—we discover a difference in their form and proportions that is well-suited to the different tasks the limbs must perform. The cup or socket at the shoulder is much shallower and flatter than it is at the hip; it is also partially formed of cartilage set around the rim of the cup. This is true despite the twists and strains to which the limbs of animals are constantly subjected.

II. The *joints*—or rather, the ends of the bones that form them—also demonstrate another purpose in their structure. It is obvious that the nerves, blood vessels, and tendons necessary for the life or movement of the limbs must travel from the trunk of the body to their destination by passing over the moving joints. It is equally obvious that, along this path, they will face the danger of being compressed or pinched by sudden movements and abrupt changes in the limb's curve.

This is achieved through the specific shape of the bones themselves. The nerves that supply the *forearm*, particularly the lower cubital nerves <term>ulnar nerves</term>, are guided at the elbow through a sort of protected passage between the condyles <term>rounded projections at the end of a bone</term>, or rather under the inner bony bumps <term>epicondyles</term> of the bone that makes up the *upper arm**. Through the hollow space between the back of these two heads—specifically under the back of the knee <term>the ham</term>, between the hamstrings, and within the recessed curve formed by the bumps on each side—pass the major vessels and nerves that lead to the leg†. To put it simply, they travel through a protected pass, like a valley between rocks. Who guided these vessels along such a well-defended and secure route? In the *shoulder* joint, on the rim of the socket <term>the cup</term> that holds the head of the arm bone, there is a notch covered at the top by a ligament. Through this protected opening, the blood vessels pass safely to their destination in the arm, instead of being forced to climb over the sharp edge of the socket‡.

III. In every joint, the ends of the bones that move against one another are tipped with *cartilage* <term>gristle</term>. In a ball-and-socket joint, the socket is lined and the ball is capped with it. The smooth surface and the elastic, durable <term>unfriable</term> nature of cartilage make it the most suitable of all materials for this specific location and purpose. ->IN THE HUMAN FRAME.<-

It has been argued that cartilage is actually only developing <term>nascent</term> or incomplete bone. This theory suggests that the bone in these areas is kept soft and incomplete because constant movement and friction prevent a more complete and rigid hardening <term>ossification</term> from occurring. If this were true, what we describe as a purposeful design advantage would actually just be an unavoidable physical result. I am far from convinced that this is a true account of the facts; furthermore, even if it were true, I do not believe it disproves the argument for design. To me, the way the ends of the bones are covered with cartilage looks more like plating them with a different metal, rather than the same metal being kept in a different state by the wear and tear to which it is exposed. In any case, we see a great specific benefit arising from a general biological rule. However, since this last point does not perfectly align with my specific argument, and because I do not wish to overstate its value, I thought it only fair to mention the opposing view.

IV. In some joints, most notably in the knees, there are loose cartilages <term>menisci</term> located between the bones and within the joint. This ensures that the ends of the bones, instead of rubbing directly against one another, move against these intermediate cartilages. Cheselden <note>William Cheselden (1688–1752), a famous English surgeon and anatomist.</note> observed\* that engineers use a similar design—a "loose ring" or washer—in machines where the friction in the joints is very high. Examples include the hinges of heavy gates or the area under the head of the main screw in large clamps <term>vices</term>. The cartilages we are discussing are shaped very much like these mechanical rings. This comparison also explains why we find them in the knees rather than in other joints. As we have seen, an engineer only resorts to this solution when there is heavy work to be done. Similarly, in the human body, the thigh—

# OF MECHANICAL ARRANGEMENT

The bone must achieve its motion at the knee while the entire weight of the body presses down upon it. Often, such as when we rise from a seat, it must even lift the body's full weight. According to Cheselden’s <note>William Cheselden (1688–1752), an influential English surgeon and anatomist.</note> account, it appears that the slipping and sliding of the loose cartilages <term>menisci</term>—though likely a small and subtle movement—assisted the motion of the end of the thigh bone. This movement was adapted to the specific shape <term>configuration</term> required for the tendons to operate effectively. This shape requires what he calls a "variable socket"—that is, a concavity whose curves change as the bones move into different angles.

V. We have now finished discussing the shape and arrangement of the joints. However, there is another exquisite feature common to all joints that is clearly adapted for their use. In my opinion, its purpose is beyond dispute: namely, the regular supply of a lubricant <term>mucilage</term> that is smoother and more slippery than oil itself. This fluid constantly softens and lubricates the parts that rub against one another, thereby reducing the effects of wear and tear <term>attrition</term> to the greatest possible degree. To ensure the continual production <term>secretion</term> of this important lubricant <term>liniment</term> and to supply the joint cavities with it, glands are positioned near every joint. The discharge tubes <term>excretory ducts</term> of these glands, dripping with their soothing contents, hang loose like fringes within the cavity of the joints. 

A recent improvement in what are called friction wheels involves a mechanism designed to regularly drop oil into a box that encloses the axle, the hub <term>nave</term>, and the balls upon which the hub rotates. This could be said, in a way, to represent the same mechanical solution found in the animal joint. However, the joint has one clear superiority: in the body, the oil is not only applied, but actually *manufactured*.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the mechanics of joints, moving from the role of lubrication to the long-term durability of the skeletal system and the design of fixed connections between bones.</meta>

->IN THE HUMAN FRAME.<-

In considering the joints, there is perhaps nothing that should move us to more gratitude than reflecting on *how well they wear*. A limb may swing upon its hinge or move in its socket many hundreds of times an hour for sixty years straight without any loss of agility. This is a remarkably long time for anything to last, especially for something that is as constantly used and exercised as the joints are. I attribute this durability partly to the measures taken to prevent wear and tear: first, the polished surfaces of the cartilage; and second, the healing lubrication of the fluid <term>synovial fluid</term>. It is also due to that astonishing property of living organisms known as assimilation <term>metabolic repair</term>, by which every part of the body—regardless of what it is made of—restores its substance and repairs its waste.

While I believe movable joints represent the most interesting aspect of bones, the way they join together even where no motion is intended or needed also shows signs of purposeful design and mechanical wisdom. The teeth, particularly the front ones, are essentially one bone fixed into another like a peg driven into a board. The seams <term>sutures</term> of the skull are like the edges of two saws pressed together in such a way that the teeth of one enter the gaps of the other. Sometimes we find one bone overlapping another, with the edges planed down; at other times, a thin plate <term>lamella</term> of one bone is received into a narrow groove in another. In all these variations, we seem to discover the same goal: namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, a firm connection without any clumsiness at the seam.

# CHAPTER IX.

## OF THE MUSCLES.

Muscles and their tendons are the instruments by which animal motion is performed. Our task will be to point out instances and characteristics showing that the arrangement of these muscles is as strictly mechanical as the wires and strings of a puppet.

I. We can observe what appears to be a universal rule: an exact relationship exists between a joint and the muscles that move it. Whatever motion a joint is capable of performing due to its mechanical construction, the attached muscles are positioned to produce that specific motion. For example, at the knee and elbow, there are hinge joints capable of moving only in a single plane. The "leaders"—that is, the muscular tendons—are placed parallel to the bone so that, through the contraction or relaxation of their muscles, they produce that specific motion and no other. Even if these joints were capable of a wider range of motion, there are no muscles positioned to produce it. In contrast, at the shoulder and the hip, where the ball-and-socket joint's construction allows for a rotating or sweeping motion, the tendons are positioned and pull in such directions as to produce the full range of motion the joint allows. For instance, the <term>sartorius</term> or *tailor’s muscle* originates from the spine <note>specifically the anterior superior iliac spine of the pelvis</note>, runs diagonally across the thigh, and attaches to the inside of the main bone of the leg <term>tibia</term> a little below the knee; this enables us, by

As we have seen, there is a specific mechanism in the bones for the rotating motions of the head and hands. There is also a specific provision in the diagonal direction of the muscles belonging to them for putting this skeletal mechanism into action. Notice the coordination of their functions: the diagonal muscles would have been useless without the <term>articulation</term> <note>joint</note>, and the joint would have been useless without the diagonal muscles. However, it is worth noting regarding the *head*—though I believe it does not change the point—that its diagonal motions and tilts are often movements in a *diagonal* line produced by the combined action of muscles lying in straight directions. But whether the pull is single or combined, the joint is always designed to be capable of obeying the action of the muscles.

The diagonal muscles attached to the head are also positioned to steady the head as well as move it. The head of a newborn infant often needs to be supported with a headband <note>The original text uses "filleted up," referring to the practice of using a "fillet" or band to support an infant's weak neck muscles.</note>. After death, the head drops and rolls in every direction. Thus, it is by the equilibrium of the muscles—through a significant and equal muscular force in constant exertion—that the head maintains its upright posture. Here, the muscles compensate for what would otherwise be a significant flaw in the joint; for while the joint in the neck is excellently suited for moving the head, it is insufficient for supporting its weight. It is not only through the remarkable structure of the bones that a person turns their head, but also by virtue of a precisely balanced muscular power that they are able to hold it up at all.

II. A muscle acts only by contraction. Its force is exerted in no other way. When the exertion ceases, it relaxes itself; that is, it returns by relaxation to its former state, but without active energy. This is the nature of the muscular fiber; and this being the case, it is evident that the reciprocal *energetic* motion of the limbs—by which we mean motion *with force* in opposite directions—can only be produced by the use of opposite or "antagonist" muscles; that is, of flexors and extensors corresponding to each other. 

For instance, the biceps and <term>internal brachial muscle</term> <note>original: *brachiæus internus*</note> placed in the front part of the upper arm bend the elbow by their contraction, and they do so with whatever degree of force the case requires or their strength admits. The relaxation of these muscles after the effort would merely let the forearm drop down. For the *return stroke*, therefore—so that the arm may not only bend at the elbow but also extend and straighten itself with force—other muscles, specifically the <term>long and short external brachial muscles</term> <note>original: *longus* and *brevis brachiæus externus*</note> and the <term>anconeus muscle</term> <note>original: *anconæus*</note> placed on the back part of the arm, use their contractile pull to fetch back the forearm into a straight line with the <term>upper arm</term> <note>The original uses "cubit," which historically referred to the forearm or the ulna.</note> with no less force than that with which it was bent out of it. 

The same principle applies to all the limbs and to every movable part of the body. A finger is not bent and straightened without the contraction of two muscles taking place. It is evident, therefore, that animal functions require that particular arrangement of the muscles which we describe by the name "antagonist muscles." And they are accordingly arranged this way. Every muscle is provided with an adversary. They act like two sawyers in a

III. Another property of the muscles, which could only be the result of careful design, is that they are almost universally positioned so as not to obstruct or interfere with one another's action. I know of only one instance in which this impediment is felt: we cannot easily swallow while gaping. This, I understand, is because the muscles employed in the act of <term>deglutition</term> <note>The act of swallowing.</note> are so intertwined with the muscles of the lower jaw that while the latter are contracted, the former cannot act freely. The obstruction in this instance causes little inconvenience, but it shows what the effect would be where it does exist, and what loss of faculty there would be if it were more frequent. IV. The following situation often occurs with the muscles: their action is needed in a place where their presence would be inconvenient. In such cases, the main body of the muscle is placed in a more convenient position at a distance and is made to connect with the point of action by slender strings or wires. If the muscles that move the fingers had been placed in the palm or the back of the hand, they would have swollen that part to an awkward and clumsy thickness. The beauty and proportions of the hand would have been destroyed. They are, therefore, arranged in the arm, extending even up to the elbow. They act by long tendons, which are strapped down at the wrist and pass under the ligament to the fingers and the finger joints that they are each intended to move. In the same way, consider the muscles that move the toes and many of the foot joints: how gracefully are they arranged in the calf of the leg, instead of forming an unwieldy <term>tumefaction</term> <note>A localized swelling or enlargement.</note> in the foot itself? The same observation can be made about the muscle that draws the <term>nictitating membrane</term> <note>The "third eyelid" found in many animals, which moves horizontally across the eye for protection and moisture.</note> over the eye. Its function is at the front of the eye, but its body is tucked away in the back part of the eyeball, where it stays safe and does not obstruct anything.

V. The great mechanical variety in the shapes of the muscles can be explained like this: it appears to be a fixed law that a muscle contracts toward its center. Therefore, the mechanical challenge in each case is to modify the shape and adjust the position of the muscle so that it produces the required motion in accordance with this law. This can only be achieved by giving different muscles a variety of shapes suited to their specific functions and their location relative to the task they must perform. For this reason,

We find them in a wide variety of forms and positions: sometimes with double or triple tendons, and sometimes with none at all; sometimes one tendon serves several muscles, while at other times one muscle serves several tendons. The shape of the organ allows for infinite variety, while the fundamental property of the muscle—the law and direction of its contraction—remains the same and is simple. In this regard, the muscular system perfectly resembles our own works of art. An artist does not change the inherent quality of his materials or their natural laws of action. He accepts them as they are. His skill and ingenuity are used to turn these materials to his advantage by giving the parts of his machine a shape and relationship where these unchangeable properties can produce the intended results.

I. The variety, speed, and precision of muscular motion are, in my opinion, most remarkable in the *tongue*. It is worth anyone's time to observe the agility of their tongue—the wonderful readiness with which it changes position and its perfect accuracy. Every syllable of spoken sound requires a specific movement of the tongue and the surrounding parts. The arrangement and shape of the mouth for every letter and word is unique. If one pays close attention, these shapes are actually visible. Indeed, observant people have used this fact to teach the deaf how to speak and how to understand others by <term>reading lips</term> <note>The text refers to the early history of lip-reading and speech training for the deaf.</note>. In any individual, once their habit of speaking is formed, only one specific position of the mouth and tongue will correctly produce a particular sound. How instantly these positions are taken up and dropped! How numerous the combinations, how varied, and yet how error-free! We do not admire random or <term>bizarre</term> <note>Original: "antic," meaning grotesque or strange.</note> variety; rather, we admire variety that follows a rule, achieves a goal, and matches the needs of infinitely diverse situations. The anatomy of the tongue corresponds with these observations about its activity. The muscles of the tongue are so numerous and so intertwined with one another that they cannot be fully traced even by the most precise dissection. Nevertheless—and this is a great perfection of the organ—neither the number, the complexity, nor what might seem to be the entanglement of its fibers in any way hinders its motion or makes the control or success of its efforts uncertain.

I now ask the reader’s permission to step a little off-track to consider *the parts of the mouth* in some of their other properties. It has been said, and by an eminent physiologist, that whenever nature attempts to achieve two or more purposes with a single instrument, she performs both or all of them imperfectly. Is this true of the tongue when regarded as an instrument of speech and of taste? Or when regarded as an instrument of speech, taste, and <term>deglutition</term> <note>The act or process of swallowing.</note>? Quite the opposite: the vast majority of people—nine hundred and ninety-nine out of a thousand—use this one organ to talk, taste, and swallow very well. 

In fact, the constant warmth and moisture of the tongue, its thin skin, and the <term>papillæ</term> <note>Small protrusions on the surface of the tongue that contain taste buds.</note> on its surface qualify this organ for the task of tasting just as much as its complex web of fibers enables the rapid movements necessary for speech. The cavity of the mouth contains more distinct functions and parts performing separate roles than I believe can be found so close together—or within the same space—in any other part of the body. These include: teeth of different shapes, first for cutting and secondly for grinding; muscles expertly arranged to perform the complex movement of the lower jaw—partly side-to-side and partly vertical—by which the "mill" is operated; fountains of saliva springing up in different parts of the cavity to moisten the food while <term>mastication</term> <note>The act of chewing.</note> is occurring; and glands to supply those fountains. 

There is also a muscular constriction of a very peculiar kind at the back of the cavity, designed to guide the prepared <term>aliment</term> <note>Food or nourishment.</note> into the passage leading to the stomach and, in many cases, to carry it along that passage. Although we might imagine this movement is caused simply by the weight of the food itself, that is actually not the case, even in the upright posture of the human neck. It is most evidently not the case with <term>quadrupeds</term> <note>Four-legged animals.</note>—a horse, for instance—in which the food is thrust upward by muscular strength while the animal is grazing, instead of descending on its own.

In the meantime, and within the same cavity, an entirely different process is taking place: that of respiration and speech. In addition, therefore, to everything already mentioned, we have a passage opened from this cavity to the lungs for the admission of air, to the exclusion of every other substance. We have muscles—some in the <term>larynx</term> <note>The voice box; the upper part of the windpipe.</note> and countless others in the tongue—for the purpose of modulating that air as it passes, with a variety, range, and precision that no musical instrument is capable of matching. The mouth, with all these purposes to serve, is a single cavity; it is one machine, with its parts neither crowded nor confused, and each unhindered by the rest—or at least free enough to achieve the intended goal. If we cannot eat and sing at the same moment, we can eat one moment and sing the next, with breathing proceeding freely all the while.

There is one case, however, of this dual office—and one of the most immediate necessity—which the mouth alone could not perform: that is, carrying on the two actions of sucking and breathing at the same time. Another route, therefore, is opened for the air, namely through the nose, which lets the breath pass back and forth while the lips, in the act of sucking, are necessarily shut tight against the body from which the <term>nutriment</term> <note>Nourishment or food; here referring to a mother's milk.</note> is drawn. This is a circumstance which has always appeared to me worthy of notice. The nose would have been necessary even if it had not been the organ of smelling. Making it the seat of a sense was adding a new use to a part already required; it was taking a wise advantage of a prior and fundamental biological necessity.

### III.
Regarding the subject of muscles, we may also observe that many of our most important actions are achieved through the combined help of different muscles. Frequently, a diagonal motion is produced by the contraction of tendons pulling in the directions of the sides of a parallelogram. As has been already noticed, this is the case with some of the oblique <term>nutations</term> <note>nodding or tilting movements</note> of the head. Sometimes the number of cooperating muscles is very large. <note>Bernard Nieuwentyt (1654–1718) was a Dutch philosopher and mathematician known for his work on natural theology.</note> Dr. Nieuwentyt, in the *Leipsic Transactions* <note>The *Acta Eruditorum*, the first scientific journal of the German-speaking lands, published in Leipzig.</note>, counts a hundred muscles that are employed every time we breathe. Yet, we inhale or exhale without reflecting on the immense work being performed, the vast array of instruments prepared for this service, or how many parts contribute to the effect. Easy breathing is a blessing of every moment; yet, of all others, it is the one we possess with the least awareness. Only a man suffering from asthma truly knows how to value it.

They are like microscopic hairs and must be magnified to be seen; yet, they are real, effective muscles. Not only that, but our most vital and precious faculties—sight and hearing—depend upon their health and action.

V. The muscles in the limbs operate with what is called a mechanical disadvantage. For example, the muscle at the shoulder that raises the arm is attached in nearly the same way a load is fixed to a <term>steelyard</term> <note>A portable balance scale consisting of a lever with unequal arms; a heavy load on the short arm is balanced by a light weight moved along the long arm.</note>. It is positioned within a few tenths of an inch from the center point upon which the steelyard turns. In this arrangement, we find that a very heavy weight is only just enough to counterbalance the force of a small lead weight placed on the long arm of the steelyard, perhaps fifteen or twenty inches away from the center on the opposite side. This is the "disadvantage" being described. It would certainly be an absolute disadvantage if the goal were to minimize the effort of muscular contraction. 

But observe how beneficial this design is for animal convenience. Engineering always aims for one of two purposes: either to move a great weight slowly through a small space, or to move a light weight rapidly through a wide range of motion. For the first purpose, a different type of lever and a different <term>collocation</term> <note>arrangement or placement</note> of the muscles might be better than what we have. But for the second purpose, the current structure is the correct one. 

As it happens, it is the second purpose, and not the first, that the needs of animal life primarily require. Regarding the human body, it is of much more importance to any person to be able to move their hand to their head with proper speed than it would be to have the power to lift a heavier load from the ground (perhaps two or three hundred pounds more than they can lift at present). This latter ability is a faculty that one might wish to possess on some extraordinary occasions, but the former is what a person needs and uses every hour or minute. In the same way, a farmer or a gardener will accomplish more work by being able to move his scythe or his rake—

We have offered our observations on the structure of muscles in general; we have also noted certain species of muscles; but there are also *single* muscles which show signs of mechanical design that are as appropriate as they are unique. From many examples of this kind, we select the following.

II. What design could be more mechanical than this: a slit in one tendon to allow another tendon to pass through it? This structure is found in the tendons that move the toes and fingers. In the foot, the "long tendon" (as it is called), which bends the first toe joint, passes *through* the short tendon that bends the second joint. This path gives the <term>tendon</term> <note>original: "sinew"</note> more freedom and a more effective range of motion than it would otherwise have been capable of achieving\*. I believe there is nothing in a silk or cotton mill—neither the belts, straps, nor ropes used to transfer motion from one part of a machine to another—that is more clearly mechanical or artificial than this *perforation*.

...and that circumstance is the tendons, which pass from the leg to the foot, being bound down by a ligament at the ankle. The foot is placed at a considerable angle with the leg. It is obvious, therefore, that flexible strings passing along the interior of the angle would, if left to themselves, snap away from it when stretched. The clear preventive measure is to tie them down. And this is, in fact, what is done. Across the instep, or rather just above it, the anatomist finds a strong ligament *under* which the tendons pass to the foot. The effect of the ligament as a bandage can be made evident to the senses; for if it is cut, the tendons spring up. The simplicity, yet the clarity of this contrivance, and its exact resemblance to established resources of engineering, place it among the most <margin>✓</margin>unquestionable manifestations of design with which we are acquainted.

<margin>✓</margin>There is also a further use to be made of this example, and that is that it precisely contradicts the opinion that the parts of animals may have all been formed by what is called *appetency*—that is, *endeavour* or effort, maintained and imperceptibly working its effect through an incalculable series of generations. We have here no such effort, but rather the reverse of it: a constant <term>resistance</term> <note>original: "renitency"</note> and reluctance. The effort is all in the other direction. The pressure of the ligament constrains the tendons; the tendons react against the pressure of the ligament. It is impossible that the ligament should ever have been generated by the exercise of the tendon, or in the course of that exercise, because the force of the tendon perpendicularly resists the fiber which confines it and is constantly trying, not to form, but to rupture and displace the threads of which the ligament is composed.

# OF THE MUSCLES.

Keill <note>James Keill (1673–1719), a Scottish physician and philosopher known for his work on anatomy</note> has counted four hundred and forty-six muscles in the human body that can be dissected and described; and he has assigned a use to every single one. This cannot be merely a product of the imagination.

Bishop Wilkins <note>John Wilkins (1614–1672), a founder of the Royal Society and Bishop of Chester</note> has observed from Galen <note>Aulius Cornelius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), an influential Greek physician and philosopher</note> that there are at least ten different qualifications to be considered in each particular muscle: namely, its proper shape, its exact size, its fulcrum, its point of action (assuming its shape is fixed), its placement with respect to its two ends (the upper and the lower), its location, the position of the whole muscle, and the entry into it of nerves, arteries, and veins. How are things that involve so many adjustments to be made—or, once made, how are they to be put together—without an underlying intelligence?

I have sometimes wondered why we are not struck by the mechanical design in animal bodies as readily and as strongly as we are struck, at first sight, by the mechanics of a watch or a mill. One reason for this difference may be that animal bodies are, for the most part, made of soft, flexible substances, such as muscles and membranes; whereas we have been accustomed to tracing mechanical design in sharp lines, in the configuration of hard materials, and in the molding, chiseling, and filing of articles such as metal or wood into specific shapes. There is, therefore, an element of habit in this case. However, it is sufficiently evident that there can be no valid reason for any distinction of this sort. Mechanical design may be displayed in one kind of substance just as well as in the other.

Although the few instances we have selected—even as they stand in our description—are perhaps nothing short of logical proofs of design, yet it must not be forgotten that, in every part of anatomy, des—

# CHAPTER X.

## OF THE VESSELS OF ANIMAL BODIES.

The circulation of the blood through the bodies of humans and quadrupeds, and the apparatus by which it is carried on, forms a system and demonstrates a design that is perhaps better understood than any other part of the animal frame. The lymphatic vessels or the nervous system may be more subtle and intricate; indeed, it is possible that their structure is even more ingenious than the <term>sanguiferous</term> <note>blood-carrying</note> system, but we do not know as much about them.

I take the utility of the blood's circulation as an acknowledged fact. One grand purpose is plainly answered by it: the distribution of nourishment, received through a single opening, to every part, every extremity, and every nook and corner of the body. What enters at the mouth finds its way to the fingertips. I think a more difficult mechanical problem could hardly be proposed than to discover a method of constantly repairing waste and supplying a fresh addition of substance to every part of a complicated machine at the same time.

This system presents itself from two perspectives: first, the arrangement of the blood vessels (that is, the laying of the pipes); and second, the construction of the engine at the center—the heart—for driving the blood through them.

I. The arrangement of the blood vessels, as far as it concerns the supply of the body, is like that of water

pipes in a city: namely, large main trunks branching off into smaller pipes (and these again into even narrower tubes) in every direction and toward every part where the fluid they carry might be needed. In this way, the water pipes that serve a town represent the vessels that carry blood from the heart. However, blood requires something that water does not: it must be carried back again to its source. For this task, a reverse system of vessels is provided. These unite at their ends with the ends of the first system and collect the divided and subdivided streamlets—first through <term>capillary ramifications</term> <note>fine, hair-like branching vessels</note> into larger branches, and then from these branches into trunks. This returns the blood to the source from which its motion began, almost exactly inverting the order in which it went out. All of this is clearly a mechanical design.

The body, therefore, contains two systems of blood vessels: arteries and veins. There are also two differences in the makeup of these systems, suited to the functions they must perform. Because blood travels from wider to narrower tubes as it goes out, and from narrower to wider tubes as it returns, the pressure and force against the walls of the blood vessels is clearly much greater in the first case than in the second. Accordingly, the arteries that carry the blood out are formed with much tougher and stronger walls than the veins that bring it back. That is one difference. The other is even more "artificial"—or, if I may put it this way, it indicates even more clearly the care and concern of the <term>artificer</term> <note>the Designer or Creator</note>. Since a wound or rupture would be more dangerous in the arteries—due to the greater force with which the blood is pushed through them—these vessels are protected from injury not only by their tex-

At other times, the arteries pass through canals formed within the very substance—even the very center—of the bone. All this care is extraordinary, yet no more than the importance of the situation requires. It has often been said of those who risk their lives in a ship that only an inch-thick board stands between them and death; but in the body itself, especially within the arterial system, there is in many places only a membrane, a skin, or a thread-like wall. For this reason, this system lies deep beneath the <term>integuments</term> <note>the outer layers of skin and tissue</note>. In contrast, the veins—where the damage that follows from injuring the walls is much less severe—generally lie above the arteries, closer to the surface and more exposed.

It may be further observed concerning the two systems taken together that, although the arterial system—with its trunk, branches, and small twigs—might be imagined to emerge or *grow* from the heart like a plant from its root or the fibers of a leaf from its stalk (which, even if it were so, would only be to explain one mechanical process by another), the <term>venous</term> <note>original: "venal"</note> or returning system can never be formed in this manner. II. The next thing to be considered is the engine that works this machinery, namely, the *heart*. For our purpose, it is unnecessary to determine the exact principle by which the heart operates. Whether it is irritation triggered by contact with the blood, by the flow of nervous fluid <note>A historical physiological concept; the 18th-century equivalent of nerve impulses</note>, or whatever else might cause its motion, it is something capable of producing reciprocal contraction and relaxation in a living muscular fiber. This is the power we have to work with, and the inquiry is how this power is applied in the case before us.

Located in the central part of the body is a hollow muscle covered with spiral fibers running in both directions, with the layers intersecting one another; in some animals, however, they appear to be semicircular rather than spiral. By the contraction of these fibers, the sides of the muscular cavities are necessarily squeezed together to force out any fluid they contain at that time. Through the relaxation of these same fibers, the cavities are dilated in turn and are, of course, prepared to receive any fluid that may be poured into them.

The great trunks—both of the arteries that carry out the blood and the veins that bring it back—are inserted into these cavities. This is a general description of the apparatus. The simplest idea of its action is that, with each contraction, a portion of blood is forced into the arteries as if by a syringe; and, with each dilation, an equal portion is received from the veins. This produces, with every pulse, a motion and change in the mass of blood equal to the amount that the cavity...

The speed with which these changes follow one another, and how this sequence is sufficient to maintain a stream or circulation throughout the entire system, can be understood by the following calculation, summarized from *Keill’s Anatomy*, page 117, 3rd edition:

> "Each ventricle contains at least one ounce of blood. The heart contracts four thousand times every hour; from which it follows that four thousand ounces, or three hundred and fifty pounds, of blood pass through the heart every hour. Since the total mass of blood is estimated to be about twenty-five pounds, a quantity of blood equal to the entire volume of blood passes through the heart fourteen times every hour, which is approximately once every four minutes."

Consider the scale of this process when we look at very large animals. The aorta of a whale has a larger diameter than the main pipe of the waterworks at London Bridge; the water roaring through that pipe is inferior in force and speed to the blood gushing from a whale’s heart. The communication of the air to the blood, upon which life depends, would—if the surface area were gathered and spread out—be equal to a surface of fifteen square feet in a human being. Now, in order to give the blood the benefit of this organization during its course (which is the part of the subject with which we are chiefly concerned), the following process takes place. As soon as the heart receives the blood from the veins of the body, and before it is sent out again into the arteries, the force of the heart’s contraction carries it—by means of a separate and additional artery—to the lungs. It is made to enter the vessels of the lungs, and after it has undergone the process, whatever it may be, of that organ <term>viscus: an internal organ</term>, it is brought back by a large vein once more to the heart. This is done so that the blood, once it is processed and prepared, can then be distributed anew throughout the entire system. This gives the heart a double office. The pulmonary circulation <term>the movement of blood between the heart and lungs</term> is a system within a system, and a single action of the heart is the source of both.

For this complicated function, four cavities become necessary, and four are accordingly provided. Two are called ventricles, which pump out the blood: namely, one into the lungs in the first instance, and the other into the main body of blood after it has returned from the lungs. The other two are called auricles <term>modernly referred to as atria</term>, which *receive* the blood from the veins: namely, one as it comes immediately from the body, and the other as that same blood returns a second time after its circulation through the lungs. Thus, there are two receiving cavities and two forcing cavities. The structure of the heart is designed specifically with the lungs in mind; without the lungs, one of each would have been sufficient. The movement of the blood within the heart itself happens in this way: the receiving cavities connect with the forcing cavities and, by their contraction, unload...

"The wisdom of the Creator," says Hamberger <note>original: "Hamburgher"; likely referring to Georg Erhard Hamberger, an 18th-century German physician</note>, "is seen in nothing more gloriously than in the heart." With every beat, it must overcome significant resistance, and it will continue this action for all that time without breaking down and without becoming tired.

...into it from the vein, which was the intended course, but back from the artery, through which it ought to be moving forward. The way to prevent a backward flow of the fluid in both these cases is to install valves. These, like floodgates, open a path for the stream in one direction and block the passage against it in the other. The heart, designed as it is, can no more function without valves than a pump can. In a pump, when the piston descends, the motion would simply push back down the water it had just drawn up if it were not for the blockage provided by the valve below. A similar result would ruin the action of the heart. Therefore, properly arranged valves—meaning they are positioned correctly to promote the necessary flow of blood—are essential to the design. *And valves arranged in this way are, accordingly, provided.*

A valve is placed in the communication between each auricle <note>modern term: atrium; the upper chamber of the heart</note> and its ventricle <note>the lower pumping chamber of the heart</note>. This ensures that when the ventricle contracts, no part of the blood flows back into the auricle; instead, the entire volume enters the opening of the artery as it should. A valve is also fixed at the opening of each of the great arteries that carry blood away from the heart. These leave the passage open as long as the blood moves forward in its proper course, but they close whenever the blood attempts to flow backward as a result of the ventricle relaxing.

There is some variety in the construction of these valves, though all the valves in the body operate on nearly the same principle and are intended for the same purpose. Generally, they consist of a thin membrane that lies flat against the side of the vessel, thereby allowing an open passage while the stream flows in one direction. However, if the fluid attempts to flow the other way, it gets behind the membrane and pushes it out from the side, blocking the passage of the blood. Where more than one membrane is used, the different membranes simply form a single

One purpose of the circulation of blood (likely among others) is to distribute nourishment to the different parts of the body. The branching of the blood vessels for that purpose is so minute and numerous, and they are spread so thickly over at least the <term>superficies</term> <gloss>outer surface</gloss> of the body, that it is proven by a single observation: we cannot prick the point of a pin into the flesh without drawing blood—that is, without hitting a blood vessel. We can even trace into every tooth, through a small hole in the root, an artery to feed the bone as well as a vein to return the excess blood from it; both of these, along with an accompanying nerve, form a thread only slightly thicker than a horsehair.

Therefore, once the nourishment taken in through the mouth has reached and mixed with the blood, every part of the body is in a position to be supplied by it. Secondly, we now have the food in the intestines converted into a pulp. Though it recently consisted of perhaps ten different dishes, it is now reduced to a nearly uniform substance and prepared to yield its essence. This essence is called <term>chyle</term>, which is a fluid that resembles milk more than any other liquid with which it can be compared. To strain this fluid from the digested food during its long progress through the body, countless thousands of <term>capillary tubes</term> (pipes as thin as hairs) open their mouths into every part of the intestinal cavity. These tubes, which are so fine and slender that they are invisible unless filled with chyle, soon join together into larger branches. 

The pipes formed by this union end in glands. From these glands, other pipes with even larger diameters emerge, carrying the chyle from all parts into a common reservoir or *receptacle* <note>Known in modern anatomy as the cisterna chyli</note>. This receptacle is a bag large enough to hold about two tablespoons. From this vessel, a main pipe or duct proceeds, climbing up the back of the chest and then creeping along the <term>gullet</term> <gloss>esophagus</gloss> until it reaches the neck. Here it meets the "river" of the blood. At this point, it discharges itself into a large vein, which soon carries the chyle—now flowing along with the old blood—to the heart. This entire route can be shown to the eye; nothing is left to imagination or guesswork. 

Now, besides the usefulness of this entire structure for a clear and necessary purpose, we may notice two or three specific details that show not only its design but its perfection. Their pipes are so fine and slender that they are invisible to the naked eye unless they are filled, and their openings into the intestines are so small that they cannot be seen even with the best microscope.

2. It does not have the nature of saliva, nor does it have the nature of bile; it is distinct from both. Experiments conducted outside the body show that neither of these secretions acts upon food substances in the same way that gastric juice does.

3. Digestion is not *putrefaction* <note>the process of decay or rotting</note>; for it resists putrefaction most stubbornly. In fact, it not only halts its further progress but even reverses the state of putrid substances.

4. It is not a *fermentative process*; for the dissolving of food begins at the surface and proceeds toward the center, which is the opposite of the order in which fermentation acts and spreads.

5. It is not *digestion caused by heat*; for the cold stomach of a cod or sturgeon will dissolve the shells of crabs and lobsters, which are harder than the walls of the stomach containing them.

In short, animal digestion bears all the marks of being a power and a process that is completely *sui generis* <note>Latin: "of its own kind"; unique</note>; it is distinct from every other process, or at least from every chemical process known to us. The most wonderful thing about it is its specific adaptation—its subservience to the particular biological system of each animal. The gastric juice of an owl, falcon, or kite will not affect grain; it will not even finish digesting the softened and half-digested <term>pulse</term> <gloss>seeds or legumes</gloss> left in the crops of the sparrows that the bird devours. In poultry, the <term>trituration</term> <gloss>the act of grinding or crushing</gloss> performed by the gizzard and the action of the gastric juice work together in the process of digestion. The gastric juice will not dissolve grain while it is whole. Grains of barley enclosed in tubes or small spheres are not affected by it. But if that same grain is broken or ground by any means, the gastric juice immediately acts upon it. Here, then, a combination of mechanics and chemistry is required, and here we find it. It only produces a slight softening <gloss>maceration</gloss>, similar to what common water would do at a temperature slightly above the average temperature of the atmosphere. But once the plant has been broken into pieces by chewing, the gastric juice begins its work: first by softening the plant’s substance, then by breaking down its natural consistency, and finally by dissolving it so completely that even the toughest and most stringy parts, such as the veins <term>nerves</term> of the leaves, are consumed.

So far, we have followed the findings of our accurate and tireless Abbe <note>Lazzaro Spallanzani (1729–1799), a priest and biologist who proved that digestion is a chemical process rather than just mechanical grinding.</note>. In 1777, Dr. Stevens of Edinburgh discovered through experiments using perforated balls that the gastric juice of sheep and oxen quickly dissolved vegetables but had no effect on beef, mutton, or other animal tissues. Dr. Hunter <note>John Hunter (1728–1793), a pioneering Scottish surgeon and anatomist.</note> discovered a most curious property of this fluid: namely, that in the stomachs of animals that feed on flesh, as irresistibly as this fluid acts upon animal matter, it only operates on **dead** tissue. **Living** tissue suffers no injury from being in contact with it. Worms and insects are found alive in the stomachs of such animals. The lining of the human stomach, when in a healthy state, is unaffected by its presence; yet, in cases of sudden...

III. The gallbladder is a very remarkable design <term>contrivance</term>. It serves as a reservoir for a canal. It does not form the main channel itself—that is, the direct connection between the liver and the intestine, which is formed by another passage called the *hepatic duct*, continuing under the name of the *common bile duct*. Instead, it sits adjacent to this channel and connects to it through its own tube, the *cystic duct*. By this structure, it is able, as the situation requires, to add its contents to the flow of bile into the duodenum <term>the first part of the small intestine</term> and increase it. The position of the gallbladder is such that it uses this structure to the best advantage. In its natural position, it touches the outer surface of the stomach and is consequently compressed when that organ expands. The effect of this compression is to force an extra quantity of bile out of the bag and into the duodenum to meet the extra demand that the filling <term>repletion</term> of the stomach with food is about to create†. Cheselden <note>William Cheselden (1688–1752), an influential English surgeon and teacher of anatomy.</note> describes‡ the gallbladder as being positioned against the duodenum, making it liable to have its fluid pressed out by the passage of food <term>aliment</term> through that cavity; this likewise ensures that the bile is received into the intestine at the right time and in the proper amount.

The entrance of the bile duct into the duodenum <term>the first part of the small intestine</term> provides another observation. Whenever smaller tubes are inserted into larger tubes, or tubes into vessels and cavities—where these receiving tubes, vessels, or cavities are subject to muscular contraction—we always find a design to prevent backflow <term>regurgitation</term>. In some cases, valves are used; in other cases, including the one now before us, a different method is used, which may be described like this: The bile duct enters the duodenum at an angle <term>obliquely</term>. After it has pierced the first outer layer <term>coat</term>, it runs about two fingers' width *between the layers* before it opens into the cavity of the intestine†. The same design is used in another part where there is exactly the same need for it: namely, in the insertion of the ureters <term>tubes from the kidneys</term> into the bladder. These enter the bladder near its neck, running at an angle for about an inch between its layers‡. In both cases, it is quite evident that this structure has a necessary mechanical function to resist backflow. Any force that acts in a direction that would push the fluid back into the openings of the tubes must, at the same time, stretch the layers of the vessels and thereby compress that part of the tube which is tucked between them.

There is no room for claiming that the movement of these parts might have gradually formed the epiglottis—I do not mean in a single individual, but over a succession of generations. The species could not wait for the gradual formation or expansion of a part that was, from the very beginning, necessary for the life of the individual.

The larynx, or rather the entire windpipe taken together (for the larynx is only the upper part of the windpipe), besides its other uses, is also a musical instrument; that is to say, it is a mechanism expressly designed for the modulation of sound. A tuneful bird is a ventriloquist; the source of the song is in the breast.

While the primary use of the lungs in the body’s system has been called obscure, one use is nonetheless plain—though, in some sense, external to the internal system—and that is the formation of voice and speech in conjunction with the larynx. They are to animal utterance what the bellows are to a pipe organ.

The wisdom of the Creator is seen not in their separate actions but in their collective action—in their mutual support and dependence, and in their contributing together to one effect and one use. We must consider how many things we do understand, to say nothing of the many more, probably, which we do not.

First, a long, hard, strong cylinder <note>the humerus, or upper arm bone</note> is required to give the arm its firmness and tension; but because it is rigid and, in its substance, inflexible, it can only move by using joints. Secondly, therefore, there are joints for this purpose: one at the shoulder to raise the arm, and another at the elbow to bend it. These joints are continually supplied with a soft lubricant <note>original: "mucilage"; referring to synovial fluid</note> to make the parts slide easily upon one another, and they are held together by strong braces <note>ligaments</note> to keep them in their proper position. Then, thirdly, there are strings and wires—that is, muscles and tendons—skillfully attached for the purpose of pulling the bones in the directions in which the joints allow them to move.

So far, we seem to understand the mechanism quite well; and in understanding this, we possess enough evidence for our conclusion. Nevertheless, we have so far only described a machine standing still: a dead organization, a mere apparatus. To put the system in a state of activity (to set it to work), a further provision is necessary: namely, a communication with the brain by means of nerves. We know this communication exists because we can see the connecting threads and can trace them to the brain. We also know its necessity because if the thread is cut, or if the communication is interrupted, the muscle becomes paralyzed. But beyond this we know little; the organization is too minute and subtle for our inspection.

To what has been listed as functioning in the single act of a man raising his hand to his head, we must also add everything that is necessary and all that contributes to the growth, nourishment, and sustenance of the limb.

# CHAPTER XI.

## OF THE ANIMAL STRUCTURE REGARDED AS A WHOLE.

When contemplating an animal body in its collective capacity, we cannot fail to notice how many instruments <term>instruments: biological organs or functional parts</term> are brought together, often within a very small space. In a canary bird, for instance—and in the single ounce of matter that composes its body (all of which seems to be fully utilized)—we have instruments for eating, for digesting, for nourishment, for breathing, for reproduction, for running, for flying, for seeing, for hearing, and for smelling. Each is appropriate to its task, and each is entirely different from all the rest.

The human frame—or indeed any animal frame—when considered as a mass or assemblage, exhibits three properties in its composition. These have long struck my mind as certain evidence, not only of design, but of a great deal of attention and accuracy in carrying out that design.

I. The first is the exact correspondence of the two sides of the same animal: the right hand matching the left, leg to leg, eye to eye, and one side of the face matching the other. This is done with a precision that, to imitate even moderately well, constitutes one of the great difficulties of sculpture <term>statuary: the art of making statues</term>. It requires the artist to pay constant attention to this property of his work, separate from every other detail.

It is one of the most difficult things possible to get a wig made evenly, yet how seldom is a *face* crooked? And what care is taken that it should not be so, the

The lower part of the face is composed in a similar way of six bones—three on each side, respectively corresponding—with the lower jaw in the center. In building an arch, could more be done to make the curve *true*—that is, to make the parts equidistant from the middle and identical in shape and position?

The exact resemblance between the *eyes* is a property of animal bodies that should be greatly admired, especially when considering how complex the structure of this organ is. One must consider how varied and delicate the shades of color are in the iris, how differently the eye may be mounted in its socket to affect its appearance, and how differently eyes are actually set in different heads. Out of ten thousand eyes, I do not know if it would be possible to match any single one except with its own fellow, or to organize them into suitable pairs by any selection other than the natural one that already exists.

This regularity of the animal structure is made even more remarkable by the following three considerations. First, the limbs, when taken individually, do not have this correlation of parts; in fact, they have the opposite. A knife drawn down the spine <term>chine: the backbone or spine of an animal</term> cuts the human body into two parts that are externally equal and alike. However, you cannot draw a straight line that will divide a hand, a foot, a leg, a thigh, a cheek, an eye, or an ear into two equal and identical parts. Those parts placed upon the middle or partition line of the body, or which cross over that line—such as the nose, the tongue, and the lips—may be divided this way, or, more accurately speaking, are double organs; but other parts cannot be. 2. The next point to be remarked is that while the cavities of the body are shaped so as to exhibit, externally, an exact correspondence between opposite sides, the contents of these cavities have no such symmetry. A line drawn down the middle of the chest divides the thorax <term>the chest cavity</term> into two exactly similar sides, yet these two sides enclose very different contents. The heart lies on the left side, and a lobe of the lungs on the right; they balance each other in neither size nor shape. The same is true of the abdomen. The liver lies on the right side without any similar internal organ <term>viscus: an internal organ of the body, especially one in the chest or abdomen</term> across from it on the left. The spleen is indeed situated across from the liver, but it matches the liver in neither bulk nor form. There is no equality of weight or balance <term>equipollency: equality in force, power, or weight</term> between them. The stomach is a vessel that is both irregular in its shape and slanted in its position. The folds and coils of the intestines do not show a matching symmetry of sides. The heart is pumping at the center at the rate of eighty strokes per minute: one set of pipes <term>arteries: blood vessels that carry oxygenated blood away from the heart</term> carries the stream away from it, while another set <term>veins: blood vessels that carry blood toward the heart</term> brings the fluid back to it again in its course. The lungs perform their elaborate office—namely, expanding and contracting their many thousand vesicles <term>vesicles: tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange occurs</term>—by a cycle that cannot cease for a single minute. The stomach exercises its powerful chemistry <term>chemistry: here referring to the digestive process of breaking down food</term>, and the bowels silently propel the changed food <term>aliment: food or nourishment</term>. As it proceeds, they collect from it and transmit to the blood a constant supply of prepared and assimilated nourishment. That blood pursues its course while the liver, the kidneys, the pancreas, the parotid <term>parotid: the largest salivary gland, located in front of the ear</term>, and many other known and identifiable glands draw off their proper secretions from it all the while. These several operations, along with others more subtle but less capable of being investigated, are going on within us at one and the same time. 

Think of this, and then observe how the body itself—the case which holds this machinery—is rolled, jolted, and tossed about, while the mechanism remains unharmed and with very little disturbance even to its most delicate motions. Observe a rope-dancer, a tumbler, or a monkey; consider the sudden inversions and contortions that the internal parts endure because of the postures into which their bodies are thrown. Or rather, observe the shocks that these parts receive, even in ordinary people, from falls and bruises or by abrupt jerks and twists, without noticeable damage, or with damage that is soon recovered. Observe this, and then reflect on how firmly every part must be secured, how carefully surrounded, and how well tied down and packed together.

This property of animal bodies has never, I think, been considered as a distinct topic, or as fully as it deserves. I may be allowed, therefore, in order to verify my observation concerning it, to set forth a short anatomical detail, though it obliges me to use...

...more technical language than I would wish to introduce into a work of this kind.

1. The heart (because such care is taken of this center of life) is placed between the two soft lobes of the lungs. It is tied to the mediastinum <term>mediastinum: the membrane-filled space in the chest between the lungs</term> and to the pericardium <term>pericardium: the sac that surrounds the heart</term>. This pericardium is not only an exceedingly strong membrane itself, but it also adheres firmly to the fold of the mediastinum and, at its tip, to the middle tendon of the diaphragm. The heart is also held in its place by the large blood vessels that emerge from it*.

2. The lungs are tied to the sternum <term>sternum: the breastbone</term> by the mediastinum in the front, and to the vertebrae by the pleura <term>pleura: the membrane lining the chest cavity and covering the lungs</term> in the back. Indeed, the primary purpose of the mediastinum (which is a membrane that runs straight through the middle of the thorax <term>thorax: the chest cavity</term> from the breast to the back) seems to be to keep the contents of the chest in their proper places. In particular, it prevents one lobe of the lungs from interfering with another, and keeps the parts of the lungs from pressing against each other when we lie on our side†.

3. The liver is secured in the body by two ligaments. The first, which is large and strong, comes from the lining of the diaphragm and penetrates the tissue of the liver. The second is the umbilical vein, which, after birth, transforms into a ligament. The first, which is the primary support, keeps the liver in its position while the body is in an upright posture. The second prevents it from pressing against the diaphragm when we lie down. Working together, both ligaments suspend the liver when we lie on our backs so that it does not compress or block the ascending vena cava‡ <term>vena cava: the large vein returning blood from the lower body to the heart</term>, which performs the vital task of returning blood from the body to the heart.

4. The *bladder* is tied to the navel by the urachus <term>urachus: a fibrous cord connecting the bladder to the navel</term>, which is transformed into a ligament. In this way, what was a passage for urine in the fetus becomes, after birth, a support or anchor for the bladder. The peritoneum also prevents the internal organs from becoming entangled with or pressing irregularly upon the bladder; the kidneys and bladder are contained in a distinct fold of that membrane, effectively partitioning them off from the other contents of the abdomen.

5. The *kidneys* are nestled in a bed of fat.

6. The *pancreas*, or *sweetbread*, is firmly attached to the peritoneum, which is the great wrapping sheet that encloses all the organs contained in the lower abdomen*.

7. The *spleen* is also held in its place by an attachment to the peritoneum and diaphragm, and by a connection with the omentum†. In my opinion, it is possible that the spleen may be merely "stuffing"—a soft cushion to fill a vacancy or hollow which, if left unoccupied, would leave the internal package loose and unsteady. Even if we suppose it answers no other purpose than this, it must still be vascular <term>vascular: consisting of or containing vessels for blood or fluid</term> and allow for circulation through it in order to be kept alive as part of a living body.

8. The *omentum* (also called the *epiploon* <term>epiploon: from Greek, another term for the omentum</term> or *cawl*) is like an apron, tucked up or doubled back upon itself at its lowest part. The upper edge is tied to the bottom of the stomach, to the spleen (as has already been observed), and to part of the duodenum <term>duodenum: the first part of the small intestine</term>. After forming the fold, the tucked-back edge comes up behind the front flap and is tied to the colon and adjoining organs‡.

9. The *septa* <term>septa: partitions or walls dividing a cavity</term> of the brain probably prevent one part of that organ from pressing with too much weight upon another part. The extensions of the dura mater <term>dura mater: the tough outermost membrane surrounding the brain</term> divide the cavity of the skull, like so—

...many internal partition walls. By doing so, they confine each hemisphere and lobe of the brain to its assigned chamber, preventing them from resting upon or mixing with neighboring parts. The great skill and care involved in "packing" is to prevent one thing from damaging another. In the head, the chest, and the abdomen of an animal body, this is provided for—among other methods—by membranous partitions and wrappings which keep the parts separate.

The above may serve as a short account of the manner in which the principal viscera <term>viscera: the internal organs in the main cavities of the body, especially those in the abdomen</term> are held in their places. However, in my opinion, by far the most curious provision for this purpose—and the one where such a provision was most needed—is found in the guts. It is quite evident that a long, narrow tube (in humans, about five times the length of the body) laid in side-to-side folds, winding in slanted and circuitous directions, and composed of a soft and flexible substance, would be constantly displaced by the various sudden and abrupt movements of the body if there were no extraordinary precautions for its safety. I would expect that, if it were not bruised or wounded by every fall, leap, or twist, it would at least become entangled or knotted within itself. At the very least, it would be shifted and shaken out of the order in which it is arranged—an order that must be preserved to carry out the important functions it performs in the animal economy <term>animal economy: the system of physical and chemical processes by which a living animal is maintained</term>. 

Let us see, therefore, how a danger so serious, and yet so natural to the length, narrowness, and tubular form of the part, is guarded against. The solution is admirable, and it is this: the intestinal canal, throughout its entire length, is attached to the edge of a broad, fat membrane called the *mesentery*. It forms the border of this mesentery, being stitched and fastened...

...to it like the edging of a ruffle. Because it is four times as long as the mesentery itself, it is what a seamstress would call "gathered on" to it. This is the nature of the connection between the gut and the mesentery; being thus joined to—or rather, made a part of—the mesentery, it is folded and wrapped up together with it. The mesentery also not only keeps the intestinal canal in its proper place and position throughout all the turns and windings of its course, but it also supports the countless small vessels—the arteries, the veins, the lymph ducts, and, above all, the lacteals <term>lacteals: lymphatic vessels that absorb fats from the small intestine</term>—which lead from or to almost every point of its linings and cavity. This membrane, which appears to be the great support and security of the digestive system, is itself strongly tied to the first three vertebrae of the lower back*.

III. A third general property of animal forms is *beauty*. I do not mean relative beauty, or the superiority of one individual over another of the same species, or of one species compared with another; rather, I mean the general provision made in the body of almost every animal to adapt its appearance to the perception of the animals with which it interacts. In our own species, for example, only consider what parts and materials make up even the most beautiful body. No further observation will be necessary to show how well these things are wrapped up so as to form a mass capable of symmetry in its proportions and beauty in its appearance. Consider how the bones are covered, the bowels concealed, and the roughness of the muscles smoothed...

and softened. A covering <term>integument: a natural outer covering or coat, such as skin</term> is drawn over the whole body, which converts the otherwise repulsive materials of a dissecting room into an object that is attractive to the eye, or at least one that can be looked upon with comfort and satisfaction. Much of this effect is due to the presence of the cellular or fatty membrane <term>adipose membrane: the layer of connective tissue and fat located just beneath the skin</term>, which lies immediately under the skin and serves as a kind of lining to it. This membrane is moist, soft, slippery, and compressible; it fills in the gaps between the muscles everywhere, thereby creating their rounded shape and smooth lines, as well as the evenness and polish of the entire surface.

All of this seems to be a strong indication of design—a design deliberately aimed at this purpose. Once it is granted that such a purpose existed for any of nature’s creations, we may, with a high degree of probability, attribute other details to the same intention. These include the tints of flowers, the feathers of birds, the fur of beasts, the bright scales of fish, the painted wings of butterflies and beetles, and the rich colors and spotted luster of many tribes of insects.

There are also parts of animals that are ornamental, where the features making them so do not serve any other known purpose. The *irises* <term>irides: the plural of iris, the colored part of the eye</term> of most animals are very beautiful, yet their beauty does not contribute at all to the perfection of vision. Nature could have used her brush nowhere else to such advantage, because no other part presents itself so conspicuously to an observer or gives such a great effect to the overall appearance.

In plants, especially in flowers, the principle of beauty plays an even more significant role in their makeup; it is even more obvious than in animals. Or, if this were not possible while maintaining the progress of plant life, why does it break into such a wide variety of colors? This is not a natural effect of age or the slowing of the sap’s rise. If it were, it would—like autumnal tints <note>original: "teints"</note>—produce a single color in a leaf, along with signs of fading and withering. It seems a weak explanation to call it a "disease of the plant," as some have done. Is it not more probable that this property, which seems independent of the plant's needs and utilities, was calculated for beauty and intended for display?

I know that an objection has been raised against this entire line of argument. This objection claims that there is no such thing as beauty at all. In other words, it suggests that whatever is useful and familiar naturally comes to be thought of as beautiful, and that things appear to be so only because they are associated with these qualities. Our idea of beauty is so easily modified by habit, fashion, the experience of benefit or pleasure, and the associations arising from that experience, that some have questioned whether beauty is entirely generated by these causes, or if it would have any real existence without them. 

However, it seems to be taking the conclusion too far to deny the existence of the principle itself—namely, a natural capacity for perceiving beauty—simply because of the influences or variations to which it is subject. We see that even the most widely acknowledged principles are liable to be affected in the same way. I would argue this instead: the question concerns objects of sight. Now, every other sense has its own distinction between what is agreeable and disagreeable. Some tastes offend the palate, while others gratify it.
