Pigs, when free to choose and in their natural state—that is, when not corrupted <note>original: "vitiated"</note> by habits forced upon them—eat and reject the same plants. Many insects that feed on particular plants would rather die than change to a different leaf. All of this looks like a natural inclination within the sense of taste itself toward specific flavors. Similarly, smells affect the nose with sensations that are either pleasurable or disgusting. Some sounds, or combinations of sound, delight the ear, while others torture it. Habit can do much in all these cases (and it is fortunate for us that it can, for it is this power which helps us accept many necessities), but does the distinction between the agreeable and the disagreeable have no foundation in the sense itself? What is true of the other senses is most probably true of the eye as well (the analogy is undeniable); namely, that it possesses an original nature <term>constitution</term> designed to receive pleasure from some impressions and pain from others.

I do not know, however, if the argument that cites beauty as a final cause <term>the ultimate purpose or reason for a thing's existence</term> depends on making this admission. We possess a sense of beauty, regardless of how we acquired it. It does, in fact, exist. Things are not neutral to this sense; not all objects suit it. Many things we see are pleasing to it, while many others are unpleasant. This is certainly not merely the effect of habit regarding a particular object, because the most pleasing objects are often the rarest, while many very common things remain offensive to us. If habit makes them tolerable, that is the most habit can achieve; they never actually become pleasant. Therefore, if this sense is acquired, it is a result—the product of numerous and complex interactions between external objects and our senses, and between the mind and its sensations. For this result to occur, there must be a certain compatibility <term>congruity</term> to allow any specific object to please us. We contend that this compatibility was intentionally considered when shaping the appearance of animal and vegetable bodies.

IV. The skin and covering of animals is the primary factor upon which their appearance depends. It is perhaps the part that is most decorated and free from impurities in all animals. But even if beauty or an agreeable appearance were entirely set aside, there is another purpose served by this <term>integument</term> (the natural outer covering or skin) and by the arrangement <note>original: "collocation"</note> of the body parts beneath it, which is of even greater importance: and that purpose is *concealment*. If it were possible to see the internal mechanism of our bodies through the skin, the sight would frighten us out of our wits. "Would we dare make a single movement," asks a lively French writer <note>Likely referring to Bernard le Bovier de Fontenelle, a popularizer of science in the 17th and 18th centuries.</note>, "or stir a step from where we are, if we *saw* our blood circulating, the tendons pulling, the lungs blowing, the <term>humours</term> (bodily fluids) filtering, and all the incomprehensible collection of fibers, tubes, pumps, valves, currents, and pivots that sustain an existence that is at once so frail and so over-confident?"

V. When considering animal bodies as physical masses, there is another property more curious than people generally realize: the faculty of *standing*. This is more remarkable in two-legged animals than in four-legged ones <note>original: "quadrupeds"</note>, and is most remarkable in man, who is the tallest and rests upon the smallest base. I believe there is more to this matter than we realize. A statue of a man, placed loosely upon its pedestal, would not be guaranteed to stay standing for even half an hour. You are forced to fix its feet to the block with bolts and solder; otherwise, the first vibration or the first gust of wind would surely throw it down. Yet this statue may perfectly represent all the mechanical proportions of a living model. Therefore, it is not merely the shape, or simply placing the center of gravity within the base, that is sufficient. Either the law of gravitation is suspended in favor of living substances, or something more is being done for them to enable them to maintain their posture. There is no reason whatever to doubt, but—

Therefore, this gift appears to me to consist of a faculty for constantly shifting the center of gravity through a set of actions that are obscure but quick-balancing, so as to keep the line of direction—the line drawn from that center to the ground—within its required limits.

Regarding these actions, it may be observed, first, that they partly constitute what we call strength. A dead body drops down. Therefore, the mere adjustment of weight and pressure, which may be the same the moment after death as the moment before, is not what supports the column of the body. Also, in cases of extreme weakness, the patient cannot stand upright. Secondly, these actions are only voluntary to a small degree. A person is seldom conscious of their voluntary powers in keeping themselves on their legs. A child learning to walk is the greatest <term>posture-master</term> (someone who masterfully controls their body's position) in the world; but this "art," if it can be called that, settles into habit. Soon, the child is able to balance themselves in a wide variety of positions without being aware of either caution or effort. 

Yet, there must still be a natural aptitude in the body's parts for habit to take hold of—a pre-existing capacity for movement that the animal is thus taught to use. The ease with which this skill is acquired is something to be admired. As has already been admitted, it is difficult to explain which parts are primarily used or how each performs its specific role. Perhaps the subtle movement of the bones of the feet plays a part in this effect. They are set in motion by every slip or <term>vacillation</term> (swaying or staggering) of the body and seem to help restore its balance. ...like the <term>last</term><note>A mechanical form shaped like a human foot, used by shoemakers.</note> of a shoe, is very remarkable. I also suspect that it would be difficult to stand firmly on stilts or wooden legs, even if their base exactly copied the shape and dimensions of the sole of the foot. The alternating arrangement of the joints—the knee joint bending backward and the hip joint forward—as well as the flexibility of the spine in every direction, especially in the lower back and neck, appear to be of great importance in maintaining the balance of the body. Regarding this last point, it is notable that the <term>vertebræ</term> (the individual bones of the spine) are so tightly restricted by ligaments that they allow no more sliding upon their bases than what is strictly necessary to absorb the shock that any violent motion might cause the body. A certain level of tension in the <term>sinews</term> (tendons and muscles) also seems essential for an upright posture; it is because of the loss of this tension that a dead or paralyzed body collapses. The entire system is a wonderful result of combined forces and highly complex operations.

We have said that this quality is most worthy of observation in the *human* body; but a *bird* resting upon its perch, or hopping upon a branch, provides an impressive example of the same faculty. A chicken runs as soon as it hatches from its egg; yet a chicken, when considered geometrically in relation to its center of gravity, its line of direction, and its balance, is a very irregularly shaped solid object. Is this ability, therefore, a natural gift or a learned skill? Might it not be said that nature has balanced the body upon its pivots with great attention?

I also notice in the same *bird* a piece of useful mechanics of this kind. When <term>trussing</term><note>The process of tying a bird's wings and legs before cooking.</note> a fowl, the cook finds that upon bending the legs and thighs up toward the body, the claws close automatically. VI. By viewing the human body as a physical mass, and considering the general structures that exist within it—as well as the specific parts related to those structures—we are led to observe what I call "interrupted analogies." The following are examples of what I mean by this term; I do not see how such crucial deviations could be explained by any possible hypothesis other than intentional design.

1. All the bones of the body are covered with a <term>periosteum</term><note>A dense layer of vascular connective tissue enveloping the bones except at the surfaces of the joints.</note>, except for the teeth. At the teeth, this covering ceases, and an ivory enamel—which saws and files can hardly scratch—takes its place. No one can doubt the usefulness and appropriateness of this difference, or that the "analogy" is thus "**interrupted**." The rule that governs the structure of the bones stops exactly where it should. If a membrane as exquisitely sensitive as the <term>periosteum</term> covered the teeth as it covers every other bone in the body, their regular use, necessary exposure, and irritation would have subjected the animal to constant pain. As common as that membrane is, it was not the type of <term>integument</term><note>A natural outer covering or coat.</note> that suited the teeth. What they required was a strong, hard, unfeeling, defensive coat—and exactly such a covering is given to them in the ivory enamel that adheres to their surface.

2. The <term>scarf-skin</term><note>The epidermis, or the outermost layer of the skin.</note>, which covers all the rest of the body, gives way at the ends of the fingers and toes to nails. A man has only to look at his hand to observe with what nicety and precision that covering, which extends over every other part, is...

## CHAPTER XII.

### COMPARATIVE ANATOMY.

Whenever we find a general plan being followed, yet with variations required by the specific needs of the subject to which it is applied, we have the strongest possible evidence of intelligence and design. This evidence is so strong that it completely excludes every other hypothesis. If the general plan resulted from some fixed necessity in the nature of things, how could it adapt itself to the various needs and uses it must serve under different circumstances and on different occasions?

Arkwright’s mill <note>Richard Arkwright (1732–1792) was an English inventor and entrepreneur whose water frame revolutionized the spinning of yarn during the Industrial Revolution.</note> was invented for the spinning of cotton. We see it used for the spinning of wool, flax, and hemp, with modifications to the original principle and variations in the same plan as the texture of those different materials made necessary. If it were possible to doubt that the machine was put together with design while we saw it in only one mode and one form, we could no longer refuse to agree once we observed it in its different applications. When we see the changes of structure, additions, and supplements that each specific use demands, we must admit the proposition that intelligence—strictly speaking (including foresight, consideration, and a focus on <term>utility</term><note>The state of being useful, profitable, or beneficial.</note>)—had been employed, both in the original...

Much of this reasoning is applicable to what has been called *Comparative Anatomy*. In their general <term>economy</term><note>The functional organization or internal management of a living organism.</note>, in the outlines of the plan, and in the construction as well as the functions of their principal parts, there exists a close resemblance between all large terrestrial animals. In all of them, life is sustained and the body nourished by nearly the same apparatus. The heart, the lungs, the stomach, the liver, and the kidneys are much alike in all. The same fluid (for no distinction in the nature of blood has been observed) circulates through their vessels, and nearly in the same order. Therefore, the same cause—whatever that cause was—has been involved in their origin and has governed the production of these different animal forms.

When we move on to smaller animals, or to those that live in a different element <note>Referring to aquatic animals living in water rather than on land.</note>, the resemblance becomes more distant and more obscure, yet the plan still follows us.

And what we can never praise enough—and which it is our current task to demonstrate—is that the plan is maintained through all its varieties and deviations by being adapted to special occasions and purposes.

I. The *covering* of different animals (though I do not know if I am correct in classifying this under their anatomy) is the first thing that presents itself to our observation. In truth, because of both its variety and its suitability to their various natures, it is as much to be admired as any part of their structure. We see bristles, hair, wool, furs, feathers, quills, prickles, and scales. Yet, despite this diversity of both material and form, we cannot swap one animal’s coat for another without clearly making it worse off. We should, however, take care to note that these coverings are, in many cases, armor as well...

Humans are the only animals that are naturally naked, and the only ones capable of clothing themselves. This is one of the characteristics that allows us to inhabit all climates and all seasons. We can adapt the warmth or lightness of our covering to the temperature of our surroundings. If humans had been born with a fleece on their backs, although they might have been kept comfortable by its warmth in northern latitudes, it would have overwhelmed them with its weight and heat as the species spread toward the equator.

However, what human skill achieves for us, nature has, in many instances, provided for those animals that are incapable of such skill. Their clothing changes automatically according to their needs. This is particularly the case with that large group of four-legged animals covered in *fur*. Every dealer in hare and rabbit skins knows how much the fur thickens as winter approaches. It appears to be part of the same biological constitution and the same design that wool, in hot countries, "degenerates" (as it is called), but in truth—most fortunately for the animal's comfort—it changes into hair. Conversely, in the dogs of the polar regions, that hair is turned into wool, or something very similar to it. To this we may add what naturalists have noted: bears, wolves, foxes, and hares—which do not enter the water—have much thicker fur on their backs than on their bellies. In contrast, the beaver has the thickest fur upon its belly, just as waterfowl have their densest feathers there. We understand the <term>final cause</term><note>The ultimate purpose or "why" behind a physical feature; in this context, the reason for the design (e.g., keeping a swimming animal's belly warm).</note> of all this, and we can find no other explanation for it.

The covering of *birds* is so remarkable it cannot escape even the most casual observation. Consider its lightness, its smoothness, and its warmth: the arrangement of the feathers all angled backward, the down surrounding their stems, the overlapping of their tips, and their different shapes in different parts of the body...

Now, the first thing an attentive observer will notice is how much stronger the feather’s beard shows itself to be when pressed in a direction perpendicular to its plane than when rubbed, either up or down, along the line of the stem. He will soon discover the structure that causes this difference: namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, that the laminae of which these beards are composed are flat and placed with their flat sides towa<unclear>r</unclear>ds each other. By this means, while they easily bend to approach each other—as anyone may perceive by drawing a finger ever so lightly upward—they are much harder to bend out of their plane. This is the direction in which they must encounter the impulse and pressure of the air, and in which their strength is needed and put to the test.

This is one particularity in the structure of a feather; a second is still more extraordinary. Whoever examines a feather cannot help but notice that the threads or laminae of which we have been speaking *unite* in their natural state. Their union is something more than the mere placement of loose surfaces next to each other; they are not parted apart without some degree of force. Nevertheless, there is no sticky <note>original: "glutinous"</note> cohesion between them. Therefore, by some mechanical means or other, they catch or clasp among themselves, thereby giving the beard or vane its closeness and compactness of texture. Nor is this all: when two laminae that have been separated by accident or force are brought together again, they immediately *reclasp*. The connection, whatever it was, is perfectly recovered, and the beard of the feather becomes as smooth and firm as if nothing had happened to it. If you draw your finger down the feather, which is against the grain, you break, pro- <note>The original text likely continues as "probably" or "producing a gap."</note>

# COMPARATIVE ANATOMY.

...probably, the junction of some of the neighboring threads; draw your finger up the feather, and you restore everything to its former state. This is no ordinary invention; and now for the mechanism by which it is achieved. The threads or <term>laminae</term> <note>thin, plate-like structures forming the vane of the feather</note> mentioned above are interlaced with one another. This interlacing is performed by a vast number of fibers or teeth, which the laminae extend *on* each side, and which hook and grapple together. A friend of mine counted fifty of these fibers in one-twentieth of an inch. These fibers are hooked, but curved in different ways. Those which extend from the thread on the side toward the tip of the feather are longer, more flexible, and bent downward. In contrast, those which extend from the side toward the base or quill end of the feather are shorter, firmer, and turn upward. 

The process that occurs is as follows: when two laminae are pressed together so that these long fibers are forced far enough over the short ones, *their* hooked parts fall into the cavity made by the hooks of the others. It is just like a latch fastened to a door entering the cavity of the catch fixed to the doorpost and, by hooking itself there, securing the door. This is exactly how one thread of a feather is fastened to another.

This wonderful structure of the feather, which is easy to see with a microscope, works perfectly for the purpose nature designed for it. That purpose was not only so the laminae might be united, but also so that when one thread or lamina has been separated from another by some external force, it might be reclasped with sufficient ease and speed*.

In the *ostrich*, this mechanism of hooks and fibers, of barbs and teeth, is missing; and we see the consequence of that lack. The filaments hang loose and separate from one another, forming only a kind of down. While this structure may make them suitable as the flowing ornaments of a lady’s head-dress, it can be considered an imperfection in the bird; this is because wings made of these feathers, while they may greatly help the bird run, do not allow for flight.

But in this current division of our subject, our concern with feathers is their role as the covering of the bird. In this regard, a unique circumstance occurs. In the small birds that stay with us through the winter, from the snipe on down, regardless of the feathers' external color, the Creator has universally given them a layer of *black* down next to their bodies. We know that black is the warmest color <note>Darker materials absorb and retain heat more effectively than light ones</note>; the purpose here is *to retain* the heat generated by the heart and the circulation of the blood. It is also remarkable that this is not found in larger birds, for which there is also a reason. Small birds are much more exposed to the cold than large ones, because they have a much larger surface area in proportion to their mass. If a turkey were divided into a number of wrens—assuming the shapes of the turkey and the wren were similar—the total surface area of all those wrens would exceed the surface area of the turkey. This would be in the same proportion as the length, breadth, or any <term>homologous line</term> <note>a corresponding line or measurement in similar shapes</note> of a turkey compared to that of a wren, which might be a ratio of ten to one. It was necessary, therefore, for small birds to be more warmly clothed than large ones, and this appears to be the method by which that need is met.

In that variety of forms, we see a more precise adaptation to their respective convenience than even that which is seen in the different structures of their *mouths*. Whether the purpose is simply the intake of food, the catching of prey, the picking up of seeds, the cropping of grass, the extraction of juices, the suction of liquids, the breaking and grinding of food, or the tasting of that food—along with the breathing of air and the making of sounds—all these various functions are assigned to this one part. In different species, these needs are provided for, as they are required, by the mouth's different physical makeup.

In the human species, because there are hands to bring the food to the mouth, the mouth is flat; because of this flatness, it is suited only for *receiving* food. In contrast, the projecting jaws, the wide gape <note>original: "rictus"</note>, and the pointed teeth of the dog and its relatives enable them to use their mouths to snatch and seize the objects of their pursuit. The full lips, the rough tongue, the ridged cartilaginous palate, and the broad cutting teeth of the ox, the deer, the horse, and the sheep qualify this group for grazing upon their pasture. They are capable of either gathering large mouthfuls at once where the grass is long (which is the case with the ox in particular) or biting close to the ground where it is short, which the horse and the sheep are able to do to a degree that one could hardly expect. The recessed lower jaw of a pig *works in the ground* after its protruding snout—acting like a prong or a plow—has cleared a path to the roots upon which it feeds. A design so perfectly suited to its purpose was not the gift of chance.

In birds, this organ takes on a new character—new both in its material and its form—but in both aspects, it is wonderfully adapted to the requirements and uses of a distinct way of life. Everything about the animal *mouth* is mechanical. The teeth of fish have their points turned backward, like the teeth of a wool or cotton card <note>a tool with wire teeth used to untangle and align fibers</note>. The teeth of lobsters work against one another like the blades of a pair of shears. In many insects, the mouth is transformed into a pump or sucker, fitted at the end sometimes with a drill-like tool <term>wimble</term> and sometimes with forceps. Through this dual design—namely, the tube and the sharp point—the insect first bores through the outer skin <term>integuments</term> of its prey and then extracts the juices. 

And, what is most extraordinary of all, one type of mouth can be changed into another as the situation requires. A caterpillar could not survive without teeth; yet in several species, the butterfly that develops from it could not use them. Therefore, the old teeth are shed along with the discarded skin <term>exuviæ</term> of the larva <term>grub</term>; a new and totally different mechanism takes their place in the adult fly. Amid these novelties of form, we sometimes forget that throughout the process, it remains the animal’s *mouth*. Whether it consists of lips, teeth, a bill, a beak, shears, or a pump, it is the same...

III. The *gullet* <term>esophagus</term> is connected to the mouth. In this part as well, comparative anatomy reveals structural differences adapted to the specific needs of each animal. In animals <term>brutes</term>, because the horizontal posture of their necks does little to help the passage of food <term>aliments</term>, the muscles of the gullet that perform this task are arranged in two tight spiral lines that cross each other. In humans, these fibers run only slightly diagonally from the top of the esophagus to the stomach; by a gentle contraction, they easily pass the food downward. In other words, for the more difficult swallowing <term>deglutition</term> required of animals—who must push their food *upward* rather than *downward*, and often through a longer neck—a proportionally more powerful muscular apparatus is provided. This system is more powerful not merely because of the physical strength of the fibers (which might be credited to constant exercise), but because of their arrangement <term>collocation</term>, which is a fixed characteristic that must have been part of the original design.

IV. The gullet leads to the *intestines*. Here again, when comparing four-footed animals <term>quadrupeds</term> with humans, we find specific differences despite a general similarity. The *valvulae conniventes* <note>Latin: "converging valves"</note>—also called semilunar valves—which are found in the human intestine, are absent in those of animals. These are folds or pleats in the innermost lining of the intestines, which serve to slow down the progress of food through the digestive <term>alimentary</term> canal. It is easy to understand why such a feature is much more necessary for a body that stands in an erect posture—where the weight of the food adds to the movement of the intestine—than in a four-footed animal, where the path of the food, from its...

# COMPARATIVE ANATOMY.

From its entrance to its exit, the intestine is nearly horizontal; however, it is impossible to assign any reason for this specific arrangement other than the "final cause" <term>the purposeful design intended by a creator</term>. Based purely on the physical movement of the organ, this horizontal structure would be more expected in a four-footed animal <term>quadruped</term> than in a human. In reality, in both cases, the structure must have been formed not by physical action, but in direct opposition to action and pressure. The resistance that would arise from pressure is greater in an upright torso than in any other posture. 

Therefore, that theory <note>Referring to the idea that bodily structures are formed purely by physical habit or pressure</note> is pointedly contradicted by the example before us. The structure is found exactly where its development—according to the method proposed by the theorist—would be the most difficult. Yet, (*observe*) it is found precisely where its effect is most useful.

The different lengths of the intestines in meat-eating <term>carnivorous</term> and plant-eating <term>herbivorous</term> animals have been noted on a previous occasion. The shortest, I believe, are those of certain birds of prey, in which the intestinal canal is little more than a straight passage from the mouth to the anus <term>vent</term>. The longest are found in the deer family. The intestines of a Canadian stag, four feet high, measured ninety-six feet*. The intestine of a sheep, when unraveled, measures thirty times the length of its body. Conversely, the intestine of a wild cat is only three times the length of its body. 

As a universal rule, when the substance an animal feeds upon is slow to digest <term>concoction</term> or yields its nutrients <term>chyle</term> with more difficulty, the passage is winding and slow. This ensures that enough time and space are allowed for the necessary chemical changes and absorption to occur. Where the food is quickly dissolved, or already partially processed <term>assimilated</term>, the body avoids an unnecessary—or perhaps even harmful—delay by providing a shorter and more direct route.

# COMPARATIVE ANATOMY.

V. In comparing the **bones** of different animals, we are struck by a **perfect suitability** in the bones of birds, which could only come from the wisdom of an intelligent and designing Creator. In the bones of an animal that must fly, the two required qualities are strength and lightness. In what ways, therefore, do the bones of birds (I am referring to the long, tubular bones) differ in these respects from the bones of four-footed animals <term>quadrupeds</term>? They differ in three properties: first, their cavities are much larger in proportion to the weight of the bone than in those of quadrupeds; second, these cavities are empty; and third, the outer shell is of a firmer texture than the substance of other bones. It is easy to observe these details even when picking the wing or leg of a chicken. Now, it is evident that if the weight remains the same, the diameter will be greater in a hollow bone than in a solid one; and, as every mathematician can <margin>V</margin> prove, with an increased diameter—**all other things being equal** <note>original: "*cæteris paribus*"</note>—the strength of the cylinder or its resistance to breaking is also increased. In short, a bone of the **same weight** would not have been as strong in any other form; yet, to have made it heavier would have hindered the animal's flight. Furthermore, this form could not be acquired through habit, nor could the bone become hollow and tubular through exercise. What **internal desire** <term>appetency</term> could hollow out a bone?

VI. The lungs of birds, when compared with the lungs of quadrupeds, also contain a specialized feature intended for this same purpose of lifting themselves into the air. Specifically, there is a connection (not found in other kinds of animals) between the air vessels of the lungs and the cavities of the body. Through the entry of air from one to the other—at the will of the animal, it would seem—its body can be occasionally puffed out, making its tendency to descend, or its **specific gravity** <term>density relative to the air</term>, lower. The bodies of birds are inflated from their lungs, which is not the case for any other animal bodies, and are thus rendered buoyant.

VII. All birds are *oviparous* <term>egg-laying</term>. This also carries out the process of development with the smallest possible increase in body weight. A heavy, pregnant uterus would have been a burdensome weight for a bird during flight. The advantage of reproducing by laying eggs is that, while the entire brood is eventually hatched together, the eggs are laid one at a time and at significant intervals. Ten, fifteen, or twenty young birds may be produced in a single clutch <term>cletch</term> or covey, yet the parent bird is never weighed down by the load of more than one full-grown egg at any given time.

VIII. A major subject for comparison among animals is their means of movement. These fall into three categories: feet, wings, and fins. I challenge anyone to say which of the three is best suited for its purpose, or whether the same perfect skill is not evident in all of them. The physical makeup of the environments in which the movement must occur is very different. The animal's actions must necessarily adapt to those conditions. The Creator, therefore—if we may speak in such terms—had to prepare for various situations and different difficulties; yet the goal is achieved no less successfully in one case than in the others. Furthermore, when comparing wings to the corresponding limbs of four-footed animals <term>quadrupeds</term>, the goal is achieved without abandoning the general design. The design is modified, not discarded. Strip a wing of its feathers, and it bears a clear resemblance to the front leg of a quadruped. The joints at the shoulder and the elbow <term>cubitus</term> are very similar; and, even more strikingly, in both cases the upper part of the limb consists of a single bone, while the lower part consists of two.

One thing is certain: if the flapping of wings in flight were simply the back-and-forth motion of the same surface area in opposite directions—whether straight up and down or along an angled path—the bird would lose as much height or momentum from one movement as she gained from the other. A skylark could never climb into the sky using such a motion; for while the downward stroke against the air with the underside of her wing would push her up, the upward stroke—when she raised her wing again—would push her back down.

A bird’s steering during flight is achieved partly by the wings but primarily by the tail. In this regard, we encounter a very remarkable circumstance. Birds with long legs have short tails; during flight, they pull their legs close to their bodies while stretching them backward as far as possible. In this position, the legs extend beyond the tail feathers and serve as a rudder, providing the steering that the short tail cannot.

From the wings of birds, it is a natural transition to the *fins* of fish. For both types of animals, these are the instruments of motion; however, there is a significant difference in the work they perform based on the following fact. Fish, unlike birds, possess nearly the same specific gravity <term>density relative to the fluid</term> as the element in which they move. Therefore, in the case of fish, there is little to no weight to support. What is required instead is simply enough thrust to move the body through a resistant medium, to maintain posture, or to support and restore the body's balance—which is always most unstable when there is no weight to anchor it. For these functions, the fins are as large as necessary, though much smaller than wings; their mechanical action, their placement, and the muscles that move them are all perfectly suited for their purpose. When the fish wants to move *backward*, a forward stroke with the pectoral fin effectively produces that motion. If the fish wants to *turn* in either direction, a single blow with the tail in the opposite direction sends it around at once. If the tail strikes both ways, the motion produced by this double stroke is *forward-moving*, enabling the fish to dart ahead with astonishing speed <note>Original: "velocity"</note>. The result is not only, in some cases, the most rapid, but in all cases the most flexible, easy, and graceful animal motion we know of. 

However, when the tail is cut off, the fish loses all power of movement and is abandoned to wherever the water pushes it. The rest of the fins, therefore, regarding movement, seem to be merely secondary to the tail. In their mechanical function, the anal fin may be considered the keel; the ventral fins, the out-riggers; and the pectoral fins <note>OCR text: "muscles"</note>, the oars. If there is any similarity between these parts of a boat and a fish, observe that it is not a resemblance of imitation, but the similarity that arises from applying the same mechanical solutions to the same purpose.

IX. The *five senses* are common to most large animals. We do not find much difference to note in their basic constitution, or at least not much that can be explained by physical mechanism.

# CHAPTER 13.

## UNIQUE BIOLOGICAL STRUCTURES.

I believe that all the examples I will collect under this title could, consistently with technical language, have been placed under the category of *Comparative Anatomy*. However, it seems to me improper how that term is currently used. In a way, it is absurd to call something "comparative anatomy" when there is nothing to "compare"—specifically, when a physical structure is found in one animal that has no equivalent in another. The examples I propose in this chapter are of this kind. The reader will see that although some of them are perhaps the strongest evidence found in any part of our subject, they are necessarily of an unconnected and miscellaneous nature. To arrange them in some sort of order, however, we will first note specific structures belonging to *quadrupeds* <term>four-legged animals</term>, birds, and fish as a whole, or to many species within those classes. The principle of the design is clear, and the application of that principle is equally clear. The purpose of the organ—to support and, at will, elevate the fish's body in the water—is proven by observation. Experiments have shown that when the bladder is burst, the fish remains at the bottom. Furthermore, flatfish like flounders, soles, and skates, which lack a swim bladder <term>historically called an air bladder</term>, rarely rise in the water, and can only do so with great effort. The way this purpose is achieved, and the suitability of the means to the end, are easy to understand.

The rising and sinking of a fish in water, so far as it is independent of the movement of its fins and tail, can only be regulated by the specific gravity <term>the density of an object compared to the water it displaces</term> of its body. When the bladder inside the fish's body is contracted—which the fish likely has the muscular power to do—the overall volume of the fish decreases along with it. Since the total weight remains the same but the volume is smaller, the specific gravity (the force that causes sinking) increases, and the fish descends. Conversely, when the muscles relax, the elasticity of the enclosed and compressed air restores the size of the bladder. The downward tendency becomes proportionally less than it was before, or is even reversed into an upward force. These are well-known properties of objects immersed in a fluid. The painted figures or small glass bubbles used in water jars <note>These are known as "Cartesian divers," a classic physics demonstration where pressure changes the buoyancy of a floating object.</note> are made to rise and fall by the same mechanism. A diving machine could be built to ascend and descend on this same principle: by placing an air vessel inside it that could contract to decrease, or expand to increase, the volume of the machine itself. This would make the machine either denser or lighter than the surrounding water. Suppose this were done;

Yet, though located in the mouth, it is built in such a way that, in its harmless and resting state, it does not interfere with the animal's regular task of eating food. It has also been observed that none of the non-venomous snakes—such as the black snake or the slow-worm <term>historically called the blind worm</term>—possess these fangs. ### II.

In being a feature shared by several different species, the previous example is similar to the one I shall mention next: the *pouch of the opossum*. This is a mechanical design in the truest sense of the word. The simplicity of this solution makes the design even more obvious than many others, though it is no less effective. A fold of skin under the animal's belly forms a pouch where the young litter are placed at birth. In this pouch, they have easy and constant access to the teats; they are carried by their mother <term>historically called the dam</term> from place to place; they are free to run in and out; and they find a refuge from surprise and danger. It is their cradle, their transport, and their *sanctuary*. 

Can the purpose of this structure be doubted? It is not merely a fold of skin, but a distinct organ equipped with its own bones and muscles. Two bones are placed in front of the pubic bone <note>original: "os pubis"</note> and are joined to that bone as their base. These support and provide an anchor for the muscles that open the pouch. There are opposing muscles <term>historically called antagonists</term> that work in the same way to close it. They perform this function so precisely that, in the living animal, the opening can hardly be seen unless the sides are forcibly pulled apart*. Is there any action in this part of the

### III.

As a specific feature, yet one belonging to more than one species, and also as something strictly mechanical, we may notice a detail in the structure of the *claws* of certain birds. The middle claw of the heron and cormorant is toothed and notched like a saw. These birds are expert fishers, and these notches help them hold onto their slippery prey. The purpose is obvious, but the structure is such that it cannot be explained by the animal’s own effort or the physical use of that part. Some other fishing birds have similar notches in their bills for the same purpose. The gannet, or Soland goose <term>Northern gannet</term>, has the sides of its bill irregularly jagged so that it can hold its prey more securely. In this case, as in the previous one, the structure cannot result from how the body part is used. The smooth skin and soft flesh of fish are less likely to create notches in a bird's bill than the hard materials eaten by many other species.

We now come to unique features in the strict sense—those limited to a single species of animal. Of these, I will select one from a quadruped <term>a four-legged animal</term> and one from a bird.

### I.

The *stomach of the camel* is well known for its ability to hold large amounts of water and to keep it unchanged for a long time. This trait makes it fit for living in the desert. Let us examine the internal organization that allows for such a rare and beneficial ability. A number of distinct sacs or bags (thirty of these have been counted in a dromedary) are found between the membranes of the second stomach. II. The *tongue of the woodpecker* is one of those unique features that nature presents us with when a specific purpose must be fulfilled. It is a specialized instrument for a specialized use; and what else but intentional design ever produces such things? The woodpecker lives mainly on insects lodged in the trunks of dead or decaying trees. To bore into the wood, it is equipped with a beak that is straight, hard, angled, and sharp. Once it has reached the insects' cells by using this drill, the tongue begins its work. This tongue is, first, of such a length that the bird can dart it out three or four inches beyond the beak, differing greatly from every other species of bird in this regard. Second, it is tipped with a stiff, sharp, bony thorn. Third—and what seems to me the most remarkable property of all—this tip is jagged on both sides, like the barb of an arrow or a fishhook. 

The description of the part reveals its use. Having exposed the insects' retreats with its beak, the bird launches this long tongue at them with incredibly fast motion, impaling them on the barbed needle at its tip, and thus draws its prey into its mouth. Nor does the animal use these upper teeth for fighting. They might therefore seem to be both unnecessary and a burden. However, observe the result: the animal hooks one of these curved upper teeth onto a tree branch and then allows its entire body to swing from it. This is its way of resting and ensuring its safety. It remains suspended by its tooth throughout the night, both comfortable in its posture and secure, being out of reach of the animals that hunt it for prey.

## CHAPTER XIV.

### PROSPECTIVE CONTRIVANCES.

I can hardly imagine a more distinguishing mark and, consequently, a more certain proof of design than *preparation*—that is, the providing of things beforehand which are not to be used until a considerable time later. This implies a contemplation of the future, which belongs only to intelligence.

The bodies of animals provide various examples of these prospective contrivances.

I. Human teeth provide an instance not only of prospective contrivance but also of the completion of that contrivance being intentionally suspended. They are formed within the gums and stop there. The fact is that their further growth to maturity would not only be useless to the newborn animal but would be extremely in its way. It is evident that the act of *sucking*, by which the infant is to be nourished for some time, will be performed with more ease for both the nurse and the infant while the inside of the mouth and the edges of the gums are smooth and soft, rather than if they were set with hard, pointed bones. By the time they are needed, the teeth are ready. They have been lodged within the gums for several months but are held back, as it were, in their sockets for as long as their further emergence would interfere with the purpose for which the mouth is then intended. Nature—namely, that intelligence which was employed in creation—looked beyond the first year of the infant’s life; yet, while she

Nature, while providing for functions that would become necessary after that period, was careful not to interfere with those that preceded them. What makes it more probable that this is the result of design is that the teeth are incomplete, while all other parts of the mouth are fully formed. The lips are fully formed, the tongue is fully formed; the cheeks, the jaws, the palate, the pharynx, and the larynx are all fully formed. The teeth alone are not. This is the case with the human mouth: the parts listed above are called into use from the beginning, whereas the teeth would only be obstacles and nuisances if they were present then. 

When a different order is necessary, a different order prevails. In the beetle larva <note>original: "worm of the beetle"</note>, as hatched from the egg, the teeth are the first things to reach development. The insect begins to gnaw as soon as it escapes from the shell, even though its other parts only gradually reach maturity.

What has been observed about the teeth is also true of the *horns* of animals, and for the same reason. The horn of a calf or lamb does not bud, or at least does not grow to any significant length, until the animal is capable of grazing in its pasture. This is because such a hard substance on the young animal's forehead would greatly interfere with the mother's teat during the act of nursing.

II. It is not very easy to imagine a more clearly forward-looking design than the *milk* of the female parent found in all mammals <term>viviparous: animals that give birth to live young</term>. The moment the young animal enters the world, its nourishment is ready for it. The details to be noted in this biological system are neither few nor insignificant. 

First, we have the nutritious quality of the fluid, which is unlike any other bodily secretion in this regard. In this, nature remains unsurpassed; neither cooking nor chemistry has been able to produce milk from grass. Second, we have the organ meant to receive and hold it. Third, we have the duct attached to it for secretion. And finally, we have the movement of the milk to the breast at the exact moment when it is needed. 

All these properties are present in the subject before us, and they are all indicators of intentional design. This last point is the strongest of all. If I were to guess beforehand, I would have predicted that when there was an extraordinary demand for nutrients in one part of the body, there would be the least likelihood of having an excess to supply another part. A female’s advanced pregnancy has no obvious or direct mechanical reason to fill the breasts with milk. From this perspective, the composition of many of their parts is, quite literally, prospective <term>prospective: designed for a future state or need</term>.

III. The eye is of no use at the time it is formed. It is an optical instrument made in a dark dungeon; constructed to refract light into a focal point and perfected for its purpose before a single ray of light has reached it. It is geometrically adapted to the properties and behavior of an element with which it currently has no contact. It is, however, about to enter into that contact, and this is exactly what proves intentional design. It is *providing for the future* in the truest sense of the phrase, for it is preparing for a future change: not for the current state of the animal, nor for any gradual progress in that same state, but for a completely new state resulting from the great and sudden change the animal undergoes at birth. 

Is it believable that the eye was formed—or, what amounts to the same thing, that the sequence of causes creating the eye was established—without considering this change? Was it done without a vision of that future condition where its structure, currently useless, will become vital? Was it done without considering the qualities of light, an element previously entirely excluded, but with which the eye would soon hold such an intimate relationship? Instead, they are suited to another element in another place.

## CHAPTER XV.

### RELATIONS.

When several different parts contribute to one effect—or, what is the same thing, when an effect is produced by the joint action of different instruments—the fitness of those parts or instruments to one another for the purpose of producing that effect through their united action is what I call *relation*. Wherever this is observed in the works of nature or of man, it appears to me to carry with it decisive evidence of understanding, intention, and art. 

In examining, for instance, the various parts of a *watch*—the spring, the barrel, the chain, the fusee <term>fusee: a cone-shaped pulley used in early watches to equalize the pull of the mainspring as it unwinds</term>, the balance wheel, and the wheels of various sizes, forms, and positions—what would capture the observer’s attention as the clearest evidence of a construction guided by thought, deliberation, and design? It is the suitability of these parts to one another: first, in the sequence and order in which they act; and, secondly, regarding the final effect produced. 

Thus, when relating the spring to the wheels, the observer sees in the spring the source that originates and sustains *their* motion. In the chain, he sees what transmits that motion to the fusee; in the fusee, he sees what communicates it to the wheels. If he looks back at the spring while considering the conical shape of the fusee, he sees the mechanism that corrects the inequality of the spring's force. When relating the wheels to one another, he notices, first, their teeth—which would have been useless or meaningless if there had been only one wheel, or if the wheels had

What struck his attention in these various parts of the watch, he might designate by the general name of “<term>relation</term>.” Observing that in every case where the origin and formation of an object can be proven by evidence, these relations are found only in things produced by art and design, he would rightly consider them characteristic of such creations.

This parallel between the digestive process and certain mechanical arts could be explored in even further detail. Spallanzani <note>Lazzaro Spallanzani (1729–1799), an Italian biologist and physiologist who made significant discoveries in digestion and animal reproduction.</note> has noted* a detailed resemblance between the stomachs of gallinaceous birds <note>Birds in the order Galliformes, such as chickens, turkeys, and pheasants.</note> and the structure of grain mills. While the two sides of the gizzard perform the function of the millstones, the <term>craw</term> or crop <note>A muscular pouch near the throat used for food storage.</note> takes the place of the hopper <note>A funnel-shaped container in a mill used to feed grain into the grinding mechanism.</note>. When our poultry are provided with plenty of food, they quickly fill their crop; however, it does not pass immediately from there into the gizzard. It always enters in very small quantities, in proportion to the progress of <term>trituration</term> <note>The process of grinding or pulverizing a solid into fine particles.</note>. This is much like a mill where a receiver is fixed above the two large stones used for grinding grain; although the grain may be poured into the receiver by the bushel, it allows the grain to trickle only in small amounts into the central hole of the upper millstone.

But we have not finished the history of digestion. There exists a general relationship between an animal's external organs, which it uses to obtain its food, and the internal systems it uses to digest it. Birds of prey, by their talons and beaks, are equipped to seize and devour many species of both other birds and four-legged animals. The constitution of the stomach corresponds exactly with the form of the limbs. The gastric juice of a bird of prey—such as an owl, a falcon, or a kite—acts upon animal tissue...

II. The relationship of the kidneys to the bladder, and of the ureters to both—that is <note>original: "i. e."</note>, the relationship between the organ that filters the fluid, the vessel that receives the filtered liquid, and the pipe laid from one to the other for the purpose of carrying it—is as obvious as the relationship between the various vessels used in a distillery and the pipes connecting them. Because the animal structure in this case is simple and the parts are easily separated, it provides an example of correlation that can be shown through dissection to anyone, or which, indeed, can be understood by anyone even without dissection. This coordination of instruments with one another proves that there was an intention behind their design.

III. The relationship of parts to one another stays with us throughout the entire biological system <note>original: "animal œconomy"</note>. Can any relationship be simpler, yet more convincing, than this: that the eyes are positioned to look in the direction in which the legs move and the hands work? It might have happened very differently if it had been left to chance. There were at least three out of four directions on the compass to have been wrong in. Any significant change in the position of the eye, or the shape of the joints, would have disrupted this alignment and destroyed the coordination between the senses and the limbs.

IV. But relationship is perhaps never so striking as when it exists, not between different parts of the same thing, but between separate things. The relationship between a lock and a key is more obvious than the relationship between different parts of the lock itself. A bow was designed for an arrow, and an arrow for a bow; the design is even more evident because they are separate tools.

Nor do the works of the Deity lack this clearest type of relationship. The sexes are obviously made for each other. They form the primary relationship of animated nature; it is universal, organic, and mechanical. V. The teats of animals that nurse their young bear a relationship to the mouth of the suckling offspring, particularly to the lips and tongue. Here also, as before, is a correspondence of parts, where these parts exist in different individuals.

These are *general* relationships—that is, the relationships of parts found either in all animals or in large classes and categories of animals. *Particular* relationships are those that exist between the specific configuration of one or more parts of certain animal species and the specific configuration of one or more other parts of the same animal. This type of relationship is perhaps the most striking, and includes examples such as the following:

I. In the *swan*, the webbed foot, the spoon-shaped bill, the long neck, the thick down, and the <term>graminivorous</term> <note>Grass-eating or plant-eating.</note> stomach all bear a relationship to one another. They all work together for one purpose: to meet the needs of a water bird that floats on the surface of shallow pools and seeks its food at the bottom. Start with any one of these specific structural features and observe how the others follow from it. The webbed foot equips the bird for swimming; the spoon-shaped bill enables it to graze. But how is an animal floating on the surface of a pond to graze at the bottom, except by the use of a long neck? Consequently, a long neck is given to it. Again, a warm-blooded animal that was to spend its life on the water required a defense against the coldness of that element. Such a defense is provided to the swan by the "muff" of thick down in which its body is wrapped. But all this external equipment would have been useless if the digestive system <note>original: "intestinal system"</note> had not been suited to the digestion of vegetable matter. I say suited...

II. This mutual relationship, which arises from various parts serving a common purpose, is also very noticeable in the anatomy of a mole. The animal’s short, strong legs; its <term>palmated</term> <note>Shaped like an open palm; webbed or spade-like.</note> feet armed with sharp claws; its pig-like nose, teeth, and velvet coat; its small external ears, keen sense of smell, and recessed, protected eyes—all these contribute to the utility or safety of its life underground. It is a specific purpose, specifically consulted in every detail. The shape of the feet defines the animal’s character. They are essentially shovels; they determine its activity to be that of rooting in the ground, and everything about its body agrees with this destination. The cylindrical figure of the mole, as well as its compact form—resulting from the <term>terseness</term> <note>In this context, the compact or shortened nature of the limbs.</note> of its limbs—proportionally lessens its labor; because, relative to its size, it requires the least possible amount of earth to be moved for its progress. It has nearly the same structure of the face and jaws as a pig and the same purpose for them. But what I have always most admired in the mole is its *eyes*. Since this animal occasionally visits the surface and needs, for its safety and guidance, to know when it does so or when it approaches it, a perception of light was necessary. I am not aware that the clarity of sight depends at all on the size of the organ. What is gained by the largeness or prominence of the eyeball is the width of the field of vision. Such a capability would be of no use to an animal that seeks its food in the dark. The mole does not need to look around; nor could a large, protruding eye have been easily protected from the irritations to which the animal’s life must constantly expose it. Indeed, how was the mole, working its way underground, to protect its eyes at all? 

In order to meet this difficulty, the eyes are made scarcely larger than the head of a <term>corking pin</term> <note>The largest size of pin used in the 18th century for heavy fabrics.</note>; and these minute globules are recessed so deep in the skull, and lie so sheltered within its velvet covering, that any contraction of what might be called the eyebrows not only closes the openings that lead to the eyes, but also provides a cushion, as it were, against any sharp or protruding substance that might press against them. Even in its ordinary state, this opening is like a pinhole in a piece of velvet, hardly allowing loose particles of earth to pass through.

Observe then, in this structure, what we call "relation." There is no natural connection between a small, recessed eye and a shovel-like, <term>palmated</term> <note>Shaped like an open palm; webbed or spade-like.</note> foot. Palmated feet could have been paired with bulging eyes;

The relationship is obvious, regardless of which of the related parts we consider first. In short: the mole's feet are made for digging; its neck, nose, eyes, ears, and skin are uniquely adapted to an underground life. This is what I call relation.

# CHAPTER 16.

## COMPENSATION.

COMPENSATION is a type of relation. It is a relation where the *deficiencies* of one part, or of one organ, are supplied by the structure of another part, or of another organ. For example:

1. The short, stiff neck of the *elephant* is compensated for by the length and flexibility of its *trunk* <note>original: "proboscis"</note>. The elephant could not have reached the ground without it. Even if we suppose that it might have fed upon the fruit, leaves, or branches of trees, how was it to drink? If it were asked, "Why is the elephant's neck so short?" the answer is that the weight of such a heavy head could not have been supported at the end of a longer lever <note>The author uses "lever" as a mechanical metaphor for the neck supporting the skull.</note>. Therefore, for a physical form that is necessary in some respects but inadequate for the animal's needs in others, a supplement is added. This supplement exactly makes up for the deficiency under which the animal labored.

If it were suggested that this trunk may have been produced over a long course of generations by the constant effort of the elephant to stretch out its nose (which is the general hypothesis recently used to attempt to explain the forms of the living world <note>Paley is likely critiquing early transformist or proto-evolutionary ideas, such as those later associated with Lamarck.</note>), I would ask: how was the animal to survive in the meantime? How would it subsist during the process, until this lengthening of the snout was completed? What was to become of the individual while the species was still perfecting itself?

<summary>Paley defines "compensation" as a design feature where one organ's limitation is balanced by another's specialized function, using the elephant's trunk as a primary example. He argues that such complex systems must be designed as a whole rather than developed gradually over time, as the animal could not survive the intermediate stages.</summary>

## COMPENSATION.

Our current task is simply to point out the relationship between this organ and the specific physical form of the animal to which it belongs. In this regard, everything corresponds. The necessity of the elephant’s <term>trunk</term> <note>original: "proboscis"</note> arises from the shortness of its neck; the shortness of the neck is made necessary by the weight of the head. If we were to examine the structure and anatomy of the trunk itself, we would see one of the most curious examples of animal mechanism. 

The arrangement of the rings and fibers serves several purposes: first, forming a long <term>cartilaginous</term> <note>made of cartilage; firm but flexible tissue</note> pipe; second, contracting and lengthening that pipe; and third, turning it in every direction at the animal's will. Additionally, there is a fleshy appendage at the end, about the length and thickness of a finger, which functions like a finger to pick up a straw from the ground. Together, these properties of the organ demonstrate not only design (which is proven by the utility it provides) but also supreme skill and, one might say, elaborate preparation in achieving that design.

II. The hook in the wing of a bat is strictly a mechanical and compensating mechanism. At the angle of its wing, there is a bent claw in the exact shape of a hook. The bat uses this to attach itself to the sides of rocks, caves, and buildings, gripping onto crevices, joints, cracks, and rough surfaces. It hooks itself by this claw, remains suspended by this grip, and takes flight from this position. These actions compensate for the weakness of its legs and feet. Without its hook, the bat would be the most helpless of all animals. It can neither run on its feet nor lift itself from the ground. These disabilities are made up for by the mechanism in its wing; and in placing a claw on

III. Birds of the *crane* kind are meant to live and seek their food in the water; yet, because they lack webbed feet, they are unable to swim. To make up for this deficiency, they are provided with long legs for wading, or long beaks for searching underwater—and usually both. This is an example of compensation. However, I believe the most important observation in this instance is how every part of nature is occupied by suitable inhabitants. Not only is the surface of deep water populated by many groups of birds that swim, but marshes and shallow pools are also home to nearly as many groups of birds that wade.

IV. The common parrot has, in the structure of its beak, both an inconvenience and a compensation for it. V. The *spider's web* is a *compensatory* contrivance. The spider feeds on flies but lacks wings to chase them. One might have thought this a case of great difficulty, yet it is provided for—and provided for by a resource that no clever strategy or effort of the animal could have produced, had not both its external and internal anatomy been specifically adapted for the task.

VI. In many species of insects, the eye is fixed; consequently, they lack the power of turning the pupil toward an object. This great defect is, however, perfectly *compensated* for by a mechanism we would not expect. The eye is a magnifying glass <note>original: "multiplying glass"</note> with a lens looking in every direction and capturing every object. By this means, although the eyeball remains stationary, the field of vision is as wide as that of other animals and is controlled on every side. When this lattice-work structure was first observed, the sheer number and tiny size of the surfaces must have added to the surprise of the discovery. Adams <note>George Adams (1720–1773), an English optician and writer on natural philosophy</note> tells us that fourteen hundred of these facets <term>reticulations</term> have been counted in the two eyes of a drone bee.

In other cases, the *compensation* is achieved by the number and position of the eyes themselves. The spider has eight eyes mounted upon different parts of the head: two in front, two on the top of the head, and two on each side. These eyes are motionless; but, by their placement, they are suited to capture every view that the needs or safety of the animal require it to take.

The *Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Sciences* from 1687 <note>Refers to the *Mémoires pour servir à l'histoire naturelle des animaux*, a landmark work in comparative anatomy by the French Academy</note> provide us with some curious details about the eye of a **chameleon** <term>camelion</term>. Instead of having two eyelids, it is covered by a single eyelid with a hole in it. This unique structure appears to be **compensatory** and corresponds to other unusual features in the animal’s shape. The neck of the chameleon is inflexible. To make up for this, the eye is so prominent that more than half of the eyeball protrudes from the head. Because of this extraordinary projection, the muscles can move the pupil in every direction, and it can be pointed toward every object. 

However, such an unusual exposure of the eyeball requires more than ordinary protection for its lubrication <term>lubricity</term> and defense, as well as a greater than usual supply of moisture. Yet, the movement of a standard eyelid would likely be hindered by the extreme curvature <term>convexity</term> of the organ. The hole in the lid solves this difficulty. It enables the animal to keep the main part of the eye's surface covered and preserved in a proper state of humidity without blocking out the light, and without needing to blink <term>nictitation</term> every moment—an action that would likely be more difficult for this animal than for others.

IX. But the works of the Deity <note>God</note> are recognized by their clever solutions <term>expedients</term>. Where we might expect to find total lack, or where we can see nothing but needs, some invention always arrives to provide for what is missing. A *snail*, lacking wings, feet, or silk, climbs the stalks of plants solely with the help of a sticky fluid <term>viscid humour</term> discharged from its skin. It clings to the stems, leaves, and fruits of plants as if using a sticking plaster. A *mussel* <term>muscle</term>, which might seem helpless against every wave that washes over it, has the unique power of spinning strong, fibrous threads <note>Known as byssus, these threads allow the mussel to anchor itself</note>. With these, it anchors its shell to rocks and timbers.

The lobster’s shell, being fitted to the limbs of the body as well as to the body itself, does not allow for either of the growth methods observed in other shells. Its hardness resists expansion, and its complexity makes it incapable of increasing its size by adding substance to its edges. How, then, was the lobster’s growth to be provided for? Was room to be made for it inside the old shell, or was it to be successively fitted with new ones? If a change of shell became necessary, how was the lobster to free himself from his present confinement? How was he to remove his breastplate <term>buckler</term> or draw his legs out of his "boots"? 

The process, which fishermen have observed taking place, is as follows: At certain seasons, the shell of the lobster grows soft; the animal swells its body; the seams open, and the claws burst at the joints. When the shell has thus become loose upon the body, the animal makes a second effort and, by a trembling, spasmodic motion, casts it off. In this state, the liberated but defenseless fish retreats into holes in the rocks. The released body now grows suddenly and rapidly. In about forty-eight hours, a new hardening of fluid <term>concretion of humour</term> on the surface—that is <note>original: "i. e."</note>, a new shell—is formed, adapted in every part to the increased dimensions of the animal. This wonderful transformation <term>mutation</term> is repeated every year.

If there are perceived defects without compensation, I suspect that they are defects only in appearance. For instance, the body of the *sloth* has often been criticized for the slowness of its motions, which has been attributed to a flaw in the formation of its limbs. But it ought to be observed that it is this very slowness that alone restrains the gluttony <term>voracity</term> of the animal. He fasts during his migration from one tree to another, and this fast may be necessary to relieve his overloaded blood vessels <term>over-charged vessels</term>, as well as to allow time for the digestion <term>concoction</term> of the mass of coarse...

## CHAPTER XVII.

### THE RELATION OF LIVING BODIES TO INANIMATE NATURE.

WE have already considered *relation* from different perspectives; however, it was the relation of parts to other parts—the parts of an animal to other parts of the same animal, or to another individual of the same species.

But the bodies of animals, in their structure <term>constitution</term> and properties, maintain a close and important relation to systems entirely outside of themselves; to inanimate substances, and to the specific qualities of these. For example <note>original: "e. g."</note>, *they maintain a strict relation to the elements by which they are surrounded*.

I. Can it be doubted whether the *wings* of birds bear a relation to air, and the *fins* of *fish* to water? They are instruments of motion, each suited to the properties of the environment <term>medium</term> in which the motion must occur, and these properties are different. Was this difference not considered when the instruments were built with different designs?

II. The structure of the animal ear relies for its use not simply on being surrounded by a fluid, but on the specific nature of that fluid. Not every fluid would work; its particles must repel one another; it must form an *elastic medium*. III. The organs of speech, voice, and respiration are no less indebted to the unique qualities of the fluid in which the animal lives <term>is immersed</term> for their successful operation than the ear is. They, like the ear, are therefore designed with the assumption that such a fluid—that is, a fluid with these specific properties—is always present. It does not change this relationship whether you claim the organ was made for the element (which seems the most natural way of looking at it) or that the element was prepared for the organ.

If this does not prove intentional design <term>appropriation</term>, I would like to know what would.

V. Throughout the universe, there is a wonderful *proportioning* of one thing to another. Take the earth as it is, and consider the correspondence between the powers of its inhabitants and the properties and condition of the soil on which they tread. Take the inhabitants as they are, and consider the substances which the earth yields for their use. They can scratch its surface, and its surface supplies all that they need. This is the extent <term>length</term> of their faculties; and such is the constitution of the globe, and their own nature, that this is sufficient for all their needs <term>occasions</term>.

When we move from the earth to the *sea*, from land to water, we experience a major change; however, a corresponding change in animal forms, functions, capacities, and needs follows us, so that a proper fit <term>correspondency</term> remains. The earth is naturally very different from the sea, and the sea from the earth; yet each suits its inhabitants just as perfectly as the other.

VII. The final relationship of this type that I will mention is that of *sleep* to *night*. This appears to me to be a relationship that was intentionally designed. Two points are obvious: first, that the animal body <term>frame</term> requires sleep; second, that night brings a silence and a stop to activity that allows sleep to occur without interruption and without loss of productive time. Animal life consists of action and slumber; nature has provided a season for each. An animal that did not need rest would live in constant daylight. An animal that is built for and enjoys action, but must have its strength restored by sleep, is fitted by its biological makeup <term>constitution</term> to the regular cycles of day and night. 

In the human species, for example, if the bustle, labor, and movement of life were sustained by the constant presence of light, sleep could not be enjoyed without being disturbed by noise. Furthermore, people would not willingly give up time for sleep because of their eager pursuit of private interests. It is fortunate, therefore, for this part of creation—meaning it fits the structure and needs of their bodies—that nature, by the very arrangement of her elements, has commanded and imposed a general break from their labor, occupations, and pursuits at regular intervals.

It is likely even more: a relationship to the entire solar system of which this globe is a part, and further still, to the vast collection of systems <term>congregation of systems</term> of which ours is only one.

# CHAPTER XVIII.

## INSTINCTS.

The order in which I place instincts immediately after relations may not seem very obvious. However, I consider them a type <term>species</term> of relation. They work together with an animal's physical structure <term>organization</term> to produce a combined effect; from this perspective, they are related to that physical structure. In many cases, they involve the interaction of one animal with another; when this happens, they become "relations" in a strictly literal sense.

An instinct is a natural inclination <term>propensity</term> that exists prior to experience and is independent of instruction. I argue that it is by instinct that the sexes of animals seek each other; that animals care for <term>cherish</term> their offspring; that a young four-legged animal <term>quadruped</term> is directed to its mother’s <term>dam's</term> nipple; that birds build their nests and sit <term>brood</term> with such patience upon their eggs; that insects which do not sit upon their eggs nevertheless lay <term>deposit</term> them in specific locations where the young, once hatched, will find their proper food; and that it is instinct which drives salmon and certain other fish out of the sea and into rivers for the purpose of laying their eggs <term>shedding their spawn</term> in fresh water.

From *this* list, we can select the incubation of eggs as an example. I have no doubt that a pair of sparrows hatched in an oven and kept separate from the rest of their species would still behave exactly like other sparrows in every task related to the production and preservation of their young <term>brood</term>. Assuming this is true, such behavior cannot be explained by any other—

In the sparrow species, when it is observed that the young brood can fly and fend for themselves, the parents abandon them forever. Although they may continue to live together, the parents pay them no more attention than they do to other birds in the same flock\*. I believe the same is true of all social <term>gregarious</term> four-legged animals <term>quadrupeds</term>.

In this part of the argument, the variety of resources, methods, and materials which animals of the same species are said to use under different circumstances and when provided with different supplies, does not contradict the doctrine of instincts. Since the propensity exists, it is likely enough that it may lead the animal to perform different actions according to different needs. This adaptation of resources may look like the result of skill and deliberation rather than instinct; however, the propensity itself remains instinctive.

I am aware of a theory which reduces instinct to mere sensation. Furthermore, the chain of intermediate effects is clearly laid out and planned with a view to that purpose. That is to say, design is as completely proven by these phenomena as it would be even if we supposed the actions began, or were carried on, by what some would call "true" instincts—that is, from desires directed toward a future goal, having no satisfaction other than achieving that goal.

Nor should we forget, in this context, how much the instinct *costs* the animal that feels it. An animal built for freedom submits to confinement during the very season when everything invites her to go outside. Furthermore, an animal that delights in and is built for motion—one whose movements are so easy and free that she is rarely at rest at other times—is fixed to her nest for many hours over many days, as securely as if her limbs were pinned down. For my part, I never see a bird in that situation without recognizing an invisible hand. This hand keeps the contented prisoner away from her fields and groves for a purpose that, as the results prove, is entirely worthy of the sacrifice—a purpose that is most important and beneficial.

This shows that the mating <term>conjugal</term> instinct is adapted with a focus on practical utility based on the specific needs of the offspring. In four-legged animals <term>quadrupeds</term>, the young animal draws its nourishment from the body of the mother <term>dam</term>. In the bird kingdom <term>feathered race</term>, however, the young bird is supplied with food brought in from the outside. To find and bring home enough food to meet the demands of a large brood requires the hard work of both parents. In this difference, we see a reason for the wandering <term>vagrant</term> instinct of the four-legged animal, and for the faithful love of the bird for its mate.
