# CHAPTER XIX.

## OF INSECTS.

We are not writing a complete system of natural history; therefore, we have not followed the specific classifications into which the subjects of that science are usually divided. Most of what we had to observe regarding different species of animals fit easily within the divisions that our line of argument led us to adopt. There remain, however, some remarks regarding the *insect* tribe that could not be properly introduced under any of those headings; we have, therefore, collected them into a chapter of their own.

The structure and the function of the parts of insects are less understood than those of four-legged animals <term>quadrupeds</term> and birds. This is not only because of their small size <term>minuteness</term> (though we can, to some extent, observe that smallness with magnifying glasses), but also because their behaviors and ways of life are so different from those of larger animals. For instance, insects, in all their variety of forms, are equipped with *antennae*, which is the name given to those long feelers that rise from each side of the head. However, the common use or necessity this universal provision serves for insects has not yet been determined. It has not been determined because it does not allow for a clear or even probable comparison with any organs we possess ourselves, or with the organs of animals that resemble us in their functions and abilities, or with which we are

I. The *elytra*, or scaly wings of the beetle genus (*scarabaeus* <note>original: "scarabæus"</note>), provide an example of this. The animal's actual wing is a light, transparent membrane, finer than the highest quality gauze and very similar to it. When spread out, it is also very large in proportion to the animal's size. To protect this delicate structure—and perhaps also to keep it sufficiently flexible and moist—nature has provided a strong, hard case in the form of a horny wing called the *elytron*. When the animal is at rest, the gauze wings lie folded under this impenetrable shield. When the beetle prepares for flight, it raises this outer covering <term>integument</term> and spreads its thin membrane to the air. 

One cannot observe without admiration the complex network of cords—that is, muscular tendons—that must run in various and complicated yet specific directions along this delicate surface. These allow the animal to either fold the wing into a precise shape whenever it wants to shelter them under the protection nature has given them, or to unfold them again when they are needed for action.

In some insects, the *elytra* cover the entire body; in others, only half; and in others, only a small part. However, in all cases, they completely hide and protect the true wings. II. Another mechanism, equally mechanical and equally clear, is the *awl* or *borer* attached to the tails of various species of flies. Naturalists describe this organ in the following way: It is a sharp-pointed instrument that, when not in use, lies hidden at the end of the abdomen. The animal can extend it at will to puncture the leaves, stem, or bark of the specific plant that is suited to nourish its young. Within a sheath that splits and opens whenever the organ is used, there is a compact, solid, notched <term>dentated</term> stem. Along this stem runs a *gutter* or *groove*. After the surface is penetrated, the egg passes through this groove—assisted in some cases by a wave-like muscular contraction <term>peristaltic motion</term>—to its intended location. In the *gadfly* <note>original: "œstrum"</note>, the boring tool <term>wimble</term> extends like the sections of a *telescope* <term>spy-glass</term>. The final segment is armed with three hooks and is capable of boring through the hide of an ox. Is anything more needed to demonstrate the mechanical design than simply stating these facts?

The sting of a bee will pierce through a goat-skin glove. It penetrates the human skin more readily than the finest point of a needle. The action of the sting provides an example of the union of chemistry <term>chymistry</term> and mechanics, such that if it is not a proof of intentional design <term>contrivance</term>, then nothing is. 

First, as to the chemistry: how highly concentrated must the <margin>v</margin>*venom* be, which, in such a small quantity, can produce such powerful effects? In the bee, we may observe that this venom is made from *honey*, the only food of the insect; yet honey is the last material from which I would have expected a potent <term>exalted</term> poison to be prepared by any process of digestion whatsoever. 

In the next place, with respect to the mechanism, the sting is not a simple, but a compound instrument. The visible sting, though tapered to an exquisitely sharp point, is strictly speaking only a sheath. Near the tip, two minute holes <term>orifices</term> can be seen through a microscope. From these holes, during the act of stinging—and, it seems, after the point of the main sting has buried itself in the flesh—two slender filaments <term>subtile rays</term> are launched out. These may be called the true or proper stings, as they are the parts through which the poison is infused into the puncture already made by the exterior sting. 

I have said that chemistry and mechanics are united here. By this observation, I mean that all this machinery would have been useless—a harmless weapon <note>original: "telum imbelle"</note>—if a supply of poison, intense in quality in proportion to the smallness of the drop, had not been provided by the chemical processing <term>elaboration</term> carried out within the insect's body.

...and that, on the other hand, the poison—the result of this process—could not have had its effect or reached its enemy if, when it was collected at the end of the <term>abdomen</term>, it had not found a mechanism there designed to deliver it to the external locations where it was to operate; namely, an awl to bore a hole and a syringe to inject the fluid. Yet these attributes, though they work together, have independent origins. The venom does not create the sting, nor does the sting produce the venom.

IV. The *<term>proboscis</term>*, which many insects possess, is the next feature to be considered. It is a tube attached to the animal's head. In the bee, it consists of two pieces connected by a joint; if it were always extended, it would be too exposed to accidental injuries. Therefore, in its resting state, it is folded up by means of the joint and lies safely under a scaly <term>penthouse</term> <note>a protective, sloping cover or roof-like structure</note>. In many species of butterfly, the proboscis is coiled up like a watch-spring when not in use. In the bee, the proboscis functions as the mouth, as the insect has no other. It is clearly much better adapted for collecting the animal's nourishment than a regular mouth would be. The bee's food is the nectar of flowers—a drop of syrup located deep at the bottom of the <term>corollas</term> <note>original: "corollæ"; the collective petals of a flower</note>, in the recesses of the petals, or down the neck of a <term>monopetalous</term> <note>a flower with petals joined into a single tube</note> flower like a foxglove. The bee thrusts its long, narrow pump into these cells, sucking up this precious fluid through the tube’s cavity, which is inaccessible by any other means. The small rings that make up the bee's proboscis, and the muscles by which it is extended and contracted, are microscopic wonders. The agility with which it moves also cannot fail to inspire admiration. But it is enough for...

...our purpose is to observe, in general, how the structure fits its use, how the means achieve their end, and especially the wisdom by which nature has departed from its most common patterns (for the general rule that animals are provided with mouths is one such pattern) when the goal could be better achieved by this deviation.

In some insects, the <term>proboscis</term>, or tongue, or trunk, is enclosed in a sharp-pointed sheath. Because this sheath is made of a much finer material than the proboscis itself and is sharpened at the tip, it pierces the substance containing the food. It then opens *within* the wound to allow the internal tube, through which the juice is extracted, to do its job. Can any mechanism be simpler than this, or surpass it in design?

V. The *metamorphosis* of insects from grubs into moths and flies is an astonishing process. A hairy caterpillar is transformed into a butterfly. Observe the change: we see four beautiful wings where there were none before; a tubular proboscis in place of a mouth with jaws and teeth; and six long legs instead of fourteen feet. In another case, we see a white, smooth, soft worm turned into a black, hard, <term>crustaceous</term> <note>having a hard shell or crust; shell-like</note> beetle with gauze wings. These, as I have said, are astonishing processes and would seem to require a correspondingly complex biological mechanism. The hypothesis that seems most probable to me is that within the grub, there exist three animals at the same time, one inside the other. All are nourished by the same digestion and by a shared circulatory system, but they are at different stages of maturity. The latest discoveries made by <term>naturalists</term> <note>scientists who study the natural world, particularly plants and animals</note> seem to support this theory. An insect already equipped with wings can be spotted under the membranes of both the worm and the <term>nymph</term> <note>the pupal or transitional stage of an insect's development</note>. In some species, the proboscis, the antennae, the limbs, and the wings of the fly have been observed folded up within the body...

This being the case, the outermost animal—which, besides its own specific form, serves as an <term>integument</term> <note>a natural outer covering or skin</note> for the other two—is the most developed. It dies, as we assume, and falls off first. The second stage, the pupa or chrysalis, then becomes visible. This also, in its turn, dies; its dead and brittle husk falls to pieces and clears the way for the appearance of the fly or moth. Now, if this is true—or indeed whatever explanation is adopted—we see a forward-looking design of the most remarkable kind. We have biological structures *three deep*, yet a single <term>vascular system</term> <note>the system of vessels that carry blood or sap through a body</note> provides nutrition, growth, and life to all of them together.

VI. Almost all insects are <term>oviparous</term> <note>egg-laying</note>. Nature keeps her butterflies, moths, and caterpillars locked up during the winter in their egg state; we must admire the various methods to which nature has resorted for the *security* of the egg. Many insects enclose their eggs in a silken web; others cover them with a coat of hair plucked from their own bodies; some glue them together. Others, like the silkworm moth, glue them to the leaves upon which they are laid so that they are not shaken off by the wind or washed away by rain. Some insects make incisions into leaves and hide an egg in each cut, while others wrap their eggs in a soft substance that forms the first <term>aliment</term> <note>food or nourishment</note> for the young animal. Others still dig a hole in the earth and, after filling it with a supply of suitable food, deposit their egg inside. In all these cases, we should notice that the strategy depends not so much on the ingenuity of the animal, but on the physical resources of its biological makeup.

The skill with which the young insect is *coiled* inside the egg also presents a subject of great curiosity wherever it can be examined. The insect, equipped with all the limbs it should have, is rolled into a shape that seems to compress it into the smallest possible space. Because of this contraction, and despite the small size of the egg, it has more than enough room in its tiny apartment. This folding of the limbs appears to me to indicate a specific design; for, if it were merely the result of being squeezed, the arrangement of the parts would vary much more than it does. Within the same species, I believe, it is always the same.

These observations apply to the entire insect category, or at least to a large portion of them. Other observations are limited to fewer species, but they are perhaps no less important or satisfying.

I. The organization within the abdomen of the *silkworm* or *spider*, by which these insects produce their thread, is as undeniably mechanical as a wire-drawer's mill. In the body of the silkworm, there are two bags remarkable for their shape, position, and purpose. They wrap around the intestine; when stretched out, they are ten inches long, even though the animal itself is only two inches. A glue-like substance is collected within these bags. Connected to these bags are two "paps" or outlets, perforated—like a <term>colander</term> <note>original: "garter"; likely an OCR error for "colander," a perforated bowl used for straining</note>—by a number of small holes. As the glue or gum passes through these tiny openings, it forms hairs of almost imperceptible fineness. When joined together, these hairs compose the silk that we unwind from the <term>cone</term> <note>a cocoon</note> in which the silkworm has wrapped itself. In the spider, the web is formed from this same type of thread. In both cases, the end of the thread is first attached to an external anchor by the animal using its sticky quality. Once the end is fastened to a point, the insect—by turning its body or by moving away from that point—draws out the thread through...

...the holes described above, by an operation—as has been observed—exactly like drawing wire. The thread, like the wire, is shaped by the hole through which it passes. In one respect, however, there is a difference. Wire is simply metal that remains unchanged except in its shape. In the biological process, the nature of the substance is somewhat changed as well as its form; for while it exists inside the insect, it is a soft, sticky gum or glue. The thread likely acquires its firmness and strength from the effect of the air upon its surface the moment it is exposed; and a thread so fine consists almost entirely of surface area. This property of the paste, however, is part of the deliberate design.

The mechanism itself consists of the bags, or reservoirs, where the glue is collected, and the external holes communicating with these bags. The action of the machine is seen in the forming of a thread (just as wire is formed) by pushing the already prepared material through holes of the correct size. The secretion process is too subtle for us to see, except for what we perceive in the final product. But one thing corresponds to another: the secretory glands match the quality and consistency required for the secreted substance, and the bag matches its storage needs. The outlets and openings are constructed not merely for emptying the reservoirs of their <term>burden</term> <note>load or contents</note>, but for processing the contents into a shape and texture that is very useful—or rather, essential—to the future life and functions of the insect.

However, these two substances—which together are of the greatest use, but are of little value without each other—come from different origins. The bee finds the honey, but it *makes* the wax. The honey is located in the <term>nectaries</term> <note>the nectar-secreting parts of a flower</note> of flowers and probably undergoes little change; it is simply collected. In contrast, the wax is a pliable, sticky paste made from a dry powder—not simply by kneading it with a liquid, but through a digestive process within the body of the bee. 

What explanation can be given for these facts, except that the animal—being intended to feed upon honey—was enabled to obtain it through a specific external physical structure? Furthermore, because it needs the honey during times when it cannot be gathered at all, the bee was also endowed with the equally necessary faculty of constructing repositories for its preservation. This faculty, it is evident, must primarily depend on the capacity to provide suitable materials. 

Two distinct functions combine to create this ability. First, there is the power of the bee to load the <term>farina</term> <note>pollen</note> of flowers onto its thighs. III. Our business is with mechanism. In the *panorpa* <note>the scorpionfly</note> genus of insects, there is a pair of forceps in the tail of the male insect, with which he catches and holds the female. Is any pair of pincers more mechanical in its structure than this provision? Or is any structure clearer or more certain in its intended design?

IV. Saint-Pierre <note>Jacques-Henri Bernardin de Saint-Pierre, a French botanist and author</note> tells us* that in a fly with six legs (I do not remember if he specifies the species), the pair of legs closest to the head and the pair closest to the tail have brushes at their tips. With these, the fly grooms the front or the back part of its body as needed. However, the middle pair has no such brushes, as the position of these legs would not allow the brushes to be used for that purpose even if they were there. This is a very precise mechanical distinction.

V. If the reader, considering our scientific categories, wishes to contemplate the chemistry as well as the mechanism of nature, the world of insects will provide an example. I refer to the light in the tail of a *glow-worm*. Naturalists seem to agree on two points regarding it: first, that it is phosphorescent; second, that its purpose is to attract the male insect. The only thing to investigate is the uniqueness, if any exists, in the natural history of this animal that would make such a provision more necessary for *it* than for others...

In this example, we also see the resources of human art anticipated by nature. One major operation in chemistry is the production of phosphorus; it was once thought to be an ingenious invention to have phosphoric matches replace lit candles. Now, this very thing is done inside the body of the glow-worm. The phosphorus is not only produced but ignited, emitting a steady and helpful beam for the purpose stated here, which I believe is the true one.

VI. This is not the only instance entomology provides in which our discoveries—or rather, our inventions—turn out to be imitations of nature. Some years ago, a plan was suggested for producing propulsion through reaction in this way: by the power of a steam engine, a stream of water was to be shot out of the rear of a boat. The force of this stream against the water in the river would push the boat itself forward. This is, in fact, the same principle by which skyrockets rise into the air. I am not speaking of the usefulness or the practicality of the plan, nor is it my place to praise its cleverness; but it is certainly a deliberate design. Now, if naturalists are to be believed, it is exactly the mechanism that nature has used...

VII. Again, Europe has lately been surprised by the lifting of objects into the air by means of a balloon. The discovery consisted of finding a manageable substance that was, volume for volume, lighter than air. The application of this discovery was to make a body composed of this substance support its own weight along with a heavier object attached to it. This device, which seems so new to us, turns out to be nothing other than what the Author of Nature has employed in the gossamer spider. We frequently see this spider's thread floating in the air, extending from hedge to hedge across a road or a brook four or five yards wide. The animal that forms the thread has no wings with which to fly from one end of this line to the other, nor does it have muscles to enable it to leap or dart such a great distance. Yet its Creator has laid out a path for it in the atmosphere in the following way: although the animal itself is heavier than air, the thread which it spins from its body is <term>specifically lighter</term> <note>the author suggests the silk is less dense than air, allowing it to float</note>. This is its balloon. The spider, if left to itself, would drop to the ground; but because it is tied to its thread, both are supported. Here we have a very remarkable arrangement; to a contemplative eye, it is a gratifying sight to see this insect wafted along on her thread, sustained by a buoyancy not her own, and traveling through regions that might seem forbidden to its nature if we examined only the body of the animal.

I must now ask the reader’s permission to introduce here, for lack of a better place, an observation or two upon the tribe of animals—whether living on land or in water—which are covered by *shells*.

I. The *shells of snails* are a wonderful and mechanical invention—and, if one may speak this way regarding the works of nature, an original design. Other animals have their proper retreats, and their *winter quarters* <note>original: "hybernacula"</note> as well; but the snail carries these about with him. He travels with his tent; and this tent, though necessarily both light and thin, is completely impervious to both moisture and air. The young snail emerges from its egg with the shell already on its back. The gradual enlargement the shell receives is derived from the slime secreted by the animal’s skin. Now, the suitability of this secretion for its purpose, its property of hardening into a shell, and the action—whatever it may be—by which the animal makes use of its gift and the specialized nature of its glands, are things that cannot likely be attributed to any cause other than intentional design. (To say nothing of the work being started before the animal is even born.) This design cannot be attributed to the animal alone; for though the animal might build the house, it could not have supplied the material. The will of the animal could not determine the chemical quality of the secretion. Additionally, the shell of a snail, with its central pillar and <term>convolution</term> <note>the spiral or coiled shape of the shell</note>, is a very intricate construction; yet a snail, it would seem, is the most sluggish and poorly equipped of all craftsmen. In the midst of such variety, there is also a regularity that would hardly be expected. In the same species of

II. Much of what has been noted about snails also applies to *shellfish* and their shells, particularly those of the univalve (single-shell) variety, with the addition of two observations. One of these concerns the immense strength and hardness of most of these shells. I do not know if, given the same weight, human skill <note>original: "art"</note> could produce a casing as strong as some of these shells. This defensive strength is perfectly suited to the life of an animal that must often endure the dangers of a stormy sea and a rocky seabed, as well as the attacks of predatory fish. The second observation concerns the property of the animal’s secretion not only to solidify but to solidify—or, as a builder would say, "set"—underwater into a chalky <term>cretaceous</term> substance that is firm and hard. This property is much more extraordinary and, chemically speaking, more specialized than simply hardening in the air, which might be considered a type of drying out <term>exsiccation</term>, like clay drying into bricks.

III. In the *bivalve* (two-shell) order of shellfish—such as cockles, mussels, oysters, etc.—what design could be as simple or as clear as the insertion at the back of a tough, tendon-like substance? This material serves simultaneously as the ligament that binds the two shells together and the hinge upon which they open and shut.

Both serve the same purpose; therefore, both require the same properties: specifically, hardness and flexibility—a covering that can...

For this double purpose, human ingenuity <note>original: "art of man"</note>, specifically applied to this subject, has not been able to create anything better than what nature provides for observation. Is this not, therefore, a mechanical design, which a craftsman—having a similar goal in mind—would adopt? If the structure of a coat of mail is attributed to human skill, should the lobster's structure—serving the same purpose—be attributed to anything less than skill?

Some who acknowledge this imitation and agree with the conclusion we draw from it might ask why such imitations are not more common. They may wonder why—if it is true, as we claim, that the same principles of intelligence, design, and mechanical ingenuity were used to create natural bodies as we use to make tools—we do not copy them more often. The answers to this question are: first, that it rarely happens that nature and human craftsmanship pursue exactly the same purpose and no other; and second, it is even rarer that we *could* imitate nature even if we wanted to. Our materials and our craftsmanship are equally lacking. Springs, wires, cork, and leather are poor substitutes for a real arm or hand. In the example we have chosen—the comparison of a lobster's shell to a coat of mail—these difficulties are less of an obstacle than in almost any other case. Consequently, as we have seen, human skill <note>original: "art"</note> gladly borrows this design from nature and imitates it closely.

But to return to insects. I believe it is in this class of animals, above all others—especially when we consider the multitude of species discovered by the microscope—that we are struck by what Cicero called "the insatiable variety of nature" <note>original: "insatiabilis varietas naturae"</note>. It is said that there are six thousand species of flies and seven hundred and sixty species of butterflies, each distinct from all the others (St. Pierre <note>Jacques-Henri Bernardin de Saint-Pierre, a French naturalist</note>). The same writer tells us from his own observation that thirty-seven species of winged insects, with clearly defined differences, visited a single strawberry plant over the course of three weeks.\* *Ray* <note>John Ray, an influential English naturalist</note> observed two hundred kinds of butterflies—both nocturnal <term>active at night, such as moths</term> and diurnal <term>active during the day</term>—within a mile or two of his own house. He also asserts (though I think without the basis of an exact calculation) that the total number of insect species, counting all types, may be no less than ten thousand.† And in this vast variety of animal forms (for this observation is not limited to insects, though perhaps more applicable to them than to any other class), we are sometimes led to notice the different methods, or rather the carefully diversified methods, by which the exact same purpose is achieved.

Regarding the function of breathing, for example, which had to be provided for in one way or another: besides the common variations of lungs, gills, and breathing holes (for insects in general breathe not through the mouth, but through holes in their sides), the pupae <note>original: "nymphæ"</note> of gnats have a specialized structure to raise their backs to the surface of the water to take in air. The water beetles <note>original: "hydrocanthari"</note> do the same by thrusting...

Considering these various forms might lead us to believe that *variety* itself, separate from every other reason, was a motive in the mind of the Creator, or of those who carry out His will.

To this great variety in organized life, the Deity has given—or perhaps there arises from it—a corresponding variety of animal *appetites* <term>instinctive desires or nutritional needs</term>. We do not have to look far for the ultimate purpose <term>original: "final cause"</term> of this. If all animals desired the same environment, shelter, or food, it is evident that far fewer could be supported and housed than those which currently live conveniently together and find plenty of food. What one species rejects, another delights in. Food that is nauseating to one group of animals becomes, by that very same property, an alluring delicacy to another group. Carrion <term>decaying flesh</term> is a treat to dogs, ravens, vultures, and fish. The vapors of decaying substances attract flies in crowds. Maggots revel in putrefaction <term>the process of decay or rotting</term>.

## CHAPTER XX.

### OF PLANTS.

I believe that a designed and carefully planned mechanism is generally more obvious in animals than in *plants*; and it is unnecessary to spend too much time on a weaker argument when a stronger one is available. However, there are a few observations about the vegetable kingdom that are so relevant to our discussion that it would be wrong to ignore them.

The one great goal of nature in the structure of plants seems to be the perfecting of the *seed*; and, as part of that same goal, the preservation of the seed until it is *perfected*. This intention shows itself, first, by the care that appears to be taken to protect and ripen—using every advantage of placement within the plant—those parts which most directly contribute to fructification <term>the process of producing fruit or seeds</term>, namely the *antherae* <term>anthers; the part of a stamen that contains the pollen</term>, the *stamina* <term>stamens; the pollen-producing organs of a flower</term>, and the *stigmata* <term>stigmas; the part of a pistil that receives the pollen</term>. These parts are usually located in the center, the hidden depths, or the intricate folds of the flower. During their delicate and immature state, they are enclosed in the stalk or sheltered in the bud. As soon as they have become strong enough to handle exposure and are ready to perform the important function assigned to them, they are revealed to the light and air by the opening of the stem or the expansion of the *petals*. After this, in many cases, the very shape of the flower while in bloom <note>original: "during its blow"</note> reflects light and warmth onto these parts from the curved inner side of the flower's cup. The *sleep* of plants is the leaves or petals arranging themselves in such a way as to shelter the young stem, buds, or fruit. They turn upward or droop downward, depending on which change of position is required for that purpose. In the growth of corn <term>likely referring to cereal grains like wheat or barley</term>, whenever the plant begins to sprout, the two upper leaves of the stalk join together to embrace the ear, protecting it until the grain <term>pulp</term> has reached a certain level of firmness. In some water plants, flowering and fertilization <term>fecundation</term> occur *within* the stem, which later opens to release the fertilized seed*. The *pea* or *papilionaceous* <term>butterfly-shaped flowers, like peas or beans</term> family encloses its reproductive parts within a beautiful folding of the inner blossom—sometimes called the "boat" or "keel" because of its shape—which is itself protected under a canopy <term>penthouse</term> formed by the outer petals. This structure is very skillfully designed <term>artificial</term>; and while its commonness might make it seem less curious, that very prevalence adds to its value. It also has this further advantage—and it is an advantage that is strictly mechanical—that all the blossoms turn their backs to the wind whenever a gale blows strongly enough to endanger the delicate parts upon which the seed depends. I have observed this a hundred times in a field of peas in bloom. It is a natural ability that results from the shape of the flower and, as we have said, is strictly mechanical; it is just as mechanical as the turning of a weather vane or a tin cap on top of a chimney. In the poppy and many similar species of flowers, the head hangs down while it is growing because of a stiff curve in the upper part of the stem; in this position, it is protected from rain or moisture. When the head has reached its full size and is ready to open, the stalk *straightens* itself, seemingly for the purpose of presenting the flower and, along with the flower, the reproductive organs...

In *trees*, especially those native to colder climates, this point is addressed even earlier. Therefore, a winter must be endured. What we should notice is how nature has prepared for the trials and harshness of that season. These delicate embryos are, first of all, wrapped up with a compactness that no human skill can imitate; in this state, they form what we call the bud. That is not all. The bud itself is enclosed in scales, which are formed from the remains of past leaves and the beginnings of future ones. Nor is this the whole of it. In the coldest climates, a third protection is added: the bud has a *coating of gum or resin* which, once hardened <term>congealed</term>, resists the strongest frosts. When warm weather approaches, this gum softens and no longer hinders the expansion of the leaves and flowers. All this care is part of that system of provisions which has as its goal and final result the production and perfecting of the seeds.

In flowers that grow upright, the pistil is shorter than the stamens <term>stamina</term>. The pollen, shed from the anthers <term>antheræ</term> into the cup of the flower, is caught as it falls by the head of the pistil, called the stigma. 

But how is this handled when the flowers hang down (as the crown imperial does, for instance)? In that position, the pollen <term>farina</term> would fall away from the stigma rather than toward it. In these plants, the relative length of the parts is reversed. The pistil in these flowers is usually longer, instead of shorter, than the stamens, so that its protruding tip may receive the pollen as it drops toward the ground. In some cases (such as the nigella <note>Also known as "love-in-a-mist."</note>), where the stalks of the pistils, or styles, are disproportionately long, they bend their ends down toward the anthers so that the necessary closeness can be achieved.

To follow this great process as it progresses: once the fertilization <term>impregnation</term>—to which all this machinery relates—is completed, the other parts of the flower fade and drop off. In contrast, the *ripening seed-vessel* <term>gravid seed-vessel</term> begins to increase in size. It always grows significantly, and in some species (the gourd and melon, for example) it reaches a surprising size compared to its start. It takes on a vast variety of forms in different plants, but all of them clearly contribute to the security of the seed. 

By virtue of this process, which is so necessary yet so varied, we eventually have the seed. In stone fruits <term>drupes</term> and nuts, the seed is encased in a strong shell, and the shell itself is enclosed in a pulp or husk, which feeds or has fed the seed within. More commonly (as in grapes, oranges, and many kinds of berries), the seeds are submerged in a sticky syrup contained within a skin or bladder. At other times (as in apples and pears), they are embedded in the heart of a firm, fleshy...

But the physical makeup of seeds is even more remarkable than either their preservation or their dispersal. Within the seed of every species of plant, or nearly every one, provisions are made for two major purposes: first, for the safety of the <term>germ (the embryo)</term> <note>original: "germ"</note>; and second, for the temporary support of the future plant. The sprout, as it is folded up inside the seed, is more delicate and brittle than almost any other substance. It cannot be touched without being broken. Yet, in beans, peas, grass seeds, grain, and fruits, it is so well-defended on all sides—so enclosed and protected—that even while the seed itself is handled roughly, tossed into sacks, or shoveled into heaps, the miniature plant, this vital particle, remains unharmed.

Our second observation concerns a general property of climbing plants, which is strictly mechanical. > “We do not see,” says Ray <note>John Ray (1627–1705), a pioneering English naturalist and theologian.</note>, “even a single tree, shrub, or herb that has a firm and strong stem and is able to grow upward and stand alone without assistance, *equipped with these tendrils.*”

It is because the stalk of the pea cannot support itself, whereas the stalk of the bean can. We may also add a detail that should not be overlooked: in the pea family, these clasps do not appear until they are needed—until the plant has grown to a height where it requires support.

The word “support” leads us to reflect on a specific property found in grasses, grains, and canes. The hollow stems of these types of plants are equipped with joints at regular intervals. These joints are not found in the trunks of trees or in the solid stalks of other plants. There may be other uses for these joints, but it appears that at least one intended purpose is to <term>corroborate (strengthen or reinforce)</term> the stem. Because of its length and hollowness, the stem would otherwise be too likely to bend or break. <margin>✓</margin>

*Grasses* are a special focus of Nature’s care. She clothes the earth with them and uses them to sustain its inhabitants. Livestock feed on their leaves, birds on their smaller seeds, and humans on the larger ones; for few readers need to be told that the plants which produce our bread grains belong to this category. In those groups more generally recognized as grasses, their extraordinary ability to survive and multiply, their hardiness, their nearly unstoppable tendency to spread, and their capacity for <term>reviviscence (the ability to come back to life or regain vigor)</term> align with nature’s intentions for them. They thrive under conditions that would destroy other plants. The more their leaves are eaten, the more their roots grow. The more they are trampled upon, the thicker they grow. Many grass leaves that seem dry and dead revive and regain their <term>verdure (greenness)</term> in the spring. In high mountains, where the summer heat is not enough to ripen seeds, grasses are abundant that are <term>viviparous (producing plantlets or bulbs on the stem rather than seeds)</term>, and they are consequently able to reproduce themselves without seed. It has also often been observed that <term>herbivorous (plant-eating)</term> animals focus on the leaves of grasses; if allowed to roam and choose freely in their pastures, they leave the stalks that support the flowers untouched\*.

<header># OF PLANTS.</header>

The general properties of plant life, or those properties common to large portions of that kingdom, are nearly all that the scope of our argument allows us to present. It is impossible to examine every individual plant species. We may, however, be permitted to select three or four of these species as worthy of particular notice, due to either a unique mechanism, a peculiar natural provision, or both.

I. In a note for line 395 of Dr. Darwin’s *Botanic Garden* <note>Erasmus Darwin’s "The Botanic Garden" (1791), a famous scientific poem.</note>, there is the following account of the *vallisneria* as it has been observed in the Rhone River. “They have roots at the bottom of the Rhone. The flowers of the *female plant* float on the surface of the water and are equipped with an elastic, spiral stalk which extends or contracts as the water rises or falls; this rise or fall, caused by the torrents that flow into the river, often amounts to many feet in a few hours. The flowers of the *male plant* are produced underwater; as soon as the <term>fecundating farina</term> <gloss>fertilizing pollen</gloss> is mature, they detach themselves from the plant, rise to the surface, and are wafted by the air or carried by the currents to the female flowers.” In this account, our attention will be directed to two details: first, to the mechanism of the “elastic, spiral stalk” which lengthens or shortens itself according to the water level; and second, to the provision made for bringing the male flower, which is produced underwater, to the female flower floating on the surface.

II. I take my second example from Withering’s *Arrangement* <note>William Withering, "A Botanical Arrangement of all the Vegetables Naturally Growing in Great Britain" (1776).</note> (Volume 2, page 209, 3rd edition). “The *cuscuta europæa* <gloss>European dodder</gloss> is a parasitic plant. The seed opens and puts forth a *little spiral body* which does **NOT** seek the earth to take root; instead, it climbs in a spiral direction, from right to left, up other plants, from which it draws its nourishment through specialized vessels.”

...the "little spiral body" proceeding from the seed is to be compared with the fibers which seeds send out in ordinary cases; and the comparison ought to regard both the form of the threads and the direction. Ordinary fibers are straight; this one is spiral. They shoot downwards; this points upwards. In both the rule and the exception, we equally perceive design.

III. A better-known **parasitic plant** is the evergreen shrub called the *mistletoe*. What we have to remark in it is a singular instance of compensation. No art has yet made these plants take root in the earth. Here, therefore, might seem to be a mortal defect in their constitution. Let us examine how this defect is made up to them. The seeds are endowed with an adhesive quality so tenacious that, if they are rubbed upon the smooth bark of almost any tree, they will stick to it. And then what follows? Roots springing from their seeds insert their fibers into the woody substance of the tree; and the result is that a mistletoe plant is produced the next winter*. Of no other plant do the roots refuse to grow in the ground; of no other plant do the seeds possess this adhesive, generative quality when applied to the bark of trees.

IV. Another instance of the compensatory system is in the autumnal crocus or **meadow saffron** (*Colchicum autumnale* <note>original: "cholcicum autumnale"</note>). I have pitied this poor plant a thousand times. And it blooms not in the spring, to be visited by summer suns, but under all the disadvantages of the declining year. When we come, however, to look more closely into the structure of this plant, we find that, instead of its being neglected, nature has gone out of

Therefore, Providence has designed its structure so that this vital task may be performed deep in the earth, beyond the reach of the usual effects of frost*.” 

In other words, in the autumn, nothing happens above ground except for the process of pollination—a transaction between the <term>antherae</term> <gloss>the pollen-producing parts of the flower</gloss> and the <term>stigmata</term> <gloss>the parts that receive the pollen</gloss>. The maturation of the fertilized seed usually occurs within a capsule exposed to the open air along with the rest of the flower. Here, however, it is carried on throughout the entire winter within the very heart of the earth—that is, “beyond the reach of the usual effects of frost.” 

But then a new difficulty presents itself. It is known that seeds, even when fully developed, will not sprout at such a depth in the earth. Therefore, our seeds, despite being safely sheltered, would ultimately fail to serve the purpose for which all seeds are intended. To prevent this, “a second remarkable provision is made to raise them above the surface once they are perfected and to sow them at an appropriate distance.” Specifically, the <term>germ</term> <gloss>the initial growth or embryo of the plant</gloss> grows up in the spring on a fruit-stalk, accompanied by leaves. ### V.

I provide the account of the *dionæa muscipula* <gloss>the Venus flytrap</gloss>, an extraordinary American plant, as some recent authors have described it. However, I am unable to say whether we are yet familiar enough with the plant to verify every part of this account through repeated and close observation. Its leaves are hinged and equipped with two rows of strong prickles; their surfaces are covered with a number of tiny glands which secrete a sweet liquid that attracts flies. When these parts are touched by the legs of flies, the two lobes of the leaf instantly snap shut, the rows of prickles lock themselves tightly together, and they squeeze the unsuspecting animal to death.*

Here, under a new model, we recognize the ancient plan of nature: specifically, the relationship of parts and provisions to one another, to a shared purpose, and to the benefit of the biological organism to which they belong. The attracting syrup, the rows of strong prickles, their interlocking position, the hinges of the leaves, and—what is more significant than the rest—that singular sensitivity of their surfaces by which they close at a touch; all of these play a contributing role in producing an effect connected either with the defense or the nutrition of the plant.

# CHAPTER XXI.

## THE ELEMENTS.

When we come to the elements, we stop discussing mechanical systems; this is because we have reached those things whose internal organization (if they are indeed organized) we are admittedly ignorant of. This ignorance is implied by their very name <term>elements</term> <note>Meaning the fundamental, irreducible components of matter</note>. To tell the truth, our scientific investigations are halted long before we even reach this point. However, it is a comfort to find that a deep knowledge of the internal constitution of the elements is not necessary for us. <margin>✓</margin> For instance, as Joseph Addison has well observed: “we know water well enough when we know how to boil it, how to freeze it, how to evaporate it, how to make it fresh, and how to make it run or spout out in whatever quantity and direction we please—without knowing what water actually is.” The observation of this excellent writer is even more appropriate now than it was when he first made it. Although the internal makeup and the constituent parts of water appear to have been recently discovered <note>A reference to the late 18th-century discovery that water is composed of hydrogen and oxygen</note>, it does not seem to me that we can make any better or greater use of water since this discovery than we did before it.

We can never think of the elements without reflecting upon the many distinct uses that are combined within the same substance. The ***air*** supplies the lungs, supports fire, conveys sound, reflects light, spreads smells, provides rain, carries ships, and sustains birds. All things come from water <note>original: "Εξ ύδατος τα παντα"</note>; ***water***, besides maintaining its own inhabitants, is the universal nour-

We could expand at almost any length we pleased upon each of these uses, but it seems sufficient to simply state them. The few remarks which I judge necessary to add are as follows:

I. Air is essentially different from earth. There appears to be no absolute necessity for an atmosphere to surround our globe (the moon, for instance, has none). Yet it does surround it, and we see how many, how various, and how important are the purposes it serves for every order of living—not to say organized—beings placed upon the Earth's surface. I think that every one of these uses will be understood as soon as they are mentioned, except perhaps for the reflection of light, which may be explained this way: If I had the power of seeing only by means of rays coming directly from the sun, I would find myself in darkness whenever I turned my back to that celestial body. If I could see by reflected light, but only by light reflected from solid masses, these masses would indeed shine and glisten, but they would do so in the dark. The hemisphere, the sky, and the world can only be illuminated as they are because the light of the sun is reflected to the eye from all sides and in every direction by particles as numerous, as thickly scattered, and as widely diffused as those of the air <note>The author is describing the phenomenon of atmospheric scattering, which allows the entire sky to appear bright rather than just the sun itself</note>.

If evaporation is a form of solution—which seems probable—then the air dissolves the water but not the salt. Regardless of what theory this is based on, the distinction is critical. By evaporation, water is carried up into the air; by the reverse of evaporation, it falls down upon the earth. And how does it fall? It does not fall by the clouds being suddenly converted back into water and descending like a solid sheet; nor does it rush down in columns like water from a spout. Therefore, knowing that these agitations of the elements tend powerfully to restore that purity to the air—which so many causes are constantly impairing—should reconcile us to them, even though we sometimes regret their destructive consequences.

II. In WATER, what should be admired in no small measure are those negative qualities which constitute its purity. Had it been like wine, oil, or acid; had the sea been filled or the rivers flowed with wine or milk; fish, as they are currently constituted, would have died. Plants, as they are currently constituted, would have withered, and the lives of animals which feed upon plants would have perished. Its very tastelessness <term>original: "insipidity"</term>, which is one of those negative qualities, renders it the best of all **solvents** <term>original: "menstrua"; substances used to dissolve other substances</term>. Having no taste of its own, it becomes the pure vehicle for every other flavor. Had there been a taste in water, whatever it might be, it would have infected everything we ate or drank with a persistent <note>original: "importunate"</note> repetition of that same flavor.

So there is an incessant circulation of the same fluid; and there is probably not one drop more or less now than there was at the creation. A particle of water takes its departure from the surface of the sea in order to fulfill certain important offices for the earth; and having executed the service which was assigned to it, it returns to the bosom which it left.

Some have thought that we have too much water upon the globe, with the sea occupying above three-quarters of its whole surface. But the expanse of the ocean, immense as it is, may be no more than sufficient to fertilize the earth. Or, independent of this reason, I do not know why the sea may not have as much right to its place as the land. It may proportionally support as many inhabitants and contribute to as large an aggregate of enjoyment. The land only affords a habitable surface; the sea is habitable to a great depth.

III. Regarding **FIRE**, we have said that it *dissolves*. The only idea which this term probably raised in the reader’s mind was that of fire melting metals, resins, and some other substances, fluxing <term>melting or fusing</term> ores, running glass, and assisting us in many of our operations, chemical <term>original: "chymical"</term> or culinary. Now, these are only uses of an occasional kind and give us a very imperfect notion of what fire does for us. The grand importance of this dissolving power—the great office indeed of fire in the economy <term>original: "œconomy"; the internal management or system</term> of nature—is keeping things in a state of solution; that is to say, in a state of fluidity. Were it not for the presence of heat, or of a certain degree of it, all fluids would be frozen. The ocean itself would be a quarry of ice; universal nature would be stiff and dead.

# THE ELEMENTS.

We see, therefore, that the elements have not only a direct relationship to the composition of living organisms, but also a relationship to each other. Water could not perform its function for the earth without air, nor could it even exist as liquid water without fire <note>referring to the heat necessary to maintain fluidity and prevent freezing</note>.

IV. Regarding **LIGHT** (whether we consider it to be the same substance as fire or a different one), it is completely unnecessary to speak at length about its usefulness. No one disputes its value. Therefore, the observations I will offer concern the little we seem to know about its physical makeup.

Light travels from the sun to the earth in eleven minutes; a distance that would take a cannonball twenty-five years to cover. Nothing more needs to be said to demonstrate the velocity of light. Driven by such velocity, with what *force* must its particles strike against objects? I do not mean just the eye—the most delicate of animal tissues—but every substance, living or non-living, that stands in its way. It would seem to be a force strong enough to shatter the hardest objects into atoms.

How, then, is this effect—the consequence of such enormous speed—prevented? It is managed by the proportionally small size of the particles that compose light. It is impossible for the human mind to imagine anything as small as a particle of light. But this extreme <term>exility</term> <note>extreme thinness, slenderness, or smallness</note>, though difficult to conceive, is easy to prove. A single drop of tallow <note>animal fat used for making candles</note> consumed in the wick of a <term>farthing candle</term> <note>the smallest and cheapest candle available, costing a quarter of a penny</note> will give off enough rays to fill a half-sphere a mile in diameter. It fills it so completely with these rays that an opening no larger than the pupil of an eye, placed anywhere within that area, will be certain to receive some of them. We cannot even estimate what floods of light are continually poured out from the sun; but the vastness of the sphere filled with its particles—even if it reached no further than the

We can somewhat calculate the orbit of the earth, and we have reason to believe that throughout this entire region, the particles of light are positioned very close to one another, at least in terms of their breadth. The <term>spissitude</term> <note>thickness or density</note> of the sun's rays at the earth is such that the number of rays falling upon a burning glass <note>a lens, such as a magnifying glass, used to concentrate the sun's rays to produce heat</note> one inch in diameter is sufficient, when concentrated, to set wood on fire.

The <term>tenuity</term> <note>extreme thinness or smallness</note> and the velocity of particles of light, as determined by separate observations, may be said to be proportioned to each other. Both surpass our greatest ability to comprehend them, yet they are balanced. It is this proportion alone which converts what would be a terrifying element into a welcome visitor.

A learned friend once observed to me—an idea that had often struck him—that if light had been made by a common artist, it would have been of one uniform *color*. However, because of its actual composition, we have that variety of colors which is of such infinite use to us for distinguishing objects; this variety adds so much to the beauty of the earth and increases our store of innocent pleasures.

To this, we may add another reflection: namely, that considering light is composed of rays of seven different colors (of which there can be no doubt, because it can be separated into these rays simply by passing it through a prism), the constituent parts must be well mixed and blended together to produce a fluid so clear and colorless as a beam of sunlight is when we receive it.

## CHAPTER XXII.

### ASTRONOMY.*

My opinion of astronomy has always been that it is *not* the best medium through which to prove the agency of an intelligent Creator; rather, once this has been proved, it shows the magnificence of His operations more than any other science. It raises a mind that is already convinced to more sublime views of the Deity than any other subject provides, but it is not as well-suited for the purpose of argument as other subjects are. We lack the means to examine the internal makeup of the heavenly bodies. The very simplicity of their appearance works against them in this regard. We see nothing but bright points, luminous circles, or the phases of spheres reflecting the light that falls upon them. 

Now, we deduce design from the relationship, fitness, and correspondence between parts. Therefore, a certain degree of complexity is necessary to make a subject suitable for this type of argument. However, the heavenly bodies do not present themselves to our observation as being composed of parts at all—except, perhaps, in the case of Saturn’s ring. This simplicity, which might be a form of perfection in them, is a disadvantage to us as researchers of their nature. They do not fall within the scope of our <term>mechanics</term> <note>the branch of science dealing with the motion of bodies and the systems of parts that produce such motion</note>.

What we say of their forms is also true of their *motions*. Their motions are carried on without any

And what would the consequence have been? The difference between a stable axis and any other axis is this: when a <term>spheroid</term> <note>an object shaped like a sphere but not perfectly round</note> in a state of rotation stays on a stable axis, it remains there; it stays steady and fixed in its position. Its poles keep their direction relative to the plane and the center of its orbit. However, while it turns on an axis that is *not* stable—and we have seen that the number of unstable axes infinitely exceeds the number of stable ones—it is always liable to shift and wobble from one axis to another. This causes a matching change in the tilt of its poles. 

Therefore, if a planet started revolving on any axis other than its shortest one or one of its longest ones, the poles on its surface would constantly change, and it would never achieve a stable axis of rotation. The effect of this instability would be that the equatorial regions of the Earth might become the poles, or the polar regions might become the equator. It was not enough to establish the law of centripetal force, even through the wisest choice; for, even under that law, it was still possible for the planets to have moved in paths possessing such a high degree of eccentricity that, in the course of every revolution, they would be brought very near to the sun and then carried away to immense distances from it. 

The comets actually move in orbits of this kind. If the planets had done the same, instead of traveling in nearly circular orbits, the shift from one extreme of temperature to another would, on our planet at least, have destroyed every animal and plant upon its surface. Now, once the distance from the center at which a planet starts and the absolute force of attraction at that distance are fixed, the shape of its orbit—whether it is a circle or a more or less elongated oval—depends on two things: the velocity and the direction in which the planet is launched. 

To produce a proper result, both of these must be brought within certain narrow limits. Only one specific velocity, combined with one specific direction, will produce a perfect circle. Furthermore, the velocity must be very close to this specific speed, and the direction must also be very close to this specific direction, to produce orbits like those of the planets—that is, ellipses with small eccentricities that are nearly circular. The velocity and the direction must both be correct. If the velocity is

If it were significantly faster than that, the body would take one of those eccentric courses—those long <term>ellipses</term> <note>oval-shaped paths</note>—whose inconveniences we have already noted. If the velocity reached the rate of seven miles per second, or went beyond that, the ball would fly off from the Earth and never be heard of again. 

In the same way, regarding the direction: out of the innumerable angles at which the ball might be sent off—meaning angles formed with a line drawn to the center of the Earth—none would work except one that was nearly a right angle. Out of the various directions in which a cannon might be pointed, upward or downward, every single one would fail except what was exactly or nearly horizontal. The same principle holds true for the planets, including our own. We are entitled, therefore, to ask and to urge the question: Why did the <term>projectile velocity</term> and <term>projectile direction</term> <note>the initial speed and angle at which the planet was "launched" into motion</note> of the Earth happen to be nearly those which would retain it in a circular form? Now, besides the fact that this attributes the lucky coincidence of velocity and direction we have been noting to mere chance, the hypothesis, as I understand it, is inconsistent with the physical laws that govern heavenly motions. If the planets were knocked off the surface of the sun, they would eventually return to the surface of the sun. Or, if we try to solve this problem by suggesting that the same violent blow which shattered the sun’s surface and separated large fragments from it also pushed the sun itself out of its position, another equally difficult question arises: once the sun was put in motion, what would *stop* it? 

The hypothesis is also contradicted by the enormous difference that exists between the diameters of the planetary orbits. The distance of Saturn from the sun—to say nothing of the *Georgium Sidus* <note>The planet Uranus, which was originally named "the Georgian Star" by William Herschel in honor of King George III</note>—is nearly twenty-five times that of Mercury. This is a discrepancy that seems impossible to reconcile with *Buffon’s* scheme <note>Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon, who proposed that the planets were formed by a comet colliding with the sun</note>. Bodies starting from the same location, regardless of the difference in direction or velocity with which they began, could not have ended up at these various distances from the center while still maintaining their nearly circular orbits. They must have been moved to their proper distances before they were launched.

# ASTRONOMY.

To conclude: In astronomy, the primary challenge is to lift the imagination to the scale of the subject, which is often done in opposition to the impressions made upon our senses. For example, we must overcome an illusion arising from the vast distance from which we view the heavenly bodies—namely, the apparent slowness of their movements. The moon may take several hours to move just "half a yard" away from a star it once touched. We might think such a deliberate motion is easily guided. But what are the facts? In reality, during all that time, the moon is racing through the heavens at a speed of considerably more than two thousand miles per hour. This is more than double the speed at which a ball is fired from the mouth of a cannon. Yet this immense speed is just as much under control as if the planet moved ever so slowly or were guided along its path inch by inch. 

It is also difficult for the imagination to conceive (though it is necessary to do so to judge the matter fairly) just how *loose*, so to speak, the heavenly bodies are. Enormous globes, held by nothing and confined by nothing, are released into free and boundless space, each following its path by virtue of an invisible principle. This principle is singular, common, and identical for all of them, and it can be scientifically determined. To prevent these bodies from becoming lost, from colliding into heaps, or from interfering with and disrupting one another's motions to a degree that would destroy any lasting order—that is <note>original: "h. e."; an abbreviation for the Latin *hoc est*, meaning "that is"</note>, to cause them to form planetary systems that can be maintained once they are created, and especially systems suited to the organized and sentient beings that the planets support (as we know is the case on our own Earth, the only place where we can truly observe this)—all of this requires an intelligent intervention. # CHAPTER 23.

## OF THE PERSONALITY OF THE DEITY.

Contrivance, if established, appears to me to prove everything which we wish to prove. Among other things, it proves the *personality* of the Deity, as distinguished from what is sometimes called "nature" or sometimes called a "principle." These terms, in the mouths of those who use them philosophically, seem to be intended to admit and to express an efficacy <term>the power to produce an effect</term>, but to exclude and to deny a personal agent. Now, that which can contrive, which can design, must be a person. These capacities constitute personality, for they imply consciousness and thought. They require a being that can perceive an end or purpose, as well as the power of providing means and of directing them to their end*. They require a center in which perceptions unite and from which volitions <term>acts of will or choice</term> flow; this center is the mind. The acts of a mind prove the existence of a mind: and in whatever a mind resides is a person. The seat of intellect is a person.

We have no authority to limit the properties of mind to any particular corporeal <term>physical or bodily</term> form, or any particular circumscription of space. These properties exist, in created nature, under a great variety of sensible forms. Also, every animated being has its *sensorium* <term>the seat of sensation or the sensory center of the brain</term>, that is, a certain portion of space within which perception and volition are exerted. This sphere may be enlarged to an inde— <note>The text continues on the next page to describe how this sphere of influence might be extended.</note>

"No man has seen God at any time." <note>original: "No man hath seen God at any time" (John 1:18)</note> I believe this fact creates the greatest difficulty for us. Another species is granted the sense of smell. This is an advancement in the knowledge of the powers and properties of nature. But if this favored animal were to infer—based on its superiority over the category of animals just described—that it perceived everything perceptible in nature, we would know (even if the animal itself did not suspect it) that it was basing its conclusion on a false and arrogant estimate of its own faculties.

However, the strength of this reasoning is sometimes lost because we settle for mere labels. We have already noted*, and we must emphasize here again, the misuse of the term "law" and the misunderstanding of what that term expresses in physics. This error occurs whenever the idea of a law is used to replace the concept of power—and especially an intelligent power—and is assigned as the cause of anything, or any property of anything, that exists. This is what we are secretly prone to do when we speak of *organized bodies (plants, for instance, or animals)* owing their production, their form, their growth, their qualities, their beauty, or their usefulness to any "law" or "laws of nature," and when we are content to stop our inquiries with that answer. I say once more: it is a misuse of language to assign any law as the efficient <term>efficient cause: the actual agent or force that produces an effect</term>, operative cause of anything. A law presupposes an *agent*, for it is only the *method* according to which an agent proceeds; it implies a *power*, for it is the *order* according to which that power acts. Without this agent, without this power—both of which are distinct from the law itself—the "law" does nothing and *is* nothing.

What has been said concerning "law" also holds true for mechanism. Mechanism is not power itself. Mechanism, without power, can do nothing. Even if a watch were designed and built with the greatest ingenuity—even if its parts were numerous, complex, finely crafted, and cleverly put together—it cannot *run* without a weight or spring; that is, without a force that is *independent of, and beyond* its mechanism. The intervention and arrangement of what are called "**second causes**" <note>Intermediary physical or natural causes that produce an effect, as opposed to the "First Cause" or God</note> fall under the same observation. This arrangement is or is not viewed as mechanism depending on whether we can or cannot trace it using our senses and means of examination. That is the only difference; and it is a difference that relates to our own faculties, not to the things themselves. Now, where the order of second causes is mechanical, what is said here of mechanism applies strictly to it. But everything would always be seen as mechanism (*natural chemistry*, for instance, would be seen as mechanism) if our senses were sharp enough to perceive it. Therefore, neither mechanism in the works of nature, nor the intervention of what are called second causes (for I believe they are the same thing), removes the necessity of an agent distinct from both.

If, in tracing these causes, it is said that we find certain general properties of matter which have nothing in them that suggests intelligence, I answer that the management of these properties—the directing and pointing of them toward the uses we see them serve—still demands intelligence in the highest degree. For example, suppose animal secretions are the result of elective attractions <note>An archaic chemical term for chemical affinity or the tendency of certain substances to bond</note>, and that such attractions belong universally to specific substances in which no intellect is involved. There must be more in nature than what we see; and, among the things unseen, there must be an intelligent, designing author. The philosopher looks with astonishment at the production of things around him. Unconscious particles of matter take their positions and range themselves in an order so as to collectively become plants or animals—that is, organized bodies with parts that have a strict and obvious relationship to one another and to the usefulness of the whole. It appears that these particles could not move in any other way than they do, for they show not the slightest sign of choice, freedom, or discretion. There may be "plastic natures" <note>An archaic term for a formative or creative power in nature</note>, specific intelligent beings guiding these motions in each case; or they may be the result of sequences of mechanical arrangements, fixed beforehand by an intelligent appointment and kept in action by a power at the center. But in either case, there must be intelligence.

The minds of most men are fond of what they call a "principle," and they like the appearance of simplicity when explaining phenomena. Yet this principle, this simplicity, is sometimes nothing more than a *name*. That name perhaps covers a diverse, complex, or progressive operation that can be broken down into parts. The power in organized bodies to produce bodies like themselves is one of these principles. Give a philosopher this, and he can proceed. But he does not reflect on what this principle (if he chooses to call it that), or what this mode of

We might as well call the casting of metals a principle: we might, as far as it appears to me, as well call spinning and weaving principles. We might even dispense, indeed, with the necessity of any artist at all, either in the manufacturing of the article or in the construction of the machinery by which the manufacturing was carried on.

<margin>v</margin>

The opinion which would consider "reproduction" <note>original: "generation"</note> as a law of nature, and which would assign this law as the cause—or try to satisfy our minds with such a cause—for the existence of organized bodies, is proven wrong in my judgment. It is refuted not only by every mark of design <note>original: "contrivance"</note> found in those bodies (for which this theory provides no designer and no explanation whatsoever) but also by the further fact that things produced by reproduction possess a clear relationship to things *not* produced by reproduction. 

If it were merely one part of a reproduced body relating to another part of the same body—such as an animal's mouth to the throat, the throat to the stomach, the stomach to the intestines, those to the replenishment of the blood, and the blood to the nourishment of the whole frame—it might be argued that this was all due to their common origin. Similarly, if it were only one reproduced body relating to another reproduced body—such as the sexes of the same species to each other, predators to their prey, or plant-eating <note>original: "herbivorous and graminivorous"</note> animals to the plants or seeds they eat—it might be contended that this entire correspondence was attributable to reproduction, the common source from which these beings proceeded.

...as a result of being struck by a comet. Having set the earth in motion by that same strike—both on its own axis and around the sun—his next difficulty is how to introduce plants and animals onto it. To solve this problem, we are asked to imagine that the universe is filled with particles endowed with life, yet lacking their own organization or senses. These particles are also supposedly endowed with a tendency to arrange themselves into organized forms. The gathering of these particles, driven by this tendency but without intelligence, will, or direction (for I do not find that any of these qualities are attributed to them), has produced the living forms we see today.

Very few of the theories that philosophers gamble on regarding these subjects claim anything more than challenging you to show that their hypothesis is strictly impossible. In this current example, there seems to be a clear and obvious objection to the entire scheme: if things were as described, *new* combinations should be constantly occurring. New plants and animals—or organized bodies that are neither—ought to be appearing before our eyes every day.

To this, however, our philosopher has an answer. Since so many forms of plants and animals already exist, and consequently so many "internal molds" <note>This refers to Buffon’s theory of "moules intérieurs," which suggested that organic molecules are shaped by internal biological structures.</note>, as he calls them, are ready and available, the organic particles flow into these molds. As far as I can recall, the only natural phenomenon mentioned by our author as a fact upon which to build his hypothesis—the only support on which it rests—is the formation of *worms* in the intestines of animals. He attributes this to the combination of excessive organic particles floating around in the digestive tract. He claims these particles have combined themselves into these simple animal forms because they lacked "internal molds" <note>Referring to Buffon's theory of "moules intérieurs," where organic molecules are shaped by existing biological structures.</note>, or found no empty spaces in existing molds into which they could be received. The example referred to is more a category of facts than a single fact, as other cases might be included under it with equal reason. 

However, to accept this as a fact at all, or to make it applicable to the question, we must start by asserting the existence of *spontaneous generation* <term>original: "equivocal generation"; the outdated theory that living organisms can emerge from non-living matter</term>. This is contrary to analogy and unnecessary. It is contrary to analogy because throughout the limits of our knowledge, wherever we can examine plants or animals, we find reproduction from a parent form. It is unnecessary because I believe it is rarely difficult to suggest ways in which eggs, spawn, or the invisible beginnings of these pests may have entered the cavities where they are found. Additionally, their *constancy* to their species—which I believe is as regular in these as in other *worms* <note>original: "*vermes*"</note>—decides the matter against our philosopher, if indeed any doubt remained on the subject.

Lastly, these wonder-working instruments—these "internal molds"—what are they, after all? When examined, what are they but a name without meaning? They are unintelligible, if not self-contradictory. At best, they differ in no way from the "essential forms" <term>the Platonic or Aristotelian idea that an object has an ideal 'form' that determines its nature</term> of Greek philosophy. One short sentence from Buffon’s work explains his scheme as follows: "When this nutritious and prolific matter, which is spread throughout all nature, passes through the *internal mold* of an animal or vegetable and finds a proper matrix or receptacle, it gives rise to an animal or vegetable of the same species." 

Does any reader attach a meaning to the expression "internal mold" in this sentence? Should it then be said that, although we have little notion of an internal mold, we have no better understanding of a designing mind? The truth is exactly the opposite of that assertion. When we speak of a craftsman or an architect, we speak of something comprehensible to our understanding and familiar to our experience. We use no terms other than those that refer us to our own consciousness and observation for their meaning; they express objects we constantly encounter. In contrast, names like the one we have mentioned <note>Referring to Buffon's "internal molds"</note> refer us to nothing. They spark no idea; they convey a sound to the ear, but I believe they do nothing more.

Another system, which has recently been proposed with much ingenuity, is that of *appetencies* <term>the theory that the desires or needs of an organism drive the physical development of its organs over generations</term>. The principle and brief summary of the theory is this: pieces of soft, flexible matter, being endowed with propensities or "appetencies" for specific actions, would—through continuous effort carried on through a long series of generations—gradually work themselves into suitable forms. Eventually, they would acquire an organization suited to the action which their respective desires led them to perform, though perhaps through obscure and nearly imperceptible improvements. Although I have introduced this theory here, I am reluctant to call it an *atheistic* scheme for two reasons. First, as far as I understand it, the original tendencies and their countless varieties—which differ greatly from the laws of mechanical nature, which are few and simple—are, within the theory itself, attributed to the decree and appointment of an intelligent and designing Creator. Second, the major assumption <term>postulatum</term> that is taken for granted throughout—the ability of living bodies to produce other bodies organized like themselves—seems to be attributed to that same cause; at least, no other explanation is attempted. 

In one important respect, however, this theory aligns with atheistic systems: namely, that in the formation of plants and animals, and in the structure and use of their parts, it eliminates final causes <term>the concept that things are designed for a specific purpose or end-goal</term>. Instead of the parts of a plant or animal—or their specific structures—having been intended for the function or use we see them perform, this theory suggests they have actually grown out of that action and originated from that use.
