This theory, therefore, does away with what we insist is necessary in every particular case: an intelligent, designing mind to plan and determine the forms that organized bodies take. Give our philosopher these "appetencies" <term>natural urges or strivings for development</term>; give him a portion of living, irritable matter (a nerve, or even a scrap of a nerve) to work upon; and also give his beginning or developing forms the power to reproduce their own kind at every stage of their alteration. If he is to be believed, he could then fill the world with all the plant and animal life that we currently see in it.

The scheme under consideration is open to the same objection as other conjectures of a similar type: namely, a total lack of evidence. No changes like those required by the theory have ever been observed. All the transformations described in *Ovid's Metamorphoses* <note>A classical Roman poem by Ovid depicting mythical transformations of humans into animals and plants.</note> might have been possible if this theory were true; yet not a single example—nor even a claim of an example—is offered of any such change being known to have occurred. Nor does the order of reproduction follow the principle upon which this theory is built. Male nipples have not vanished through disuse <term>inusitation</term>; <note>original: "nec curtorum, per multa sæcula, Judæorum propagini deest præputium"</note> nor has the foreskin disappeared from the offspring of Jews, despite centuries of circumcision. It is easy to say, as has been said, that the process of change is too slow to be perceived; that it has been carried out through immeasurable spans of time; and that the present order of things is the result of a gradual progression of which no human record can trace the steps. It is easy to say this; and yet it remains true that the hypothesis is entirely without evidence.

The analogies which have been alleged are of the following kind. The hump of a camel is said to be nothing more than the effect of carrying heavy loads—a service in which the species has been employed since the most ancient times. The first generation, by the daily loading of their backs, would probably find a small, lumpy swelling <term>grumous tumour</term> to be formed in the flesh of that part. The next offspring would bring this swelling into the world with them. The life for which they were destined would increase it. Since the cause which first generated the lump <term>tubercle</term> continued, it would go on increasing in size through every successive generation until it attained the form and bulk under which it now appears. 

This may serve for one instance; another, and that also of the passive sort, is taken from certain species of birds. Birds of the *crane* kind—such as the crane itself, the heron, bittern, and stork—have, in general, thighs that are bare of feathers. This lack of feathers is accounted for by the habit of wading in water and the effect of that element in checking the growth of feathers on those parts. In consequence of this, the health and growth of the feathers declined through each generation of the animal; the tender down, exposed to cold and wetness, became weak, thin, and sparse until the deterioration ended in the result which we see today: absolute nakedness. 

I will mention a third instance because it is drawn from an active habit, whereas the last two were from passive habits; and that is the *pouch* of the pelican. The description which naturalists give of this organ is as follows: "From the lower edges of the lower jaw <term>under chap</term> hangs a bag, reaching the whole length of the bill to the neck, which is said to be capable of containing fifteen quarts of water. The bird has the power to wrinkle this bag up into the hollow of the lower jaw. When the bag is empty it is not seen; but when the bird has fished with success, it is..."

These, or arguments of this kind, are the analogies relied upon. The senses of animals appear to me completely incapable of being explained by the origin story this theory provides. Including under the word "sense" both the physical organ and the mental perception, we are given no account of either. How will our philosopher explain *vision*, or the creation of an eye? How could a blind animal strive for sight, when we know blind animals have neither a concept of it nor a desire for it? This objection remains valid no matter how much importance you assign to the passage of time, the power of habit, or changes too slow to be observed by man or compared to the past. No laws, no processes, and no powers of nature that exist today—nor any similar to them—could bring a new sense into existence. It is useless to inquire how something might progress if it could never actually *begin*.

I believe the senses are the most inconsistent part of the animal body <term>frame</term> with the hypothesis we are discussing. However, other parts are just as problematic. ## CHAPTER XXIV.

### OF THE NATURAL ATTRIBUTES OF THE DEITY.

**I**t is a profound conclusion that there is a God—a perceiving, intelligent, and designing Being who stands at the head of creation and from whose will it originated. Assuming His existence is proven, the attributes of such a Being must be equal to the magnitude, extent, and complexity of His works. These works are not only vast beyond comparison with those performed by any other power, but—as far as our understanding of them goes—they are infinite, because they are unlimited in every direction.

Yet, contemplating a nature so exalted overwhelms our mental faculties, however certainly we arrive at the proof of its existence. The mind feels its powers fail under the weight of the subject. One consequence of this is that, to escape the strain of abstract thought, our minds seek relief in physical images. From this, we can explain the ancient and almost universal tendency toward substituting idols for God. These idols are the resources of a struggling imagination. False religions usually give in to this natural tendency; true religions, or those derived from the truth, resist it.

It is one of the advantages of the divine revelations we acknowledge that, while they reject idolatry and its many harmful effects, they introduce the <term>Deity</term> <note>God</note> to human understanding through a concept that is more personal, more definite, and more within our mental grasp than <term>natural theology</term> <note>the study of God based on observed facts and experience apart from divine revelation</note> can—

The foundation of divine "omnipresence" in <term>natural theology</term><note>The study of God based on observed facts and experience rather than divine revelation</note> rests on this: in every part and place of the universe with which we are acquainted, we perceive the exercise of a power which we believe, either directly or indirectly, proceeds from the <term>Deity</term><note>God</note>. For instance, in what part or point of space that has ever been explored do we not discover attraction? In what regions do we not find light? In what accessible portion of our globe do we not meet with gravity, magnetism, or electricity, together with the properties and powers of organized substances in vegetable or animal nature? Furthermore, we may ask: what kingdom of nature is there, or what corner of space where anything can be examined by us, where we do not encounter <term>contrivance</term><note>Deliberate mechanical invention or planning</note> and design?

Perhaps the only reflection that arises in our minds from this view of the world around us is that the laws of nature prevail everywhere—that they are uniform and universal. But what do we mean by the "laws of nature," or by any law? Effects are produced by power, not by laws. A law cannot execute itself. A law refers us to an agent. Now, an agency so general that we cannot discover its absence, or identify a place where some effect of its continued energy is not found, may—in popular language at least, and perhaps without much deviation from philosophical strictness—be called universal. With similar and considerable propriety, the person or Being in whom that power resides, or from whom it is derived, may be understood to be **omnipresent**. He who sustains all...

"Eternity" is a negative concept given a positive name. It assumes that the subject currently exists and is the denial of a beginning or an end to that existence. As applied to the <term>Deity</term><note>God</note>, this has not been disputed by anyone who acknowledges a God at all. Most certainly, there never was a time in which nothing existed, because that condition would have continued forever. A universal blank must have remained; nothing could have emerged from it; nothing could ever have existed since, and nothing could exist now. Strictly speaking, however, we have no concern with time prior to the existence of the visible world. Regarding this point of theology, therefore, it is sufficient to know that the Designer necessarily existed before the design.

"Self-existence" is another negative concept—namely, the denial of any preceding cause, such as a parent, a maker, an author, or a creator.

"Necessary existence" means an existence that can be logically demonstrated.

"Spirituality" expresses an idea made up of a negative part and a positive part. ## CHAPTER XXV.

### THE UNITY OF THE DEITY.

The proof of the "unity of the <term>Deity</term><note>God</note>" is the *uniformity* of the plan observable in the universe. The universe itself is a single system; each part either depends upon other parts or is connected to them by some common law of motion or by the presence of some common substance. The same principle of gravitation causes a stone to fall toward the earth and the moon to orbit around it. A single law of attraction carries all the different planets around the sun. This is something <term>philosophers</term><note>natural philosophers or scientists</note> demonstrate. There are also other points of agreement among them which may be considered marks of the identity of their origin and of their intelligent author. In all of them are found the convenience and stability derived from gravitation. They all experience the cycles of day and night and the changes of seasons. They all—at least Jupiter, Mars, and Venus—derive the same advantages from their atmospheres as we do. In all the planets, the axes of rotation are stable. Nothing is more probable than that the same gravitational influence, acting according to the same rule, reaches to the fixed stars; but if this is only probable, another thing is certain: namely, that the same element of light does. The light from a fixed star affects our eyes in the same manner, and is refracted and reflected according to the same laws, as the light of a candle. The velocity of light from the fixed stars is also the same as the velocity of light from the sun, as reflected from the <term>satellites</term><note>The original text ends mid-word with the catchword "satel."</note>.

<summary>This page argues that the unity of God is proven by the uniform laws of nature, such as gravity and light, which operate consistently across the solar system and the distant stars.</summary>

On our globe, the case is even clearer. New countries are continually being discovered, yet the old laws of nature are always found within them. We may find new plants or animals, but they are always found alongside plants and animals we already know, and they always possess many of the same general properties. We never encounter such unique or entirely different forms of life as to suggest that we have entered the domain of a different Creator or are under the direction of a different will. In truth, the same order of things stays with us wherever we go. The elements act upon one another, electricity operates, the tides rise and fall, and the magnetic needle finds its position in one region of the earth and sea just as it does in another. A single atmosphere surrounds and connects every part of the globe; one sun provides light, and one moon exerts its specific gravitational attraction upon all parts. If there is variety in natural effects—as, for example, in the tides of different seas—that very variety is the result of the same cause acting under different circumstances. In many cases, this has been proven; in all cases, it is probable.

The inspection and comparison of *living forms* add countless examples to this argument. The structure of all large land animals is very much alike. Their senses are nearly the same. Their natural functions and passions are nearly the same. Their <term>viscera</term><note>internal organs</note> are nearly the same in substance, shape, and function. Digestion, nutrition, circulation, and secretion proceed in a similar manner in all of them. The primary circulating fluid is the same; for I believe no difference has been discovered in the properties of blood, regardless of which animal it is drawn from. The experiment of transfusion proves that the blood of one animal will sustain another. The skeletons of larger land animals also show specific variations, but—

# CHAPTER XXVI.

## THE GOODNESS OF THE DEITY.

The proof of *divine goodness* rests upon two propositions, each of which, as we contend, can be proven by observations drawn from the appearances of nature.

The first is, "that in the vast majority of instances in which design is perceived, the purpose of the design is *beneficial*." <note>Paley uses the word "contrivance" to describe the purposeful arrangement of parts within a mechanism or organism.</note>

The second is, "that the Deity has added *pleasure* to animal sensations beyond what was necessary for any other purpose, or even when the purpose, so far as it was necessary, could have been achieved through the operation of pain."

First, "in the vast majority of instances in which design is perceived, the purpose of the design is *beneficial*."

No products of nature display design as clearly as the parts of animals; and I believe that all animal parts have a real—and, with very few exceptions, a known and understandable—usefulness to the animal. Now, when we consider the multitude of animals, the number of parts in each, their shape and fitness, the faculties depending upon them, the variety of species, the complexity of their structure, and the success and happiness of the result in so many cases, we can never reflect upon the character of that Being from whom all these things have proceeded without the deepest adoration. We cannot help acknowledging what a great exertion of benevolence creation was—a benevolence that is as detailed in its care as it is vast in its scope.

<summary>Paley introduces two arguments for the goodness of God: that natural designs are almost always intended for the benefit of the creature, and that God added pleasure to life beyond what was strictly necessary for survival.</summary>
<keywords>Divine Goodness, benevolence, design, contrivance, animal sensations, creation, purpose of nature</keywords>

--- Page 334 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Goodness of the Deity," shifting from abstract propositions to empirical observations of the animal kingdom as evidence of a benevolent Creator.</meta>

-># THE GOODNESS OF THE DEITY.<-

When we examine the parts and faculties of animals, and their limbs and senses in particular, I believe we find the appropriate evidence for the conclusion we wish to establish. I will not say that the inanimate parts of nature were made solely for the benefit of living creatures; however, when we consider the benevolence of the Deity, we can only understand it in relation to sensitive beings <term>beings capable of feeling or perception</term>. Without this connection, or if applied to anything else, the concept of goodness has no target, and the term has no meaning. Inanimate matter is nothing in this regard. Therefore, although the parts of animals—especially the limbs and senses—make up only a small fraction of the physical world by mass and quantity, they are the only things capable of perception. Because of this, they represent the entirety of visible nature when we are trying to judge the intentions of its Author. Consequently, it is in these living beings that we should look for His character. It is through them that we can prove that the world was created with a benevolent design.

And this design has not failed. After all, it is a happy world. The air, the earth, and the water overflow with joyful life. On a spring afternoon or a summer evening, no matter where I look, thousands of happy creatures fill my sight. “The insect youth are on the wing.” <note>Paley is quoting Thomas Gray’s poem, "Ode on the Spring."</note> Swarms of newly hatched *flies* are testing their wings in the air. Its life seems to be pure enjoyment—it is so busy and so content. The *young* of all animals seem to me to receive pleasure simply from exercising their limbs and physical faculties, without aiming for a specific goal or any practical purpose for that effort. A child, knowing nothing of the use of language, is nonetheless highly delighted by being able to speak. A child is delighted with speaking without having anything to say, and with walking without knowing where to go. Even before these stages, I am inclined to believe that the waking hours of infancy are pleasantly occupied with exercising the sense of sight—or perhaps more accurately, with learning how to see.

In one important way, the elderly have the advantage: generally speaking, a state of ease is more attainable than a state of active pleasure. Therefore, a physical constitution that can enjoy ease is preferable to one that can only experience enjoyment through active pleasure.

This same sense of ease often makes old age a condition of great comfort, especially when "riding at anchor"—secure and still—after a busy or stormy life. It is well described by Rousseau as the interval of rest and enjoyment between the frantic pace of life and its conclusion. We cannot judge with certainty how far this same principle extends to other animal species. However, the apparent satisfaction with which most animals seek and enjoy rest as their activity slows down gives us reason to believe that this source of pleasure is granted to advanced life in most, if not all, of its various forms.

Regarding the species we know best—our own—I am far from thinking, even as a secular observer of human life, that youth is the happiest season, let alone the only happy one. As a Christian, I am inclined to believe there is a great deal of truth in the following description provided by a very devout writer and excellent man:* 

“To the intelligent and virtuous, old age presents a scene of peaceful enjoyment, of controlled desires, of well-regulated emotions, of mature knowledge, and of calm preparation for immortality. What we see in different stages of the same life is even more clearly illustrated in the lives of different animals. Animal enjoyments are infinitely diverse. The ways of life dictated by the physical makeup of different animals are not only various but often completely opposite. Yet each animal is happy in its own way. For instance, predators live mostly alone, while animals with a milder nature live in society. Yet the herring, which lives in shoals, and the sheep, which lives in flocks, are no happier in a crowd or more contented among their companions than the pike or the lion is in the deep solitude of the pond or the forest.

However, some might argue that the examples I have presented—whether of high energy or of rest, or the apparent enjoyment derived from either—are carefully selected and favorable cases. In each individual, many things must function correctly for it to be at ease; yet, what a large proportion of every species is in that state at any given second?

But, to do justice to the question, the system of animal destruction ought always to be considered in strict connection with another property of animal nature: namely, *<term>superfecundity</term>* <note>the capacity of organisms to produce much more offspring than can possibly survive</note>. These are offsetting qualities. One exists by balancing the other. Therefore, in treating the subject from this perspective (which I believe is the correct one), our task will be, first, to point out the advantages gained by nature’s power of superabundant multiplication; and then, to show that these advantages provide the reasons for establishing that system of animal hostilities which we are trying to explain.

In almost all cases, nature produces her supplies in profusion. A single codfish spawns more eggs in one season than there are inhabitants in all of England. A thousand other instances of prolific reproduction could be cited which, though not equal to this, would still cause a species to increase with a rapidity that defies calculation and reaches an immeasurable extent. The advantages of such a system are twofold: first, it tends to keep the world always full; and second, it allows the proportion between various species of animals to be modified as different purposes require, or as different environments provide room and food for them. Where this vast fertility meets a vacancy suited for a species, it operates with its full effect; there it pours in its numbers and fills the void. We complain about what we call the excessive multiplication of certain troublesome insects, not reflecting that large portions of nature might be left empty without it. If the reports of travelers can be trusted, immense tracts of forest in North America...

Is it a subject of complaint, and not of praise?

What we call blights are, oftentimes, legions of animated beings claiming their portion in the bounty of nature. What corrupts the produce of the earth for us prepares it for them. And it is by means of their rapid multiplication that they take possession of their pasture; a slow propagation would not meet the opportunity.

Regarding the human species, it may be a part of the design of <term>Providence</term> <note>divine guidance or God’s plan for the universe</note> that the earth should be inhabited by a shifting, or perhaps a circulating, population. Within this economy of nature, it is possible that there may be several advantages. When old countries become exceedingly corrupt, simpler modes of life, purer morals, and better institutions may rise up in new ones, while fresh soils reward the cultivator with more plentiful harvests. Thus, the different portions of the globe come into use in succession as the residence of man. In his absence, these lands host other guests who, by their rapid multiplication, soon fill the void. In domesticated animals, we find the benefit of their <term>fecundity</term> <note>fertility; ability to produce offspring</note> to be that we can always command sufficient numbers. We can always have as many of any particular species as we please, or as many as we can support. Nor do we complain of an excess of them; it is much easier to regulate abundance than it is to provide for a scarcity.

But this <term>superfecundity</term> <note>the capacity of organisms to produce much more offspring than can survive</note>, though of great occasional use and importance, exceeds the ordinary capacity of nature to receive or support its offspring. All superabundance implies destruction, or else it must destroy itself. There is perhaps no species of land animal that would not overrun the earth if it were permitted to multiply in perfect safety, nor any fish that would not fill the ocean. At the very least, if any single species were left to its natural increase without disturbance or restraint, its maintenance would exhaust the food sources of all other species. 

It is necessary, therefore, that the effects of such prolific faculties be curtailed. Along with other checks and limits, all serving the same purpose, are the "thinnings" which take place among animals through their actions upon one another <note>this refers to predation and competition for resources</note>.

In some instances, we ourselves experience the benefit of these natural conflicts quite directly. One species of insects rids us of another species, or at least reduces their ranks. A third species perhaps keeps the second within bounds, and birds or lizards act as a defense against the excessive increase by which even these last species might plague us. In other instances—more numerous and possibly more important—this arrangement of things may be necessary and useful to certain other species, even if it is less necessary for us or less observed by us. It may even be essential for preventing the loss of certain species from the universe, a misfortune that Nature seems to carefully guard against. Although there may be the appearance of failure in some of the details of Nature’s works, she never fails in her major purposes. Her species never go extinct. The provision that was originally made for the continuous repopulating of the world has proven itself to be effective through a long succession of ages.

What further shows that the system of destruction among animals has a direct connection to the system of <term>fecundity</term> <note>fertility; the ability to produce many offspring</note>—that they are indeed parts of one balancing scheme—is that, in each species, the fertility is proportional to the smallness of the animal, its weakness, the shortness of its natural lifespan, and the dangers and enemies that surround it. An elephant produces only one calf, but a butterfly lays six hundred eggs. Birds of prey seldom produce more than two eggs; however, the sparrow family and the duck family frequently sit upon a dozen. In the rivers, we find a thousand minnows for every one pike; in the sea, a million herrings for every single shark. Compensation applies throughout. <margin>✓</margin> Vulnerability and destruction are repaired by high reproductive rates.

Our *first* proposition, and the one which we have been defending until now, was "that in a vast majority of instances in which *contrivance* <term>deliberate design or planning</term> is perceived, the design of the contrivance is beneficial."

Our *second* proposition is "that the Deity has added *pleasure* to animal sensations beyond what was necessary for any other purpose, or in cases where the purpose, so far as it was necessary, might have been achieved through the operation of pain."

This proposition may be explained in this way: The capacities which, according to the established course of nature, are necessary for the support or preservation of an animal—however clearly they may be the result of an organization designed for that purpose—can only be considered an act or a part of the same will that decreed the existence of the animal itself. This is because, whether the creation proceeded from a benevolent or a malevolent being, these capacities must have been given if the animal were to exist at all. Therefore, animal properties that fall under this description do not strictly prove the goodness of God. It involves capacities for pleasure in cases where—so far as the survival of the individual or the species is concerned—they were not required, or where the same purpose might have been secured through the operation of pain. A coincidence is required here that no accident can explain. There are three possible theories regarding this subject, and no more. First: that the sense, by its original makeup, suited the object. Likewise, the degree of dullness or sharpness in the sense itself is not a random thing. To preserve the harmony mentioned here, the sense must exist in an exact or near correspondence with the strength of the sensory impression.

Rather, this power of adaptation <term>accommodation: the ability to adjust or adapt to circumstances</term>—to the extent that it exists—was designed and provided by the Creator of their physical structure and is part of their perfection.

This is, in other words, the goodness of the Author of nature toward his sentient creation.

## THE ORIGIN OF EVIL

No universal solution has been discovered for the ORIGIN OF EVIL; by this, I mean no solution that addresses every possible case of suffering. The most comprehensive explanation is the one that arises from the consideration of *general rules* <note>This argument, common in natural theology, suggests that God governs the world through consistent laws rather than constant miracles, which allows for a predictable environment but occasionally results in collateral harm.</note>. I believe we can, without much difficulty, be brought to accept the following four points:

1. First, that significant advantages benefit the universe when the natural order operates according to general laws.
2. Second, that general laws, no matter how well-designed and established, often conflict with and counteract one another.
3. Third, that these conflicts and intersections will frequently result in specific hardships.
4. Fourth, that our observations support the idea that these hardships do occur to some degree within the works of nature.

These points may be accepted; it may also be argued that the general laws we are aware of are intended for beneficial ends. On the other hand, we are completely unaware of many of these laws, or we are totally unable to follow their various branches and see how they function. The result of this ignorance is that these laws cannot serve as standards by which we regulate our own conduct. The preservation <note>original: "conversation"</note> of these laws may be important in other respects, or to other beings, but we are not informed of their specific value or use. Consequently, we do not know when or to what extent they may or may not be suspended—or their effects turned aside—by a presiding and benevolent Will, without causing greater evils than those which would be...

The doctrine of *imperfections*—or, as it is called, "evils of imperfection"—provides an explanation that, like the previous one, is based on a view of the entire natural world. The doctrine is briefly this: it is probable that creation is better filled by various kinds of sentient beings than by sentient beings who are all of one type. It is also probable that it is better filled by different levels of beings organized in a hierarchy rising one above another, rather than by beings who all possess equal degrees of perfection. Now, a hierarchy of such beings naturally implies a hierarchy of imperfections. No class of being can rightly complain of the imperfections that belong to its specific place in the scale, unless it were also valid to complain that a scale of being <term>scale of being: the "Great Chain of Being," a concept where all things are ranked in a hierarchy from the simplest matter to the most complex life and divinity</term> was established in nature at all. There appear to be reasons of wisdom and goodness for this arrangement.

In the same way, *finiteness*—or anything that can be reduced to being limited—in non-living objects can never be a fair subject of complaint. If it were ever a problem, it would always be a problem; by this, we mean that we can never reasonably demand that things should be larger or...

Therefore, I would add that we should not complain about certain other evils that are justified by the same reasoning as these acknowledged "evils of imperfection" <term>evils of imperfection: the inherent limitations or "gaps" in a creature's abilities or environment compared to a theoretical state of perfection</term>. But for us, what is the difference between a smaller globe and a portion of our current globe being uninhabitable? The inhabitants of an island might be prone to grumble about the barrenness <term>sterility: the state of being unproductive or unable to grow crops; barrenness</term> of certain areas, such as its rocks, sands, or swamps. However, no one feels entitled to complain simply because the island isn't larger than it is. Yet, these two complaints are essentially the same.

The points mentioned above are the two metaphysical <term>metaphysical: relating to abstract reasoning or the fundamental nature of existence rather than physical evidence</term> answers that have been offered for this major question. They are not less valid for being metaphysical, provided they are based on sound reasoning (which I believe they are). However, they are too broad in scope for us to fully survey, and it is often difficult to apply them to specific details. Therefore, our reflections might be more useful if they are confined to a narrower focus.

Pain itself is also not without its *alleviations*. It may be intense and frequent, but it is rarely both intense and long-lasting; its pauses and breaks actually become a source of positive pleasure. Death itself, as a method of removal and succession, is so connected with the entire order of our animal world that almost everything in that world would have to be changed to be able to do without it. It also seems impossible to separate the fear of death from the enjoyment of life, or the awareness of that fear from rational beings. Animals are, in large part, delivered from all anxiety on this account because of their lower mental faculties. Or rather, they seem to be equipped with the apprehension of death just enough to drive them toward the means of self-preservation, and no further. But would a human being wish to buy this immunity by losing those mental powers which enable him to look forward to the future?

Death implies *separation*, and the loss of those whom we love must necessarily be accompanied by pain. For the animal kingdom, nature seems to have stepped in with some secret provision for their relief when their attachments are broken. In their instincts toward their offspring, and those of the offspring toward them, I have often been surprised to observe how ardently they love and how soon they forget. The persistence of human sorrow (upon which time also, at length, lays its softening hand) is probably, therefore, connected in some way to the qualities of our rational or moral nature. One thing, however, is clear: namely, that it is better for us to possess affections—the sources of so many virtues and so many joys—even though they are exposed to the incidents of life and the interruptions of mortality, than to be reduced to a state of selfishness, apathy, and <term>quietism</term> <note>A state of total passivity or withdrawal from the world</note> by the lack of them.

# THE GOODNESS OF THE DEITY

...evil, as far as it arises from that which is external to us.

*Social evils*, or the hardships of life in society, are much more easily explained than physical evils. This is because they are, in truth, much smaller in scale, and also because they result from a kind of necessity. They arise not only from the basic constitution of our nature but from a part of that nature which no one would wish to see altered. The case is this: mankind in every country will *reproduce* up to a certain point of distress. That point may vary in different countries or ages, according to the established standards of living in each. It will also shift on the scale—allowing for a greater or smaller number of inhabitants—depending on how much food is either produced in the country or imported from elsewhere.

But there must always be such a limit, and the species will always grow until it reaches it. The rate of human reproduction proceeds by something like a *geometrical progression* <note>Exponential growth (e.g., 2, 4, 8, 16).</note>. The increase of food supplies, even under the most favorable circumstances, can only grow in the form of an *arithmetic series* <note>Linear growth (e.g., 2, 4, 6, 8).</note>. It follows from this that the population will always catch up to the food supply; it will pass the line of plenty and continue to increase until it is stopped by the difficulty of getting enough to eat <note>This entire paragraph summarizes the "Malthusian Trap," a theory famously proposed by Thomas Robert Malthus in his 1798 work, *An Essay on the Principle of Population*.</note>. Therefore, such difficulty, along with the circumstances that follow it, *must* be found in every established country. These circumstances are what we call poverty, which necessarily results in hard labor, domestic service, and social restraint.

It seems impossible to populate a country with inhabitants who are all in comfortable circumstances. For even if we suppose that could be done, there would be such frequent marrying and having children among them, as...

The social distinctions of civil life are often viewed as evils by those who occupy lower positions, but in my opinion, there is very little reason for that view.

<margin>✓</margin>
In the first place, the advantages that higher social conditions are supposed to provide are not worth nearly as much as the advantages bestowed by nature. The gifts of nature always surpass the gifts of fortune <term>wealth and status</term>. How much better, for example, is physical activity than being served by others <term>attendance</term>? Or beauty, compared to fancy clothing? Or a healthy appetite, good digestion, and comfortable <term>tranquil</term> bowels, compared to the tricks of professional cooking or forced, expensive, and exotic <term>far-fetched</term> delicacies?

Nature has a strong tendency toward equality. Habit, the instrument of nature, is a great leveler; the familiarity it creates dulls the intensity of both our pleasures and our sufferings. Habitual luxuries keep us comfortable but cannot provide much more than that. So, regarding the pleasures our senses are capable of feeling, the difference in enjoyment is by no means proportional to the amount of luxury owned. In fact, as far as excess leads to boredom and pickiness <term>fastidiousness</term>, the difference is actually worse for the wealthy.

I am not arguing that the advantages derived from wealth are nonexistent (under proper management, they are certainly significant), but rather that they are not greater than they ought to be. *Money* makes human labor <term>toil</term> more bearable; it is the substitute for forced labor <term>coercion</term>; it reconciles work with liberty. Moreover, it is the incentive for enterprise in all projects and undertakings, as well as for diligence in the most beneficial arts and professions. Natural theology has always been challenged by this question: why, under the rule of a supreme and benevolent Will, does there appear to be so much *chance* in the world? The question in its full scope lies beyond our understanding; however, just as with the origin of *evil*, there are answers that carry significant weight in specific instances and apply to a wide range of situations.

<margin>v</margin>
I. There must be *chance* even in the midst of design. By this, we mean that events which are not intended necessarily arise from the pursuit of events which are intended. For example, one man traveling to York meets another man traveling to London. Their meeting happens by *chance* and is accidental—or at least would be considered such—even though the journeys that led to the meeting were both undertaken intentionally and with careful planning. The meeting, though accidental, was nonetheless <term>hypothetically necessary</term> <note>A necessity that follows logically from certain prior conditions, rather than being a core requirement of nature.</note> (which is the only kind of necessity that makes sense). If the two journeys began at the exact time, followed the exact path, and moved at the exact speed they did, the meeting could not have been avoided. Therefore, the fact that it happened by *chance* did not make it any less inevitable. Furthermore, the meeting might be highly unfortunate, even if the errands that each person set out to accomplish were perfectly innocent or even praiseworthy. The side effect may be unfavorable without calling into question—

attainment of the intended purpose for which the sequence of events was set in motion. Even though no cause acts without a good purpose, accidental consequences like these may be either good or bad.

II. The *appearance of chance* will always be proportional to the ignorance of the observer. The roll of a die follows the laws of motion just as regularly as the ticking of a watch. However, because we can track the operation of those laws through the visible gears and movements of a watch, but cannot track them while the die is being shaken and thrown—even though the laws are the same and apply equally in both cases—we call the result of the die "chance." Meanwhile, we call the movement of the watch's hands "machinery," "order," or some other name that excludes chance. 

It is the same with events that depend on the will of a free and rational person. A jury's verdict, a judge's sentence, the resolution of an assembly, or the outcome of a contested election will seem more or less like "chance"—and might be more or less likely to be the subject of a bet—depending on how much or how little we know about the reasons that influenced the decision. The difference lies in the information available to the observer, not in the event itself. In all the cases mentioned, the outcome proceeds from intelligence, from a mind, from deliberation, and from design.

Now, when we apply this single cause for the appearance of chance—namely, the ignorance of the observer—to the workings of the Deity, it is easy to foresee how many difficulties and instances of apparent confusion it will produce. We only have to think of God to realize the immense variety of objects, the vast distances of time, and the enormous extent of space and action that His plans may, or rather must, encompass. Is it any wonder then, that among the purposes which...

<summary>This page argues that "chance" is merely a label for our own ignorance of the underlying laws and designs governing an event. Whether in physics or human decision-making, what looks like luck is actually the result of complex, intentional processes that are simply too vast for us to fully comprehend.</summary>

III. In a great variety of cases, including those with numerous sub-categories, it appears for many reasons to be better that events occur by *chance*—or, more accurately, with the appearance of chance—than according to any observable rule. This is often the case even in human arrangements. Each person’s place and precedence in a public meeting may be determined by *lot* <term>the use of objects, such as straws or dice, to decide something by resource to random chance</term>. Work and labor may be *assigned*. Tasks and burdens may be *assigned*.

Military service and stations may be *assigned*. The distribution of provisions may be made by *lot*, as it is in a sailor’s mess; in some cases, the distribution of favors may also be made by *lot*. In all these cases, it seems to be acknowledged that there are advantages in allowing events to happen by chance that are superior to those which would or could arise from strict regulation. In all these cases, though events occur in the way of chance, they do so by appointment.

In other events—specifically those independent of human will—the reasons for this preference of uncertainty over a fixed rule appear to be even stronger. For example, it seems beneficial that the length of a human life should be uncertain. If death followed any fixed rule, it would produce a sense of security in those who were far from it, which would lead to the greatest social disorders; meanwhile, it would produce a horror in those who approached it, similar to what a condemned prisoner feels on the night before his execution.

However, for death to remain uncertain, the young must sometimes die as well as the old. Furthermore, if deaths were never *sudden*, those in good health would be too confident in life. The strong and the active, who *most* need to be warned and kept in check, would live without fear or self-restraint. On the other hand, if sudden deaths were very frequent, the sense of constant jeopardy would interfere too much with the degree of ease and enjoyment intended for us; human life would be too precarious for the business and interests that belong to it. There could not be enough dependence upon either our own lives, or the lives of those with whom we are connected, to carry on the regular duties of human society. Therefore, the manner in which death is made to occur contributes to the purpose of providing a warning without overthrowing the necessary stability of human affairs.

Since *disease* is the forerunner of death, there is the same reason for its attacks to come upon us under the appearance of chance as there is for the uncertainty in the timing of death itself.

The *seasons* are a mixture of regularity and chance. They are regular enough to authorize expectation, while their being irregular to a considerable degree creates a necessity for the cultivators of the soil to exercise personal attention, activity, vigilance, and precaution. It is this necessity which creates farmers; which divides the profit of the soil between the owner and the occupier; and which—by requiring expedients <term>practical strategies or solutions</term>, by increasing employment, and by rewarding expenditure <term>investment of capital or labor</term>—promotes the agricultural arts and agricultural life, which is the best of all modes of life. I believe it is found to be a fact that where the soil is the most fruitful and the seasons are the most constant, the condition of the cultivators of the earth is the most depressed <term>impoverished or socially stagnant</term>. Therefore, uncertainty has its uses, even to those who sometimes complain about it the most.

It may be the result of a beneficial rule that the fortunes or honors of a father pass down to the son; and it seems to be an even more necessary rule that the lowly or laborious condition of a parent is shared by his family. However, with respect to the successor himself, it is like drawing a ticket in a lottery. Therefore, inequalities of fortune—at least the greatest part of them, namely those which attend us from our birth and depend upon our birth—may be left to chance, as they currently are, without any just cause for questioning the sovereignty of a supreme Disposer of events <note>God</note>.

The accessibility of social advantages ought, perhaps, to a considerable degree, to be left to the mercy of chance. It also appears to be true that the demands of social life require not only an original variety of external circumstances, but also a mixture of different abilities, tastes, and temperaments. Of all the views under which human life has ever been considered, the most reasonable in my judgment is the one that regards it as a state of *probation* <term>probation</term> <note>a period of testing or trial to assess a person's character or conduct</note>. If the course of the world were separated from the intricate designs of nature, I do not know if it would be necessary to look for any other explanation for it than the claim—if it can even be called an explanation—that events happen by chance. 

But since the designs of nature decidedly demonstrate intention; and since the course of the world and the designs of nature have the same author; we are, by the force of this connection, led to believe that the way events take place is consistent with the idea of a design on the part of the Deity. It is enough that they are consistent with this theory (and it is undoubtedly true that they may be consistent, even if we cannot personally explain how they are so). 

However, a mind that contemplates the works of nature—and sees in those works so many means directed toward specific ends, beneficial effects achieved through wise methods, and coordinated chains of causes leading to the happiest results; in short, so much wisdom, intention, and benevolence—such a mind, I say, having developed this habit of thought, can hardly look at the condition of our own species without trying to imagine some purpose or design for which our current state is suited and which it is intended to serve. 

Now, we claim that the most probable theory is that life is a state of moral probation, and that many things in it fit this hypothesis while fitting no other. It is not a state of pure happiness, or simply about happiness; it is not a state of intended misery, or simply about misery; it is not a state of retribution <term>retribution</term> <note>the distribution of rewards and punishments based on past actions</note>; it is...

If there were no evils in the world except those that were clearly and understandably punishments, benevolence would simply stand in the way of justice. Within a consistent system of moral government, such evils could not be prevented or eased—that is, they could not be forgiven in whole or in part—except by the authority that inflicted them, or by a higher, appellate authority. This consideration, which is based on our most widely accepted understanding of the nature of criminal justice, may carry weight in the Divine councils <note>God's plans or wisdom</note>. 

Virtue is perhaps the greatest of all goals. Among human beings, "relative virtues" <term>relative virtues</term> <note>virtues that arise from the relationships between people, such as compassion, patience, and charity</note> make up a large portion of our character. Now, relative virtue requires not only the existence of evil—without which it would have no purpose and no material to work with—but also that these evils appear, at least, to be misfortunes; that is, the...

## CHAPTER XXVII.

### CONCLUSION.

IN all cases where the mind feels itself in danger of being overwhelmed by variety, it is certain to rest upon a few strong points, or perhaps even upon a single instance. <margin>✓</margin> Among a multitude of proofs, it only takes one to prove the point. If we observe in any argument that hardly any two minds focus on the same instance, this diversity of choice shows the strength of the argument, because it demonstrates the sheer number and quality of the examples. There is no subject in which the tendency to dwell upon select or single topics is so common, because there is no subject whose scope, in its full extent, is as vast as natural history applied as proof of an intelligent Creator. 

For my part, I take my stand in human anatomy. The mechanical examples I would be inclined to select from the extensive list it supplies are: the pivot on which the head turns <note>referring to the atlas and axis vertebrae</note>; the ligament within the socket of the hip joint; the pulley—or trochlear muscle—of the eye; the epiglottis <term>epiglottis</term> <note>the flap of cartilage that covers the windpipe during swallowing</note>; the bandages <note>the annular ligaments</note> which tie down the tendons of the wrist and instep; the slit or perforated muscles in the hands and feet; the attachment of the intestines to the mesentery <term>mesentery</term> <note>a fold of membrane that attaches the organs to the body wall and holds them in place</note>; the path of the chyle <term>chyle</term> <note>a milky fluid containing fat droplets, drained from the small intestine into the lymphatic system during digestion</note> into the blood; and the distinction between the sexes as extended throughout the whole of the animal creation. But, for the majority of those who read arguments to prove the existence of God—whether in this book or any other—it might be said that they end exactly where they began. They were never ignorant of this great truth and never doubted it; therefore, it may not seem clear what is gained by research that teaches no new opinion and addresses a subject where no proofs were requested. 

Now, I answer that through *investigation*, the following points are always gained in favor of doctrines—even the most widely acknowledged ones (assuming they are true)—namely: stability and impression. Circumstances will arise that test the strength of our most habitual beliefs. On those occasions, it is incredibly useful to feel our foundation—to find support in reasoned argument for what we had previously accepted on authority alone. In the present case, the arguments on which the conclusion rests are exactly the kind that a truth of universal importance should rely on. I believe the situation to be this: perhaps almost every living person has a particular train of <insert>✓</insert> thought into which their mind falls when at rest from the impressions and ideas that occasionally stimulate it. ### CONCLUSION.

Once we arrive on our globe, we can then follow that connection through all the organized—and especially the living—beings it supports. We can observe signs of a shared relationship, both among themselves and with the elements that make up their environment. Therefore, one mind has planned, or at least has prescribed a general plan for all these creations. One Being has been involved in them all.

We live under this awe-inspiring Being. Our happiness and our very existence are in His hands. Everything we hope for must come from Him. Nor should we feel that our situation is insecure. In every part of nature, and in every portion of nature that we can observe, we find attention paid even to the smallest details. The hinges in the wings of an *earwig* and the joints of its *antennae* are as expertly crafted as if the Creator had nothing else to complete. We see no signs that His care diminishes because there are so many objects, or that His attention is distracted by their variety. Therefore, we have no reason to fear being forgotten, overlooked, or neglected.

The existence and character of the Deity is, from every perspective, the most compelling of all human subjects of study. # CONCLUSION.

[In]deed <note>Original: "deed"; likely "Indeed," continuing from the previous page.</note>, those who believe that perception consists of physical organization are supposed to find more difficulty than others in accepting a transition at death to a new state of conscious existence, because the old organization is clearly dissolved. However, I do not see why even these people should fear any impossibility. Even under their hypothesis, this change is not far removed from the analogy of other operations that we know for certain the Deity is carrying out. 

In the ordinary reproduction of plants and animals from one another, a particle—which is often smaller than any assignable or even conceivable dimension; a breath, a vapor, or an infinitesimal—determines the organization of a future body. It does nothing less than decide whether what is about to be produced shall be a plant, a merely conscious animal, or a rational being; whether it will be an oak, a frog, or a philosopher. This particle creates all these differences and gives the future body its qualities, nature, and species. 

Furthermore, this particle, from which a whole future nature springs and is determined, itself comes from and owes its structure to a previous body. Nevertheless—as seen most clearly in plants—the beginning organization, though formed within, through, and by a preceding organization, is not corrupted by that parent's decay or destroyed by its dissolution. On the contrary, it is sometimes released and developed by those very causes. It survives and comes into action when the purpose for which it was prepared requires its use. 

Now, a system <term>economy</term> <note>Modernized from "œconomy," referring here to the functional arrangement or management of nature.</note> which nature has adopted to transfer an organization from one individual to another may have something analogous to it when the purpose is to transmit an organization from one state of being to another state. Those who base thought in physical organization may see something in this analogy applicable to their difficulties; for whatever can transmit a similarity of organization will satisfy their pur-
